TLDR;

Premise: 10/10
Graphics: 8/10
Game Play Loop: 10/10
Stability: Fluctuates, 0/10 - 8/10, no between
Satisfaction: Could be 8/10 if not for poor QoL
Story: Non-Existent/10
QoL: 0/10 (Worst of any game I've played, not an exaggeration)


Oh you're still here? Let's talk about Hydroneer, starting at the best pieces and rounding out the most painful. Please take all of this with a grain of salt as I only have ~50 hours in the game, begrudgingly so as I really wanted to enjoy this.

The premise of this game is interesting and a cool take on the factory automation genre. Managing water as your "energy" is cool and different. Voxel style art is well placed here. Existing in the same space as Factorio or Satisfactory while being distinctly different is good, we like that. Same sort of gameplay loop, nothing revolutionary here, get things, make things, sell those things to purchase better things that get things, repeat. Simple but hey, if you were interested in this game at all, you're probably the sorta person who likes that kind of game.

Unfortunately, this is the end of the gravy train, and the beginning of the driving your car into oncoming traffic....train?

Stability is mostly fine except for some seemingly edge cases that start to happen every 5 minutes. The autosave timer by default is 5 minutes, and that's where problems typically occur. Mined items when traveling through any amount of automation can occasionally get stuck, which is not a big deal if it were just one. The problem is that it is never just one, and it is most frequently triggered when an autosave causes enough of a stutter that rivals changing all blocks in your friends Minecraft world into TNT and lighting it just to see how long their machine will become a brick for. Ever see a game with an option to delete all raw resources or dirt on the pause menu? This is why. Imagine you're peacefully mining things, building your new house, or running some quests and you get one stutter, and then 3, and then so many you start to wonder if your PC has a speech impediment. 

Story is nonexistent, although if you want to lump in the quests with it then good news, they're also awful. Basically people in the world ask you to make something, and then you make it, and then they give you a cool alternate currency that is painfully slow to acquire but you need it to get items that introduce a semblance of QoL. Except that QoL item will cause stability issues too.

To this game's credit, this loop should be very satisfying, but there's two other issues it presents. Number 1, this questing/alternate currency has very little impact on mining and and has more focus on terrain preparation in the form of vehicles. The best vehicle for this you think would be the Mole, however; the Mole makes you want to taste test a lead pipe hitting you harder than Gwen Stacy hit the ground (that's right, we getting elite nerd jokes in here). The Mole has 3 dig modes: down, straight, and up. Your second mistake (after purchasing this game) is believing that those are the 3 modes. The 3 dig modes are actually more down, less down, and don't. For sake of brevity because my 'tism is slowly turning into rage, basically down works, straight doesn't, up gets the vehicle stuck on the terrain it's supposed to be digging. Number the other one, No one probably told you there is farming/fishing in this game. That's all you really need to know about farming/fishing in this game.

Lets talk about QoL, which obviously I'm an expert at given that I've spent 45 minutes writing this homage to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ yourself at the DMV. The thing you'll see in most of these reviews is the inventory system, or rather the total lack of one. No tool belt, no back pack, not even a static currency slot (super helpful in a game with multiple currencies). You can't even buy in bulk because items have collision so stacking is a pain unless you drive a vehicle into a purchase zone (if it's accessible) which causes items to lose collision, except you still have to carry each item one by one into the vehicle, which by the way also has collision so large items don't drop in easily. Getting out of the early game isn't a grind, buying items to start the early game is a grind. Also the whole game is a grind. All of it's a grind. Except not the grind you want in a game like this. Once you finally have your factory up and running, it actually moves pretty quick, it's the 17 years of walking you have to do to set up your factory that piques my interest in swallowing a waffle iron. Terrain prep takes forever unless you have a vehicle, in which case it takes longer because you are lulled into the belief that bigger machines makes it go faster, when actually bigger machines means sticking all your fingers into Chinese Finger Traps and then trying to do microsurgery with a Play-doh (TM) knife. Honestly, I think having a colonoscopy would be less intrusive than the complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ this game gives you.

On the bright side, the price is actually not bad compared to any medical procedure in the US.


(Edit) ~For the Dev's
Thought about this a bit more, because this game could easily be a favorite with some fixes and honestly something I'd pay $30 - $40 for if we saw these improvements.

MAJOR ITEMS
-Inventory system/hot bar. I don't care if I have to buy it in game, if it's a static addition from the start, whatever. Building is too much of a hassle without it, and there is still plenty of instances where we sill still need to manually move things around one by one, redesign our layouts, etc. It doesn't remove the individual item movement need, just makes it infinitely more accessible.

-Purchase process. Give us a hotkey that auto-moves items to purchase zone and moves purchased items to the nearest vehicle or inventory. Allow purchasing in stacks. Remove item collision within a store zone. I hate myself enough as it is, I don't need this experience to add to that sentiment.

-Vehicle navigation/Terrain Manipulation. The people playing this game likely have OCD or the ability to name every train ever made, and random blobs of terrain is an amazingly efficient way to throw us into an uncontrollable rage that rivals the fury of 1000 suns. The Mole should lock on to specific block layers or at least give us options in the dig settings. Up, down, straight, but also clean dig vs. wild dig. Same for mining/digging tools. Give me modes or make sure the tool/vehicle does exactly what it says it should do. Give me block outlines for what is affected how.

MINOR THINGS

-Remove collision on items moving through/on automation pieces. Prevents Items getting stuck, stops lag from to many objects from occurring.
-More story/questing that is meaningful. Give us upgrades, new items, skill trees, lore, etc. The world is your oyster for us to explore, but this sea is three inches deep.
-Overhaul farming/fishing. There doesn't seem to be any purpose for this being in the game currently. Make it meaningful, otherwise why'd you put it in here in the first place.
-DLC. The one you have I honestly haven't touched. I have no reason to. Despite being available as soon as you have the money, I have no reason to go to it. Give some story progression to unlock, give me some goal to accomplish, make it meaningful, etc. I want to play your game but you haven't given us a reason to play, let alone spend more money on something I have no reason to play.
-Tool tips. I want to know exactly how everything can/should work. Tutorial videos for items, tips and tricks for anything relevant, not just a select few.
-New items/materials. Handheld drills/automation tools. Painting items for blocks/tools/equipment. We love organization and efficiency, and being able to color code everything is incredible in this endeavor.

The reason why the game feels poorly polished is probably because Unreal Engine was a bad choice for a game with so many physics updates. Even on fairly strong mid-range PCs, the game stutters heavily when unloading resources from buckets. On top of that, the autosave system is not asynchronous, so because the game autosaves so often, it constantly causes hard lag spikes.

The game is also completely unbalanced. In the very first hole, I already had enough money to buy basically everything, so there was no real reason to keep earning more. Another problem is the two currencies you need, which are completely RNG-based. You can only get them randomly from missions in one specific area, and each mission only gives around 20 to at most 100 T currency. Meanwhile, everything that requires this currency costs several hundred T coins.

The worst part is that you cannot actually farm this currency consistently because it completely depends on random mission rewards. That means you are forced to wait for the right missions to appear, while also earning way too little. Because of that, it would literally take months, if not over a year, to upgrade to Tier 3, especially since Tier 3 pipes alone already cost around 300 to 600 T coins.

review:
I've been eyeing this game for a few years now, waiting for it to become more fleshed out and to leave early access. Today, I thought it would be a good moment to try it out. And, to be honest, I feel like I've just wasted my time playing this. 

The start is very rough, the early automation mechanics are poorly explained and very finicky. Digging by hand is extremely inefficient yet you'll be forced to do it in order to even make space for the machines that do it for you. The machines themselves seem to need very specific black magic to work, to the point that your drill can become "buried" by the same medium it's supposed to drill through, just because you missed some small lump of dirt in the bottom left. Yeah, experience in-game may help me improve these situations, but it's not experience I would gain to "improve" the overall gameplay but to make it "tolerable".

The bottom line is: There's way better automation games out there.

It's impressive how rough around the edges this game still is after all these years. The lack of an inventory system, the completely pointless day/night cycle, the soulless towns, and the wonky physics are supposedly "intentional" by the developers to differentiate their game from others, which is like putting garbage in your soup to differentiate it from your grandma's. However, its biggest problem is that the early gameplay loop is quite unsatisfying, and feeling some kind of satisfaction for your hard work would be the only real reason to endure such a tedious game until it "gets good".

요약 : 인벤토리의 소중함을 알려주는 게임
참고로 돈도 직접 손으로 들고다녀야함
다른 공장게임은 메뉴에서 건물이나 시설물 그냥 딸깍해서 공장건설하면
이 게임은 파이프 하나하나 죄다 상점에서 사 온 다음 그걸 또 하나하나 집어서 공장 만들어야함
나야 뭐 그럭저럭 재밌게하고 추천한다 표시는 하는데 실제 의견은 비추천임
공장 다 만드는 성취감 자체는 있는데.. 공장짓다가 부품하나 없어서 상점가서 다시 사와야하면 진짜 짜증남
그래서 초반공장 돌려서 돈 넉넉하게되면 무슨 부품이든간에 정말 넉넉하게(없으면 다시 가서 사와야되니까)
사서 공장부지 근처에 흩뿌려둠
그리고 ESC눌러보면 우하단에 왠 날자원 다 지우기 같은게 있는데 돈도 없고 자동화도 안 되서 광석만 뱉어내고
그 광석 제련시설이 안 갖춰져있는데 그 날자원상태로 잠수타고오면 답이없는 경우가 있음
난 한 2시간 잠수타고 자석으로 그 자원들 자석으로 옮겨서 제련하려다가 한 3번쯤 팅겼음 PC사양 첨부함
그리고 자동화 제대로 굴러가기 시작하면 또 답없는 자원이 있는데 바로 보석류
이 게임은 철, 금, 클로니움, 중심석(코어스톤)의 4가지 광자원과(+DLC한정 하드스톤)
에메랄드, 사파이어, 루비, 오닉스(+DLC 한정 다이아몬드)의 4가지 보석들이 있는데
광자원들은 용광로에 넣어서 물상태로 있으니 상관없는데 보석들은 날자원마냥 한개한개 쌓여가는데
그걸 압축기가 자동으로 압축해주는게 아니라 일일이 작동시켜야돼서 오랜만에 가보면 보석들이 넘쳐있다
결국 나중엔 보석들을 그냥 논리 파괴자(=파쇄기)에 넣고 갈아버린다. 그거 놔두면 게임 버벅이니까 그냥 갈아버리자
자꾸 괄호넣는거 보면 알겠지만 번역이 그리 중요한 게임은 아니긴한데 한글 번역도 그냥 번역기 넣고 돌렸다.
중간중간 일본어도 나오는데 주민 잡담이라 그리 중요한건 아닌데 그것도 짜치긴한다.

그래도 해 볼 사람들을 위한 추천 테크트리
튜토리얼 해 보면 초반 돈 버는법만 가르쳐주고 이 게임의 중요한 공장돌리는거도 안 알려주고 덩그러니 내던진다.
메인겜 시작하고 아무것도 알려주지 않아서 강가에 갔더니 양동이랑 붓만 있고 왜 삽이 없지?
싶었는데 삽은 또 시작지점 간판에 있더라 그리고 그것도 튜토리얼이라고 자원 많이 튀어나오게 해 둔 거였고 진짜 그렇게 양동이에 물넣고 흙넣고 붓질해서 광얻고 보석상인에게 내다팔고 하려면 지겹다.
그나마 정석으로 빠른 방법은 낚시인데 낚싯대 52코인인가 까지만 광을 수작업으로 팔아서 돈 얻고
낚시를 하는데 희귀물고기를 낚아서 번스크로프트 마을 강가에 낚시대 바꿔주는 곳에 바꿔먹고 갈아타면서
물고기 팔아먹으면 되는데 물고기를 또 일일이 손으로 집어서 물고기바구니에 담아서 상인에게 갖다 팔아먹는거보다
시작지점 남동쪽 브리지푸어마을에 식료품상점주인이 물고기 사주는데 그 상인 매대에서 강가를 보고 낚시대를
던진다음 매대에 물고기가 낙하하게 시점을 조정하고 낚시줄이 흔들거리는 것만 보고 클릭하면 낚인다.
양형들은 소리듣고 낚으라는데 도저히 소리가 안 들려서 낚시줄 흔들리는거 보고 낚는다. 그 외에 낚시찌가
물에 닿고나서 8초, 흔들흔들4번이라니까 그냥 타이밍만 기억해도 됨.
어쨌든 물고기 팔아먹고 희귀물고기 갖다줘서 좋은 낚시대 얻어서 갈아타고 하는데 6랭크 낚시대가 돈벌기 가장
좋다고함. 8랭크는 오히려 돈을 못 번다고(부츠를 많이 낚으니까)
대신 도전과제 있으니 낚시대 바꿔먹기까지만 해도 됨
정석은 이렇게 낚시로 자동화할정도의 돈을 벌고 공장 자동화로 시작하는거고 그냥 나는 보물지도 공략보고
초반 돈 걱정없이 하겠다 하면 Hydroneer Relic 치면 유튜브에 자세한 위치 공략나옴.
나는 중반이후 도전과제용으로 공략봤는데 대략적인 위치만으로는 찾기 힘들고 핀포인트로 찾거나
아예 근처를 굴착기계로 다 갈아버려야하는데 그래도 땅사고 곡괭이 사고 하는 비용으로 2500코인쯤 필요한듯
그렇게 얻은 유물을 시작지점 옆의 동굴에 4개 전시하면 보물이 나오는데 팔면 6만코인 조금 넘게 주니
돈 걱정없이 바로 시작하고 싶으면 괜찮겠다 싶었음. 물론 이런게임 특성상 공장자동화가 시작되면
돈 걱정이 바로 끝나니 초반이 편한거 외엔 없음.
대신 이 정도로 돈걱정이 없으면 이 게임을 하는 누구나 추천하는 공장부지가 있는데 바로 아이스헬름
다른 모든 땅은 지하로 파고들어가야돼서 계단식으로 땅파고 만드는데

developer_response:
On very rare occasions Hydroneers save files can be corrupted. This generally happens when someone closes the game while it is saving. We’ve added in measures to prevent this from corrupting but there are some outlying cases. 
We have also noticed that some anti-virus programs prevent Hydroneer from saving. Please list Hydroneer as an accepted program or consider disabling your anti-virus programs. (Windows Defender is fine, but other AV programs can have this issue)
We also have added in ‘backup’ saves to prevent total data loss. Try finding this backup, by opening up the game, pressing ‘continue’ on the main menu, then ticking the ‘Show Backup’ box. This will show a backup save file which hopefully won’t be corrupted.

If you’d like any more help with this or another issue, you can reach out to us by email: support@foulballhangover.com. If this has resolved your issue please consider updating your review. We’re a small team and reviews really help us out, thanks!

review: this game it really good

This game is very good at the idea it's going for. On top of that, it is incredibly addicting plumbing everything together and making the automated setup of your dreams. 

But this game does NOT value your time. 

It is going to run you back and forth across the map, sloooooowly dig out each and every piece of dirt to get money to start, make you carry items one at a time, either slowly dig out mines or wrestle with the driving controls on an expensive machine, and even the most automatic setup requires you to come by and pull levers and push buttons. 

If your time is not at a premium and you want a soothing, relaxing, methodical manual mining experience, this game is for you. If you want something fast, snappy, and working with you to build a mega factory... I mean, you can do that last part, but you'd probably want to go for Satisfactory or Factorio or something similar instead.

On very rare occasions Hydroneers save files can be corrupted. This generally happens when someone closes the game while it is saving. We’ve added in measures to prevent this from corrupting but there are some outlying cases. 
We have also noticed that some anti-virus programs prevent Hydroneer from saving. Please list Hydroneer as an accepted program or consider disabling your anti-virus programs. (Windows Defender is fine, but other AV programs can have this issue)
We also have added in ‘backup’ saves to prevent total data loss. Try finding this backup, by opening up the game, pressing ‘continue’ on the main menu, then ticking the ‘Show Backup’ box. This will show a backup save file which hopefully won’t be corrupted.

After 30.4 hours in Hydroneer, I think the best way to describe this game is: slow at first, but incredibly satisfying once it clicks.

The early game can honestly feel rough. Hand mining, carrying resources around, and earning enough for your first automation setup takes patience. I can easily see why some players stop before reaching that point. But the moment you build your first working drill and harvester system, the game changes completely. Suddenly it stops feeling like work and starts feeling relaxing.

What surprised me most is how satisfying simple efficiency becomes. Not giant mega factories, not chaos everywhere — just building a small optimized setup and watching it run smoothly without problems. Seeing your machines work perfectly together gives a weirdly calming feeling that’s hard to explain unless you’ve played it yourself.

I actually lost my original world because of corrupted save data after already reaching tier 2 progression, which normally would make me quit a game completely. Instead, I restarted from scratch. That alone says a lot about how enjoyable the core gameplay loop is.

This is definitely not a game for impatient players. But for people who enjoy relaxing sandbox progression, gradual automation, and the satisfaction of improving their own systems step by step, this game becomes extremely rewarding.

It’s not fast-paced.
It’s not flashy.
But somehow it keeps pulling you back for “just one more improvement” to the factory.

So I bought this game cause on paper it looked really cool, the idea behind is very very interesting, but the execution is... bad.
I played the tutorial, one of the worst tutorials I've ever played, anyway, that's okay-ish. 
The items don't show you their name when you hover the mouse, you see name of stuff only when you pick it up, honestly pretty dumb already.
The tutorial appears in the down side, there's no highlight on the map, no arrows, no pointer, no glowy thingy, so most you really have to figure out the most basic things yourself. 
My real problem is the control system.
So I generally hate grab stuff with E and use with mouse click, I'm more of a left / right click person, but that's fine cause I can technically rebind stuff, I thought I can still give it the benefit of the doubt; what genuinely angered me the most was the "use system".
So apparently I have only one hand, cause I can hold only one item per time (already a huge minus for me), so I either hold the shovel or the lamp. Ok, I can handle one hand games, in theory.
So I go grab the pan, fill it with water and drop it on the floor. It's already too many interactions to fill a pan but whatever. Later I need grab the bucket, position it close to the dig site, drop it (again I have only one hand), the terrain is uneven and the darn bucket doesn't stay upright, that triggered me a lot. Anyway after 10 tries I manage to get the bucket to stay upright, I grab the shovel, shovel dirt into the bucket (the tutorial is pretty luck laster but whatever), and finally after I fill it, I need to drop the shovel, take the bucket, go to the pan, and empty the bucket in the pan. This mechanic is the dumbest, cause the drop "shadow" is basically just a shadow, almost invisible to my poor eyes, so guess where the dirt goes 9/10 times? On the floor. Whatever, I drop the bucket, get the dirt and push it in the pan  manually. 
There's no pour system, it's immediate, so holding E doesn't change anything, that's extremely dumb, cause I would've loved a very basic aiming system, since the drop shadow is completely useless.
I go sell stuff, theres no coin purse, right cause I have one hand and no pockets apparently, (despite I see like 10 pockets on my dress), so the money stay in the bucket, took me 5 mins to figure that out; another very dumb mechanic. 
I Go buy stuff, some items needs a hologram to be placed, some don't. Why? Just why? If you can do a dam hologram for the furnace why the drop is so annoying and imprecise? 
The furnace itself is another level of rage, the placement (even with the hologram) suck, no explanation on how it should be placed, it can be half underground or completely above ground, no explanation on what's the correct one, the crucible instead doesn't have a hologram and as I say before for the bucket, 9/10 times I drop it wrong on the furnace.
Melt stuff is also very poorly explained. And craft.... Craft really was the straw that broke the camel back.
I push the anvil (without a hologram) and without a way to lock it in place, I try to click to operate it, and I can just pick it up. No advice, no hold click, just pick up. Seriously? 
I choose the recipe that obviously is just a drawing on the anvil, push things on the slot, very not self explanatory honestly, hammer the nothingness (it also took a couple of tries) and I made a ring. Give birth was easier not gonna lie.
After I finish the tutorial I tried to create a world to play, I saw the city, how much stuff was far away, how much things looked messier and I just gave up and request a refund. Absolutely not. 
I genuinely expected this game to be relaxing to play, I was so nervous by the end that I had to take a break from the pc entirely.

Great game for those who enjoy the hobo-cart genre. 

You don't have an inventory and can only carry one item at a time. So you'll always be walking around the village with a bucket, or a pallet if you're fancy, to peddle your wares for coin. Which you can use to buy a bigger hobo cart or mining equipment to slowly automate your factory.
Before the optimization update, the fps would drop to single digits with just 2-3 T3 miners. Now the game runs great! Props to the devs for figuring it out after 2 years.
As for the dlc, unless you really hate yoursef, I recommend waiting a year or two after finishing the main game. To give yourself enough time to forget all the tedious parts of the game.

I'm sure there's a unique and fun experience to be had in this game for the right crowd, but after 6.6 hours I was barely able to grind enough money to afford some very basic automation that exposed some incredibly janky design limitations. 
I just didn't have the motivation to push past my confusion of how you are 'supposed' to automate and build things.. Nor did I really want to keep doing the very slow and tedious process of trying to manipulate items in the game's physics to smelt and make things to sell until I could afford MORE automation parts to hopefully understand better and get around the janky limitations.

I'm sure if I watched some videos it would make sense, but I always go into things blind.

I picked this game up on sale for $4.49 and got about 16 hours of playtime before I came to the conclusion that I didn't want to continue. For some that may be a fine transaction, but I'm still going to call this a "no" due to a lack of meaningful depth. The best part of this game is when you have a problem and you work on solving it. Early on you're finding tricks or ways to speed up the manual process of panning for resources, then you're solving how to automate the basics of machinery to bring the resources to you. The problem is that once you solve that initial automation problem, you've essentially solved the rest of the game.

Yes there are tasks where the NPC's ask you to get them specific things with increasing scale, but that just nets you tokens that you spend on higher tier equipment that ends up serving the same purpose. It's not a particularly fun problem to have to produce a 1000 weight bar to complete a task, it's just more of what I had already solved.

This game sits in a weird position of being a relaxing automation game with no active threat or timer, but also no strong driving force that incentivizes the player to go deeper into the tiers of tech. This driving force is often a promise of new and complex systems that the player would have to grapple with in order to increase production. Here, as I previously said, once you've solved that initial tier 1 drill -> tier 1 harvester -> separate resources, you've essentially solved the most complex issue you'll face and everything else is just that again with a different coat of paint.

„Hydroneer ist irgendwie wie ein Baumarktbesuch auf Energy-Drinks – chaotisch, laut und trotzdem macht’s Spaß. 😄
Die Grafik sieht überraschend gut aus, die Engine läuft sauber und der komplette Spielaufbau mit Graben, Craften und Automatisieren motiviert echt lange. Besonders wenn die ersten Maschinen rattern, fühlt man sich wie ein Goldgräber mit Ingenieursabschluss.

ABER… Multiplayer mit Kumpels ist aktuell noch eher ‘Baustelle mit Warnschild’.
Split-Screen only ist schon speziell, und dass einer Maus/Tastatur nehmen MUSS während der andere Controller spielen MUSS, sorgt regelmäßig für Diskussionen wie:
‚Wer darf heute die gute Steuerung haben?‘ 😂

Dazu kommen Tasten mit Doppelbelegung — einmal falsch gedrückt und statt zu craften verschiebt man plötzlich das halbe Gebäude. Innenarchitekt wider Willen.

Trotzdem: Das Grundgerüst ist richtig stark. Wenn die Steuerung, das Multiplayer-System und die Belegungen verbessert werden, kann das Spiel ein absoluter Dauerbrenner werden. Mit Freunden definitiv lustig — auch wenn man sich zwischendurch mehr mit den Tasten als mit dem Goldabbau prügelt. 👍“

review:
Hydroneer is genuinely one of the greatest sandbox games ever created because it understands something most modern games completely forget: making the player feel progression matters more than throwing explosions and cutscenes at the screen every five minutes. Hydroneer takes the simple idea of mining for resources and transforms it into one of the most satisfying gameplay experiences ever made.

Everything about the game feels rewarding. From the very first scoop of dirt to massive fully automated mining operations, every step forward feels earned. The progression is nearly perfect. You begin with almost nothing, just a shovel, a pan, and determination, but over time your tiny mining setup evolves into a gigantic industrial empire powered by conveyors, drills, sorters, pressure systems, and machines clanking together like a beautifully chaotic orchestra.

The feeling of accomplishment in Hydroneer is unmatched. Few games make success feel this personal. When your automation finally works after hours of building and experimenting, it feels incredible because you made it happen. The game never hands you victories for free. Every machine, every upgrade, and every improvement becomes part of your own creation.

The creativity the game allows is honestly amazing. Hydroneer gives players freedom without overwhelming them. You can build clean, efficient mining systems that look like professional engineering projects, or create absolute conveyor-belt insanity that somehow still functions perfectly. No two mining operations ever feel the same, and that freedom makes the game endlessly replayable.

The atmosphere is another huge reason why the game stands out. Hydroneer has this cozy industrial charm that no other game really captures. The stylized visuals give the world personality, and everything feels warm and inviting despite being centered around heavy machinery and mining. It’s relaxing in a way that’s hard to explain until you actually play it.

Then there’s the sound design, which is honestly phenomenal. The sounds of water rushing through pipes, drills hammering into the ground, conveyors rattling, and resources clinking through machinery create this strangely satisfying industrial soundtrack. Once your mining setup grows large enough, your base starts sounding alive, like a giant machine powered entirely by ambition and engineering.

One of the best things about Hydroneer is how addictive the gameplay loop becomes. Digging for resources never loses its appeal because there’s always another goal waiting. Bigger drills. Faster systems. Better automation. More efficient layouts. The game constantly motivates you to improve your setup without ever forcing you into a strict path.

The sense of scale is incredible too. Looking back at your tiny starter setup after building a massive automated mining operation feels unbelievably satisfying. Few games capture growth this well. You can literally see your progress spread across the landscape as your machinery expands into a sprawling industrial masterpiece.

Hydroneer also deserves massive credit for respecting the player’s intelligence. It encourages experimentation instead of overexplaining everything. Discovering better methods, smarter layouts, and creative solutions feels natural and rewarding. The game trusts players to learn through experience, which makes every breakthrough feel meaningful.

What makes Hydroneer truly special, though, is how memorable it becomes. It’s not just a game you play for a few hours and forget. It’s the kind of game where you constantly think about new ideas for your mining setup even when you aren’t playing. You start mentally redesigning conveyor systems while trying to sleep. You suddenly care deeply about water pressure. You become emotionally attached to giant automated machines made entirely out of metal, dirt, and determination.

Very few games manage to feel this immersive without relying on giant stories or cinematic moments. Hydroneer creates memorable experiences entirely through gameplay, creativity, and progression, and that’s what makes it such a masterpiece.

It’s relaxing, addictive, creative, rewarding, charming, and endlessly satisfying all at once. Every hour spent in the game feels productive in the best possible way. Watching your mining empire slowly grow from a tiny dirt pit into a massive automated operation is one of the most satisfying experiences gaming has to offer.

review:
This is a deeply interesting take on a factory game. I got it on sale for $5, at that price I couldn't recommend it enough. At full price I would still recommend it, but with some reservations based on your personal taste. At the end of this little review I'll throw in some tips for new players, it'll help smooth out those first few hours.

What the game does well: 
It's incredibly tactile. You don't have an inventory. Does that sound tedious? Well, it can be, but it's fun figuring out how to work around that limitation. You start out literally shoveling dirt into a bucket, then brushing it to reveal ores and gems, walking the pans of raw ores and gems up the road to a shop, and then selling them. Sell enough to get an extra bucket and pan at the shop so you can shovel and scrub dirt more efficiently. Shovel, dump, scrub, shovel, dump, scrub. Eventually you can afford a furnace, then you can melt the ore into bars and sell for more. Then an anvil to make them into crafted good for even more. Eventually you can full automate your setup, and that slow beginning to full automation is rewarding as hell. 

What the game does poorly: 
- Terrible onboarding. It's a complex game and it doesn't explain jack sh*t about how it works. 
- Awkward interactions. Learning to work around those interactions is interesting, but it's also a lot when you're new. 
- Bad economy and endgame: Early to mid game gives a nice sense of progression, but it quickly becomes a sandbox. Most of the content in the game is accomplished through shopping, shortly after you automate you'll have more coin than you can reasonably use. Then some of the content is gated behind coins obtained by quests. This is a bit more interesting, but it's also tedious to run around gathering quests, and you'll soon have enough coin through that to buy the guild coin goods too. After you get the big ticket items through guild coin quests, you'll probably only be in the  middle of tier 2 (out of 3) and wonder why you should bother going to tier 3. I  don't have that answer for you, I'm a progression person and I ran out of steam at this point

I still got 20 hours out of this game, and I'm going to buy the DLC and play it, I feel like the enjoyment I got would've been worth full price. I can sit here and whine about what I want the game to be because I see a lot of potential in it, but I truly did enjoy it for what it was. 

Tips for new players: 
- Go into options and change the cursor color. The default is black, which looks like a little shadow on the ground. It's impossible to see except under perfect bright conditions, save yourself a headache and change it to white.
- Press and hold "E" to do precise dropping. Then you can use scroll wheel to bring it closer or place it further away 
- The cart is magic. When you put an item on it, it disables the collision box, so you can put essentially infinite items on a cart. A bit of a pain to unload sometimes, but you can go to the store, put everything you want in the cart, put the cart on the scale, pay, and be on your way, easy. 
- Pans are magic. They have the same property as the cart for a limited number of items and they're a great way to carry small items around efficiently
- One of the first automation tools you can unlock is the hand sorter. The hand sorter is *very* reliable, but it will give you headaches figuring it out. You'll think it's just randomly spraying the sorted material. IT'S NOT. Get 3 of the concrete blocks from the shop, they're $5. Place them in a line with the sorter on top of one of the end blocks and the output facing the other 2 blocks. Take your catch pan and put it dead center on between the other 2 blocks, right on the seam. It will catch the output every time. 
- You can rotate items (PIPES) around different axes with "t" and "y"
- The truck outside the shop is yours, you don't need to buy it. That "2" in the funny font? It's a "Q". Press Q to drive. I didn't figure this out until after I had bought a level 2 truck. I'm a moron, don't be like me. 
- There's a map on the first dig site, you'll see "Bridgepour", that's where you can shop for most advanced items and it's the first place you want to check out when you're feeling confident in your first dig site
- Dirt comes in tiers, the lower you are in a tier the better reward you'll got, so dig deep. The ores you get will be heavier. The first plot only goes down to tier 1 before hitting bedrock, every other plot you can buy hits tier 3, often with different gimmicks
- Everything is by weight. You can smelt an infinite amount of ore into a single bar (it'll increase in size, up to a point), and it gets more valuable as you add more to it. Same thing with gems later on. You can cut bars and gems in half, and there's a scale in the shop. Don't feel the need to smelt a lot of tiny bars to make more items, just craft them into ultra heavy items and save yourself a trip, You can also re-melt bars to combine them.

review: Empecé a jugarlo a las 5pm porque se veía entretenido, son las casi las 12am y creí que tenía 1-2 horas jugándolo

At the moment, it just isn't worth it. It feels like an early access game but isn't advertised as such. These are my biggest problems:

1. The early game is unbelievably bad. The cycle of [i] dig dirt -> fill bucket -> fill pan with dirt bucket -> fill pan with water -> brush -> fill cauldron -> put cauldron on fire -> wait until melted -> fill mold -> put bar on fire -> wait until hot -> put on anvil -> hammer into item -> carry to jewler -> make 20c [/i] is just mind numbing. Now this wouldn't be so bad if you could move more than ONE ITEM AT A TIME. 

2. The lack of inventory, while unique, is just NOT fun. It would be fine to carry all the pipes and machines one at a time but then you have to drop the shovel to carry the bucket and drop the bucket for the pan and over and over... it gets tedious. Apparently you don't even have pockets for the coins you get. That's right, you need to [b] carry the coins in your one free hand. [/b] Luckily using the buckets, cauldrons, and carts does lock everything in place, and they usually don't have collision, so its not [i] as bad [/i] as it could be. It still doesn't make it any less tedious to fill the pans one item at a time, including ores. This does get largely mitigated later in the game but it leads me to my final complaint.

3. The automation just... kind ends? From what I've gathered, the farthest you can get is automating bar smelting, and there are logistics systems, but you still have to craft everything and sell it by hand. If this isn't the case, the game does not do a good job of showing it. Also the machines have durability need to be repaired, which is also very tedious. You can mitigate it by filtering the water but it doesn't completely negate it. If there is a way to completely negate it the game, again, doesn't explain it well. There are other things to do like farm and fish, but I really want to make a factory in this factory game. I did not at all engage with the quest system or stock market as they felt tedious and not really worth the rewards. 

There are a few other things that annoy me, like how dark the game is by default, or how you have to aim the shadows of the thing you're holding to drop it, but they're pretty minor compared to everything else. Optimization is also not the greatest. Had many stuttering episodes, even with my decent rig.

TLDR; the game is very meh. As far as automation goes, its lackluster, but there's charm. It could be interesting but the execution feels lackluster. Quality of life goes a long way in these types of games, which this game lacks. Not sure who to recommend this to but if you do want to try it, get it on heavy discount. If you want a similar physics based automation game, try something like Mine Mogul, or just get Satisfactory.

developer_response:
On very rare occasions Hydroneers save files can be corrupted. This generally happens when someone closes the game while it is saving. We’ve added in measures to prevent this from corrupting but there are some outlying cases. 
We have also noticed that some anti-virus programs prevent Hydroneer from saving. Please list Hydroneer as an accepted program or consider disabling your anti-virus programs. (Windows Defender is fine, but other AV programs can have this issue)
We also have added in ‘backup’ saves to prevent total data loss. Try finding this backup, by opening up the game, pressing ‘continue’ on the main menu, then ticking the ‘Show Backup’ box. This will show a backup save file which hopefully won’t be corrupted.

If you’d like any more help with this or another issue, you can reach out to us by email: support@foulballhangover.com. If this has resolved your issue please consider updating your review. We’re a small team and reviews really help us out, thanks!

review:
I would really like to give this a thumbs up. There's a lot to like, but the bad outweighs the good. The game lacks functional, precise systems for interacting with it. Everything is more difficult than it needs to be, and the frustration soils the otherwise great experience.

EXAMPLE
Sorting machines shoot resources out, and you are supposed to place pans to catch the resources, but the spray is wide enough and the pans small enough that unless you get lucky, the resources end up on the floor instead of in the pan. And then you get to spend 30-40 minutes picking up 300 INDIVIDUAL clumps of ore ONE AT A TIME and putting them into a pan BY HAND so you can try and sort them again. I assume this problem will go away once I have conveyor belts, but the jury is out on whether or not I push through the pain to get there, as this is only one of many examples of how the interface is a struggle to engage with.

POST DEVELPOER RESPONSE EDIT
I've decided to change my review to positive. I was only just on the side of the negatives, and getting any response at all from developers, let alone a positive constructive one, is more than enough to bump me to the other side of the fence. Thanks!

I figured about the conveyers, but that's a lot of time and effort away. 

I have the magnet stick already, but it doesn't load them into the pan the same way that dropping them does. From hand or machine, resources stack in the pan so you can carry an infinite amount; with the magnet stick, they don't stack so you can only get maybe 20 resources in at once, and taking the pan up to your sorter and back for ~20 resources a time is a slower than grabdrop spamming into a pan and doing a single run.

SUGGESTIONS
1.) Maybe you could reduce the spread of machine outputs and/or give them an indicator of where it will drop its output?
2.) It would be really great if the map was something you picked up once and then pressed the "M" key instead of needing to haul a physical map around.
3.) Getting energy bars into a vertical Pressure Tube is... a struggle. Precise placement doesn't work.
4.) The Construction Hammer is cumbersome. Same fix as the map, or maybe give players a toolbar for tools that can be cycled through with the middle mouse button. It would be a MASSIVE QoL improvement, though I understand it would be a lot of work to implement. :(
5.) Change object placement orientation default to the original setting instead of the last used setting; I never want to play my stone blocks so that the flat part isn't up, but I often have to wrestle with the Y/R/T keys to get them back to upwards.
6.) Placing objects precisely is also a pain because the placement distance can't be changed, and is too far away. It's a nightmare trying to build in cramped holes in early game.
developer_response:
Hey there. Sorry you're not enjoyng the game, let me just fire off some recommendations for you which will help your experience:
- The hand sorter is only a primitive device meant to be used in the early game. Later on you can use conveyor sorter belts which do this for you manually which are far easier to handle and more predictable. I recommend building some floor foundations when using the hand sorter so you can see exactly where it outputs to.
- You can make picking up multiple objects easier by using the "magnet on a stick"
It will make errors a lot easier to deal with. Buy it from the Bridgepour tools and equipment store.

If this has been helpful and you want to give Hydroneer another go, please consider updating your review. We're a small team and reviews really help us out :) Thanks!

review: Very fun and enjoyable, one of my favourite games!

An absolute gem of a game, brother. Hydroneer is a unique take on the automation genre. Yes, it's a little old now, but it holds up 100%. It's insanely chill. No enemies. No ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The only "downsides" are the multiplayer system and the optimization. Honestly, we are lucky they added any multiplayer. The optimization is a real head scratcher, but whatever. It's not an action/shooter. 
Buy this game, especially if it's on sale.

As someone who enjoys base building and automation games I expected this to be right up my alley. Unfortunately I didn't find the fun here at all. After 6 hours I have a basic camp with initial automation and can see the next 30 hours ahead, however I have no interest in playing them.

It starts with a bad impression thanks to a terrible tutorial. This was a rare game where I had to resort to google before the tutorial was even over thanks to a combination of janky controls and unintuiative mechanics. I have no words to describe how the item dropping mechanic makes the most simple action unnecessarily difficult.

The game itself is a sandbox. There's no purpose to your mining other than to build a bigger mine. A few villagers do have quests, however these quests ask you to build the same items you are already crafting as part of the craft-sell-buy-expand game loop. Thus they don't introduce anything new or challenging.

From the start you can visit nearby towns and see the items you can buy later in the game. I explored each town, saw the options, and lost motivation to play any further.

Ultimately I think this may be an issue of the reward not being worth the effort. I completed some basic automation, delivered the first couple of villagers quests, and explored the map. Looking through the achievement list there doesn't appear to be any challenge here, just more of the same. Nothing to unlock, nothing to learn, and no new mechanics in the future. Time for me to move on.

[h1]Hydroneer deserves a sequel — here's why[/h1]
[b]3 days after [url=https://steamcommunity.com/app/1106840/eventcomments/834998218919000178?snr=2_9_100015_]the news post[/url] = 150 comments.[/b] Top-tier games would die of envy. I want to throw in my two cents too.
I'm a little disappointed to hear that players coming back still see their big factory lagging. But it's bearable. You can live with it.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]What I'd love to see added[/h2]
Personally, I'd love to see some new gadgets and gizmos. For example — [b]a logic speaker[/b] with adjustable pitch (and duration, if possible) using the existing keyboard. We really need this. Right now I'm using bare wires, but a proper speaker is needed.
Of course, if you build two parameters into the speaker — [i]pitch[/i] and [i]duration[/i] — it would need one input to trigger it and two more for the parameters. A 3-digit number could be used as a piano frequency, from 001 to 999. That covers several octaves.
We're also missing [b]signs to hang on walls and label things[/b] — small thing, but still.
I'd love to see more interesting updates in the logic section — devices and functions. If there are a lot of ideas, you could even add a separate vendor for them.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Anvil improvements[/h2]
An anvil upgrade wouldn't hurt either. The anvil is great, but I'd love to see more recipes for jewelry and weapons — [b]a crown, a scepter, something else[/b]. Three slots on the anvil for resources and gems would allow way more combinations. I tried to make a mod using AI, but it never worked out.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Creative mode wishlist[/h2]
In creative mode I'm missing [b]more free-form building[/b] — so when you're building, the item respawns infinitely in your hand until you switch to something else. Right now I have to keep running back to the shop or using the magic wand that multiplies items. I'm building a big digital factory and I have several thousand wires on it. Maybe I'm the only one like this, so I won't push too hard on that one.
But still — [b]please[/b], more anvil crafting recipes and an expanded logic shop window. [i]Pretty please![/i]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Story and world[/h2]
The game is really interesting. There's still a lot of space in the world. I'd love to see [b]more inhabitants and quests![/b] More story — forge a scepter and crown for the king, that kind of thing. I haven't reached the king yet and don't know what's there, but it's so engaging when the gates gradually open and you get access deeper and deeper into the castle. I remember the plot of Gothic. Here, the mechanics of many games are intertwined into one universe. A beautiful, atmospheric universe.
That's the kind of thing — story content — that I want more of in this beautiful world of logic and pure energy.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Where Hydroneer sits in my library[/h2]
Hydroneer is currently [b]4th place[/b] in my library, after Dota 2, Satisfactory, and Farming Simulator 25. But despite how much I love Cities: Skylines II, Valheim, The Forest, Crime Simulator, CS and other games I've fully completed — [b]Hydroneer has surpassed them all and is fighting its way to 3rd place.[/b]
I'm a big fan of Satisfactory and Farming Simulator, and I'm amazed that a game like Hydroneer not only stands shoulder to shoulder with the giants but is capable of challenging them for the throne in my heart.
[i]Games about digging, mining, conveyor belts, farms, and factories are very popular — there are plenty of them — but Hydroneer has become a legend in its own right.[/i]
[hr][/hr]
[h1]My honest pitch to the devs: make Hydroneer 2[/h1]
I believe there should either be a [b]sequel[/b] to this game or [b]serious continued care[/b] for the first one.
I'm not giving silly advice. I suggest the developers pay attention to the number of comments — people want to see proposals. As a developer myself, I understand you want to build one thing and then move on to something else. But look at the result — a massive fanbase.
[h3]What Hydroneer 2 could be:[/h3]
A new world with the [b]old mechanics plus new ones[/b]. The same character (or a different one) tries to start over in another land. Essentially you'd only need to write a new story and draw a new, interesting location. Keep the old mechanics, add details. The speaker. More anvil combinations.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]A note on your next game[/h2]
Yes, I'll buy your new game Die Trying out of curiosity and to support the developer. But I don't think I'll actually play it. [b]I want Hydroneer![/b]
And since you need to develop something to make a living — let's meet halfway and make [b]Hydroneer 2![/b] A new adventure with the old heroes. Or new heroes. =)
[hr][/hr]
[h3]I'm serious.[/h3]
I haven't even finished the main story yet, and I'm planning to play the DLC. I'm honestly telling you — Hydroneer will fight its way into my library's top hours alongside legends I've already 100%-ed multiple times.
I got stuck somewhere in the middle of the story and I'm just slowly enjoying building in this [i]world of pure energy and entertaining logic![/i]
GOOD GAME

Du positif, du négatif, et de l'inconnu.

Négatif ou mitigé :
Le jeu est en solo, et c'est très dommage.
Le tutoriel est un peu faiblard, aucun guide à l'arrivée dans une nouvelle partie c'est un peu manquant, obligé de regarder sur internet certains éléments. Par exemple la balance est OBLIGATOIRE mais je n'ai su qu'elle existait dans un shop en regardant sur internet. Autre exemple j'ai vu qu'il y a un système d'électricité ? Ou un système logique ? Pour l'instant aucune idée de comment on s'en sert. Aussi on découvre qu'on peut pêcher et faire des soupes avec des légumes, je n'ai pas essayé mais je n'ai pour l'instant aucune idée de comment on obtient des légumes.
On doit faire beaucoup d'aller-retour pour acheter des constructions, c'est un peu long surtout quand on ne sait pas de quoi on a besoin, et qu'on oublie des trucs.
Les sauvegardes auto font freeze, ce n'est pas super embêtant mais ça reste un point à soulever.

Positif :
Bien que le début soit un peu lent, une fois qu'on comprend comment le jeu fonctionne et comment on peut automatiser certains éléments (c'est un peu le but du jeu) ça devient un peu plus sympas.
Le concept est pas mal, le fait que le jeu soit basé sur la physique est cool (ça me fait un peu penser à Minemogul).
Des mods qui rendent l'expérience meilleure sans détruire le jeu. Bien que je vienne de commencer, je suis assez expérimenté dans ce genre de jeu et ai installé des mods qui me semblent corrects directement, et franchement c'est plutôt bien.
Il y a quelques quêtes que donnent les PNJ qui donnent aussi un objectif à atteindre et des crafts à faire, à voir où sa mène.

A voir avec les zones après la zone de départ, mais globalement en poussant quelques heures (3-4 heures) ceux qui aiment l'automatisation devraient pouvoir y trouver plaisir.
J'espère aussi qu'on peut miner avec d'autres choses que la foreuse de départ, parce que de ce que je vois, je ne peux en acheter qu'une.
Il y a de bonnes idées, j'aime bien le concept, c'est assez chill, pas de grosse prise de tête avec de la micro gestion à la satisfactory pour gérer du rendement.
Un petit système de craft que je n'ai pas encore exploré, j'attends d'automatiser complètement ma première zone.
Il y a du potentiel, à voir lorsque j'aurai avancé un peu plus dans ma partie, si c'est la même chose à faire sur chaque zone ça va être barbant, mais sinon je pense qu'il peut y avoir plusieurs dizaines d'heures à passer sur le jeu.

We also have added in ‘backup’ saves to prevent total data loss. Try finding this backup, by opening up the game, pressing ‘continue’ on the main menu, then ticking the ‘Show Backup’ box. This will show a backup save file which hopefully won’t be corrupted.

If you’d like any more help with this or another issue, you can reach out to us by email: support@foulballhangover.com. If this has resolved your issue please consider updating your review. We’re a small team and reviews really help us out, thanks!

review:
Hydroneer has a really interesting core idea. Building and expanding your own mining operation, setting up machines, and slowly automating everything can be genuinely satisfying. The progression feels rewarding, especially when your systems finally start working together smoothly.

Unfortunately, the game is heavily dragged down by its awful controls. I honestly haven’t seen such clunky and frustrating interaction design in a long time. Simple tasks often feel harder than they should because fighting the camera and handling objects is unnecessarily awkward.

The translation (playing in Polish) is also very poor. Some prompts are confusing, and at times the displayed buttons don’t even match the actual controls, which becomes incredibly annoying in a game focused on manual interactions.

What frustrated me the most was the lack of a proper inventory system. Constantly carrying items back and forth stopped being immersive very quickly and just became tedious and exhausting.

Hydroneer has good ideas and some enjoyable mechanics, but the terrible controls, bad localization, and tiring item management made it difficult for me to stay invested.

review: Good
good
goood game

The core mechanics and system are very promising, the depth and framework really invites you to dive in. Unfortunately that's where the glitter ends, you are quickly met with the most tedious and mind numbingly annoying  preventions to crafting/base-building.

Lets assume you are about 4-6 hours into your first game, you keep repeating to yourself in your head "this is really fun already but boy do I wish I could just set things on the ground." You'll ignore that voice and continue to push on, only for another voice to pop up and say "hey why is the pick up item and drop item key the exact same by default, its really annoying when you try and set down a pan only to pick up your drill." The cherry on top for this exact situation is finding out you now have to scrap and rebuild your entire automation chain because once an element is removed it is NOT going back where it was. I found saving practically every time I did something helped, but funnily enough you cant even load a file while you are in game, you have to go back to the menu without saving. Another lil tidbit of extremely interactive gameplay I had was finding out the sorting bench isn't really meant for sorting. Its actually meant to fling all your ♥♥♥♥ all over the dig site and force you to pick it up again because it gets set out with the force of 1000 suns.

4/10 game, if the player QOL is brought up to the modern standard this is easily an 8-9/10 automation game with a fun simplified blacksmithing aspect. Just simple things like being able to set something down on the ground instead of having to pick it up and drop it 20x to make it land right, some more info when it comes to building would be nice ex: its red but I have 0 idea why I cant place it here.

The dev seems to be fairly petty too, just going through the recent reviews and im seeing my pain points echoed over and over. This would be a good indication that change is needed, instead they prod at the customers.

We played through the tutorial, really liked the concept, only then realizing as we were getting ready to play together, that it was splitscreen only. Which, really wouldn't be a problem, if it wasn't Steam remote play, streaming the game to one another and having network fluctuations nearly constantly, effecting the gameplay to a practically unplayable degree. It certainly seemed fun and my best friend and I were excited to give it a shot, being fans of Deep Rock Galactic and all, but... Yeah, if you were looking for a regular online co-op game, that isn't the case for this, as of now, at least. Fingers crossed, they'll release non-splitscreen sometime, but until then... I don't know, maybe give Deep Rock Galactic a shot if you're a fan of similar games. -- Recommended for solo, but for any sort of multiplayer outside of couch co-op, this isn't quite the one.

review:
It looks like a nice game and it might be good but the start is incredibly long. You have to dig and smelt manually which is fine. Moving items has the clunkiest control that i've met in a while. You hold the resource in your hand and when you release it it falls down slightly to your right side where the object is rendered. That means that if you are looking at something, the resource will fall next to it. You literally have to learn how to move items and I don't think this is what the game should be about.
And when you are not doing the resource logistics on the 5 square feet which is your mining site, you are moving your slow as hell transport cart to a shop to sell your stuff that is also using phsycs models, so you move your items in and out one by one because the game gave you one hand which is your entire inventory slot.

It pretty much feels like the game deliberately slowed progression down (which would be fine in this genre, it is about automation after all) but game controls are making this experience feel like work. And it's a shame because if I didn't have to move almost everything on a snails pace and if I had an actual inventory, this game would be nice. And it's not like the game wouldn't do things like this in places. When you get water you literally have to drop a bucket in water and then pick it back up. But time it right or your bucket will roll away because physics. When you dig, you grab the shove and click the ground. When you have dirt on your shovel, you click the bucket to put dirt there. And I get it that after I have automation this gets better but if the game is about automation then why does the beginning need to be so painful. It's like the first few hours of satisfactory where you need to keep collecting plants to make power before you can actually use coal. It's pointless grind.

This way sadly it's a refund after one hour.

developer_response:
Hey there Galliant Light
Sorry you didn't enjoy the DLC or our implementation of multiplayer - in short, with the extreme complexity of a game with a large amount of physics operations, making the game in a traditional multiplayer way is impossible, so splitscreen over remote play was the best (and frankly, the only) option to get players multiplayer.
If you'd like to read further on this, I created a post about it here: 
https://steamcommunity.com/app/1106840/discussions/0/3203748171375176286/

As you may know, Hydroneer is a finished product and we've moved our team on to the next project. Our console port was done by an outside porting company, and they've done a fantastic job. They're the best team we could possibly find with the best track record, and whilst porting the game to consoles they found a few opportunities for us to optimize the game, that our lesser experienced team did not know about.

They kindly shared this knowledge with us and we applied these optimizations to the PC version, and we wrapped it up as a free update rather than just ignoring them and focusing on our new game.

For the record, the game already does have A TON of optimizations. We supported the game for years after the 1.0 launch, and a lot of this was optimizations. 

So that's it - we're not working on Hydroneer, but we decided to dedicate some time in revisiting the game for the benefit of players.

I hope this extra information has been useful, and perhaps changed your perspective on the situation :)

review:
Hydroneer is one of those games that looks simple at first, but slowly turns into something much deeper and more addictive than expected. At the start, it seems like a basic mining and crafting game where you dig dirt, wash it, sell resources, and upgrade your tools. But after playing for a while, you realize that the real fun comes from building your own systems, automating your work, improving your base, and slowly turning a tiny mining operation into a huge machine-powered money-making setup.

The game has a very satisfying progression system. You begin with basic tools, doing almost everything by hand. You dig the ground yourself, carry buckets, wash dirt manually, and sell small amounts of gold or iron for money. It feels slow at first, but that is actually part of the charm. Every upgrade feels earned. When you finally buy better equipment, pipes, drills, harvesters, conveyors, or vehicles, the game starts opening up a lot more. You can clearly feel the difference between the early game and the later game, and that makes the progression rewarding.

One of the best parts of Hydroneer is the automation. Building a system that takes dirt, processes it, filters it, separates resources, and sends everything where it needs to go is extremely satisfying. It almost feels like a mix between a mining game, a building game, and a factory game. You constantly think about how to make your setup more efficient. Maybe your pipes are messy, maybe your machines keep getting clogged, maybe your resources are not going where you want them to go, or maybe your whole system needs to be redesigned. Fixing those problems is a big part of the fun.

The building system gives you a lot of freedom. You can create simple mining setups or giant industrial-looking systems with pipes, conveyors, machines, storage areas, and workshops. The game does not force you to play in one specific way. You can focus on mining, crafting, farming, fishing, building, or just experimenting with weird machine setups. That freedom makes the game feel relaxing, but also very engaging if you like planning and improving things.

The physics-based gameplay also gives Hydroneer a unique feeling. Items are actual objects in the world, not just numbers in an inventory. You physically move tools, resources, buckets, machines, bars, gems, and everything else. This can be very fun because it makes the world feel more interactive and real. Selling a big pile of gold or carrying materials around feels more satisfying because you actually see everything in front of you.

However, this same physics system can also be frustrating sometimes. Items can get stuck, fall in awkward places, or become messy if you are not careful. When your mining operation gets bigger, managing hundreds of objects can sometimes become chaotic. It is not always a bad thing, because some of that chaos is funny and part of the game’s personality, but it can occasionally feel clunky.

Graphically, Hydroneer has a simple but charming style. It is not trying to be ultra-realistic, but it has a clean and colorful look that fits the gameplay well. The different plots of land, tools, machines, vehicles, and resources are easy to recognize, and the world has a cozy sandbox feeling. The visuals are good enough to make building and exploring enjoyable without distracting from the main gameplay.

The sound design is also decent. The sounds of machines running, dirt being processed, water flowing through pipes, and resources dropping onto conveyors help make your setup feel alive. It is especially satisfying when you finally get an automated system running properly and can hear everything working together. The game has a calm atmosphere, which makes it easy to play for long sessions while relaxing.

Hydroneer is also very good for players who enjoy setting their own goals. The game does not constantly tell you exactly what to do. Instead, it gives you tools and systems, and then you decide what you want to build or improve. Some players might love this freedom, while others might feel a bit lost at first. If you are someone who likes games with strict missions and clear objectives, Hydroneer might feel a little slow. But if you enjoy sandbox games where you create your own projects, it is very easy to get hooked.

One of the biggest weaknesses of Hydroneer, though, is the multiplayer. The game is very good overall, but the multiplayer features feel lacking compared to what the game could have. Hydroneer seems like the perfect game to play with friends. Building a mining operation together, dividing jobs, designing automation systems, driving around, and expanding a base should be amazing in co-op. And while multiplayer does exist, it does not feel as polished or complete as it should.

The multiplayer can feel limited and sometimes awkward. It does not always feel like a fully developed co-op experience, but more like a single-player game that had multiplayer added on top. There is so much potential here, because Hydroneer’s gameplay would work extremely well with multiple people. One person could mine, another could build pipes, another could handle crafting, and another could organize resources. But the multiplayer side does not feel as smooth or deep as it could be.

This is probably the main area where the game needs improvement. Better multiplayer stability, better shared progression, smoother co-op tools, and more features designed specifically for multiple players would make the game much better. Hydroneer is already fun alone, but with stronger multiplayer, it could become an amazing co-op sandbox game. Right now, it is still enjoyable with friends, but it feels like it is missing some important quality-of-life features.

Another small issue is that the game can sometimes feel repetitive. The main loop is mining, processing, selling, upgrading, and building better systems. If you enjoy that loop, it is great. But if you do not like repeating tasks while slowly improving your setup, the game might become boring after a while. The fun mostly comes from your own creativity and motivation to expand. The game gives you the tools, but you need to make your own goals.

Performance can also depend on how large and messy your setup becomes. Because the game uses many physical objects and machines, very large builds can sometimes cause lag or weird behavior. This is not always a huge problem, but it is something to keep in mind if you like building massive automated systems.

Despite these issues, Hydroneer is still a very good game. It has a unique style, satisfying progression, fun automation, and a relaxing sandbox atmosphere. It is the kind of game where you tell yourself you will only play for a short time, but then suddenly you have spent hours redesigning your mining system, fixing pipes, upgrading machines, or trying to make everything more efficient.

The best thing about Hydroneer is how rewarding it feels to improve. Every small upgrade matters. Every machine you add makes your setup feel more advanced. Every problem you solve makes your base feel more personal. It gives you that nice feeling of starting with almost nothing and slowly building something big through your own work.

Overall, Hydroneer is a very enjoyable and creative mining sandbox game. It is especially good for people who like automation, building, experimenting, and slowly progressing from basic tools to advanced systems. It has some clunky moments, and the multiplayer features definitely need more work, but the core game is strong and very fun. The lack of deeper multiplayer support is disappointing because the game has huge co-op potential, but even with that weakness, Hydroneer is still absolutely worth playing.

Final rating: 8/10

Hydroneer is a great game with a lot of charm, creativity, and satisfying progression. It is very good as a single-player sandbox automation game, bu

Hydroneer is one of those games that looks simple at first, but after a few hours it completely takes over your brain. You start with a shovel, a bucket, and a tiny piece of land, thinking you are just going to dig up some gold for a few minutes. Then suddenly it is 3 AM and you are redesigning an entire automated mining system because your conveyor belts are slightly inefficient. That is the real magic of this game.

The core gameplay loop is incredibly satisfying. Digging dirt by hand in the beginning feels slow, but it gives you a strong sense of progression later when you build giant automated machines that sort, crush, smelt, and process resources for you. Watching your own mining setup finally work perfectly after hours of planning is one of the most rewarding experiences I have had in a sandbox game. The game constantly gives you new goals without directly forcing anything on you. You can focus on mining, automation, building, farming, forging weapons, fishing, or just creating an absurdly overcomplicated industrial machine because you felt like it.

The voxel terrain system is one of the best parts of Hydroneer. Being able to completely reshape the land makes your base actually feel like yours. You are not just placing blocks on a flat map. You are carving giant mining pits into the earth, making tunnels, building bridges, and designing your operation however you want. It creates a very natural progression from “guy with shovel” to “industrial mining company CEO.” The freedom is amazing.

The automation system is where the game truly shines. Pipes, pressure systems, drills, harvesters, sorting machines, logic systems, conveyors, smelters — everything connects together in a way that feels both complicated and rewarding. The game never feels overly simplified. You actually need to think about efficiency, organization, and resource flow. When you finally get a huge machine running without breaking, it feels earned. Few games capture that engineering satisfaction this well.

Another thing Hydroneer does extremely well is atmosphere. It is weirdly relaxing. There is no constant combat pressure, no giant list of quests screaming at you, no battle pass nonsense, no forced online garbage. You just exist in the world and slowly build your mining empire. The sound design helps a lot too. The clanking machines, running water, conveyor noises, and ambient environment make the whole experience feel cozy despite operating massive industrial equipment.

The progression is also balanced very well. Early game manual labor makes money feel important, and later game automation genuinely feels powerful because you remember how much work things used to take. Some sandbox games throw huge machines at you too quickly, but Hydroneer makes you slowly earn everything. That makes every upgrade satisfying.

Visually, the game has a simple style, but it works perfectly. It does not try to be ultra realistic. Instead, it focuses on readability and charm. The low-poly look gives the game personality, and honestly it helps the machines stand out better. Watching dozens of moving conveyor belts and drills would probably look messy in a hyper realistic art style. Here, everything is easy to understand while still looking good.

The developers also deserve credit for continuing to improve the game over time. The amount of content compared to launch is much larger now, and the community around the game is surprisingly dedicated. Steam reviews remain “Very Positive,” with tens of thousands of positive reviews overall.

Now for the main negative: multiplayer.

Hydroneer technically has co-op, but it is not proper online multiplayer. It relies on Steam Remote Play Together and split-screen systems rather than native multiplayer servers. Multiple community discussions mention issues with controller requirements, split-screen limitations, latency problems, and awkward setup processes. The second player usually needs a controller, and there is no true standalone online world hosting like you would expect from modern co-op sandbox games.

This is honestly the game’s biggest weakness by far. A game built around massive mining operations and automation feels like it should have proper multiplayer support. Building giant factories with friends would be incredible. Instead, the multiplayer feels more like a workaround than a fully designed feature. Some players manage to enjoy it, but there are enough technical limitations that it can become frustrating.

But outside of that issue, Hydroneer is genuinely awesome.

If you enjoy automation games, sandbox progression, mining, factory building, or relaxing games where you slowly create something massive from nothing, this game is absolutely worth playing. It scratches the same kind of brain itch as games like Factorio, Satisfactory, Minecraft tech mods, or automation-focused simulators, but it still feels unique because of the physics systems and terrain manipulation.

Hydroneer is not perfect. Sometimes it is janky. Sometimes machines behave strangely. Sometimes organizing pipes becomes a nightmare. But honestly, those rough edges almost become part of the charm. The game feels creative, ambitious, and genuinely fun in a way many modern games do not.

Overall, Hydroneer is one of the best mining and automation sandbox games available on Steam. The multiplayer situation is disappointing and definitely needs improvement, but everything else about the game — the progression, automation, freedom, atmosphere, creativity, and satisfaction of building your own industrial empire — is fantastic. Once the game hooks you, it is extremely hard to stop playing.

review: THIS GMAE IS SOOO GOOD THAT I WANT TO KILL MYSELF

I love automation games, especially first person and crafting types.  Satisfactory is one of my favorites.

I played this game for a bit and absolutely loathed it.  The crafting seems ok and there are some interesting ideas but the UI and controls are so janky and clunky and awkward that it actually made the game wholly unpleasant.  I quit after about half an hour because I just couldn't stand the awkward cursor selections.  In a game like this you should be focused on organizing the next steps, not worried about fighting with the mouse cursor to see if you can actually pick something up.  It was really dreadful.  Very disappointed.

The tutorial I also felt was really quite bad.  It doesn't really tell you what you need to know, or at least I felt that in several cases it just missed really important details.  It also doesn't really explain any of the surrounding info.  It's a generally very low effort tutorial that should have had a lot more thought put into it.

In a game like this, or really in any game, you cannot skimp on the early game effort.  People get 1 to 2 hours to judge a game before refunds expire, and if you can't give a good impression in that time, it doesn't matter how good the game gets later.

I don't even know if this game has potential at mid or later stages because the beginning was just too awful for me to get through, primarily due to the cursor, UI, and control issues above.

On very rare occasions Hydroneers save files can be corrupted. This generally happens when someone closes the game while it is saving. We’ve added in measures to prevent this from corrupting but there are some outlying cases. 
We have also noticed that some anti-virus programs prevent Hydroneer from saving. Please list Hydroneer as an accepted program or consider disabling your anti-virus programs. (Windows Defender is fine, but other AV programs can have this issue)
We also have added in ‘backup’ saves to prevent total data loss. Try finding this backup, by opening up the game, pressing ‘continue’ on the main menu, then ticking the ‘Show Backup’ box. This will show a backup save file which hopefully won’t be corrupted.

If you’d like any more help with this or another issue, you can reach out to us by email: support@foulballhangover.com. If this has resolved your issue please consider updating your review. We’re a small team and reviews really help us out, thanks!
