An interesting take on Factorio-style automation games, where it's first person 3D and the focus is more on the challenges of developing and managing your construction sites, moving placeable objects around and organizing them, and actually assembling things, than it is about the logistics of moving raw and finished goods around.

The defining feature of this game is that you have NO INVENTORY, as opposed to games like Satisfactory where you have a "pocket dimension" that holds impossibly large stacks of pretty much everything.  Instead, you can carry ONE item at a time, including containers, or you can load them into your truck and drive them around.

When constructing your setups, you have to manually pick up each item one by one and place it on the voxel grid.  Easier said than done, because you have to figure out which items and how many you'll need, procure them from the appropriate vendors/manufacturers, drive them to your construction site, and unload them nearby with some semblance of organization.

Not to mention, a certain amount of verticality is required because the only way to convey resources from one machine to the next is usually by having them fall down.  This in turn means that you might need to construct a rudimentary scaffolding so that you can actually REACH wherever you need to put the items -- much like a real construction project.

In short, the lack of inventory is an intentional design feature that creates its own set of gameplay challenges which significantly differ from other games in its genre.  The amount of manual steps involved can be very frustrating at first, but the game forces you to get good at at streamlining and/or automating these steps wherever possible -- even mundane tasks such as shopping trips, moving stuff around your site, loading/unloading, digging/tunneling, cutting resources to the required size, and more.  So far I really appreciate this unique take.

Hydroneer is a classic case of a maybe recommendation. In fact I would love to recommend it! There's a great game at its core but due to numerous issues I can only recommend it with some huge caveats hence the negative recommendation.

tl;dr this is a game which could have been Satisfactory/Factorio tier if the dev had continued to work on and refine it but as it stands it's essentially a janky, buggy, generous demo with a huge amount of unrealised potential. That said, for a certain type of player, there's a fun few hours to be had here if you can make your own goals with the tools provided and look past the many, many janky parts.

My main positive take away was that interacting with everything physically feels great - when it works. You really feel like you're the one mining and smithing. For example, physically digging a hole in the dirt and panning the soil for riches feels fantastic and initially sold me on the game. Although automation is fiddly, again, physically putting all the pipework, conveyors, logic, and machines together then watching it run is extremely satisfying. What's here is enjoyable and oddly compulsive while it lasts.

Additionally the world itself is extremely charming. They've nailed that idyllic fantasy feel and while the music, graphics, and art direction aren't anything to write home about they come together to give the world a relaxing vibe which makes it cosy and pleasant to exist in. And trust me, you'll need that relaxing atmosphere when all the issues kick in.

And there are so, so many issues to deal with:
[list]
  [*]Autosave literally freezes the game for seconds
  [*]The game slows down when too many items exist at the same time or a container gets too full (in a game where you're generating many items per second this quickly becomes a problem)
  [*]It's easy to spill these many items everywhere with a misclick and the in built solutions for this are horrible
  [*]Collision is enabled in such a way that just putting things down can be a trial which massively exacerbates the above issue
  [*]Only holding one thing at a time isn't necessarily a bad design choice but the way it's implemented is less than ideal
  [*]The game doesn't respect players time outside of the main game loop of mining, e.g. shops are spread out all over the place, each item is bought one at a time when you often need dozens, each item has to be loaded and unloaded onto and off of vehicles one at a time, etc.
  [*]Once you solve early automation that's the solution for the whole game. As a result there's no real game progress past early automation - there are some in-game quests but they quickly get repetitive
  [*]There are multiple types of currency for no reason other than to support the repetitive quests. You need to carry those multiple types of currency one at a time to buy from the stores that use them (although you can use a cart which make it slightly less painful)
  [*]The economy is a mess for the main currency. You'll have more money than you'll ever need once you crack early automation which also helps the game feel pointless to continue with
  [*]The final kick in the teeth was enabling some mods to try and fix some of these issues and then finding out that achievements have been permanently disabled for that save file even if I were to disable them. I understand the decision to disable achievement in a fully functional game but here those mods are just cleaning up issues that shouldn't be in the game in the first place. To go further and essentially irrevocably brick achievements on that save file is just a baffling decision.
  [*]I could go on listing stuff but you get the point. For every fantastic mechanic or idea there are multiple issues present
[/list]

Although there's a big list of negatives there, playing Hydroneer has been such a frustrating experience because I've hugely enjoyed it despite all it's faults. The games greatest issue is that it essentially just ends once you have automation up and running for the first time. If there were more and varied automation challenges to solve I would be happy to continue playing it as it's genuinely just that fun to physically interact with the world despite all the jank. Honestly, it feels like the dev had enough of building the game and punted it out of early access at an arbitrary point when there's still so much work left to do. No shade on the dev, making games is hard and I completely understand how that would happen, especially given the game was made by just one dev, but it's still a shame to see all this potential go to waste.

I like the game but there just isn't much game to be had, it feels more like a proof of concept for the mechanics instead of a full fledged game.

The initial gearing up was a slog but it did feel fulfilling to go from working with a bucket and brush to getting the starter machines. It even felt good letting those machines run to build up enough to get them hooked up with basic belts and sorters so I could finally move to whatever is next... and then it just ends.

There's nothing left that needs doing, you can buy more plots sure and you can run around doing some other random side stuff that doesn't matter but there's zero chase or goals. If you do buy more plots it's just redoing what you already did after making more machines.

I think the implied goal is to work on ramping up production so you can get more of the same machines to continue ramping up production so you can get more slightly faster versions of the same machines? This... doesn't make sense to me, there's no new automation to get and nothing to do with anything you'd get from doing it. Yes I can continue to do exactly what I did already and set up some more parallel production lines but there's no reason to to do.

To compare to another game it's like if Factorio didn't have enemies and only gave you access to coal miners and furnaces then expected you to just make more of those forever. It's... interesting... and I could see some people having fun making hundreds of them while continuing to fill them and make more but there's no point to it.

It also feels like there's a lot of tiers of automation and progression missing leaving many tasks fully manual. Constantly running around repairing filters and crafting items to sell or get more drills only reinforces the proof of concept feeling with nothing coming after.

There's also some bugs with gems getting stuck floating and not going off of the belts correctly which would be frustrating if there was reason to ramp up production... kinda funny that infinitely stacking floating gems aren't really a problem since by this point there isn't anything left to do.

Again I don't hate it, there just isn't really anything here past a proof of concept sandbox. The start is a slog since there's no inventory and once things start to get better with the machines it just ends.

This is one of the very few games that I think are worth a review, as it is one of the best I have ever played. It is rather affordable, the DLC is the size of the main game, if not bigger (And only for £10!) and the graphics are stunning. OF course, that is hardware dependant, but at max settings, it looks like a full team of professionals worked on it, rather than the solo developer and later the small group. The game is good for many reasons, one of which being its replayability. Since it is a (mostly) free build game, there are literally thousands of designs you can use to build a factory. This brings us on to our second point, "But what if It's too confusing?". Hydroneer is one of the few design and factory games that don't take too much thinking, though it doesn't come without its own difficulties of course. I would dare say it is better than even Satisfactory, due to the simplicity to complexity range between the 2 games. The final point goes for how rewarding it feels when you build a full factory, and how fun the process itself is. Turning that valve after a few hours' work feels like youv'e just struck gold (pun intended) and it is a damn good feeling. Anyway, I would recommend this game to anyone, from lazy people who want a basic setup to complex builders who may want to use logic and such. 5/5 stars! Kudos!

On the surface, this game checks a lot of boxes for me - automation, progression, base building, etc. In reality, the terrible controls, item placement jank, lack of an inventory, and excessive grind (at least in the early game) killed it for me. Here is the game loop for the first 90 minutes:

1. Drop the bucket near you on the ground
2. Pick up the shovel by pressing E
3. Left click the ground, left click the bucket. Repeat 4 times.
4. Drop the shovel by pressing E
5. Look at the full bucket and pick it up by pressing E
6. Walk over to your pan, drop the bucket by pressing E
7. Pick up the pan and drop it in the water with E to fill it
8. Pick up the full pan with E, drop it on the ground with E, hope it lands face up
9. Pick up the bucket again by pressing E, get the shadow to align with the bucket (which isn't centered in the viewport), then left click to pour the bucket into the pan
10. Drop the bucket with E
11. Pick up the brush with E
12. Left click the pan with the brush to reveal 1-4 nuggets
13. Go to step 1 and repeat ~5-10 times.
14. Once you have a bunch of nuggets, pick up all of your nuggets one by one and place them into the pan so you can sell them for a small amount of coins in town.

Once you have enough money you can buy an anvil, furnace, etc. to slightly increase your earnings. Eventually you can buy machines to help automate this, but by 90 minutes in I wasn't even halfway there.

I could potentially forgive the grind if the controls weren't terrible and I had an inventory, but all of the picking up and dropping of individual items to complete tasks is a terrible play experience.

Ich bin hin und her gerissen und daher kann ich nur eine 50%ige Kaufempfehlung aussprechen.

Das Konzept bzw. die Spielidee ist gut und auf jedenfall eine Empfehlung wert. Aber was mir negativ aufgefallen ist, ist folgendes:

- ich habe gerade mal Tier 1 Technik und ein paar Cloutium-Rohre bei einer Spielzeit von ca. 36 Stunden und produziere aktuell mehr Hydroneer-Coins als ich brauche. Man kann sagen, das man das Spiel auch ohne Tier2 und Tier3 schon durchgespielt hat.

- die Steuerung ist aus der Hölle! Ich habe ja schon einige Spiele in meinem Leben gespielt und mittlerweile haben sich bestimmte Steuerungen durchgesetzt. Daher verstehe ich nicht warum die Steuerung in Hydroneer ein neu erfundenes Rad sein muss. Man steigt mit Q in Fahrzeuge (wobei das Q dank der Schrift wie eine 2 aussieht - nicht gut durchdacht). Die Interaktion findet teilweise mit der E-Taste und teilweise mit der linken Maustaste statt. Das hat mich Anfangs massiv verwirrt und tut es auch jetzt noch oft. Und warum muss es zwei "Fadenkreuze" geben?! Es gibt einmal ein Fadenkreuz in der Mitte des Bildschirms und einmal die Ablageposition der Hände die mehr rechts ist. Das macht einen so wirr. Warum hat man nicht gleich beides auf die Mitte gelegt oder gleich das Fadenkreuz versetzt. Was soll das egtl. bringen. Das macht das Spiel nicht interessanter oder unterhaltsamer sondern nervt egtl. nur. Ich finde, das sollten die noch einmal überarbeiten. Auch steht in den Einstellungen einmal "Fahrzeug einsteigen" und einmal "Fahrzeugmodus". Letzteres ist irgend etwas anderes gewesen und hat gar nichts mit Fahrzeugen zu tun.
- Leider gibt es auch keinerlei Erklärungen im Spiel. Ich musste wegen dem Trichter im Internet erst suchen. Dann wegen den Cloutiumbarren. Es wäre gut wenn es da eine In-Game Referez gäbe. Ich meine wieviel Druck braucht man? Wie regelt man den Druck? Für was sind die Kristalle? Alles das muss man googlen weil das Spiel nichts verrät. Das hätte ich mir schon ein bisschen besser gewünscht.
- Ein Verbesserungsvorschlag wäre auch das Item-Handling. Egtl. stört es beim einfachen Spielablauf nicht , das es kein Inventar gibt. Aber wenn man sein Feld voller Items (in meinem Fall Rohre nach Versuchsbauten) hat, wäre ein besseres Handling schon wünschenswert. Denn nach 20 Rohren vom Feld zum LKW tragen hat man egtl. schon keine Lust mehr auf das Spiel. 

Fazit: Die Spielidee ist gut und wenn man das Prinzip nach googlen versteht und sich mit der Steuerung anfreundet geht es, aber einige Verbesserungen wären echt toll. Damit kann jeder selbst abwägen ob er das Spiel spielen will.

Ich bin eigentlich durch Zufall über Hydroneer gestolpert, weil ich nach einem entspannten Spiel gesucht habe, bei dem ich einfach mal „abschalten“ kann. Tja, aus „mal reinschauen“ wurde ein richtiges kleines Goldgräber-Abenteuer – und ich liebe es! 😄

Das Grundprinzip ist simpel: Du startest mit Schaufel und Eimer, buddelst ein Loch, findest Erz und versuchst, daraus Geld zu machen. Aber genau diese Einfachheit ist es, die das Spiel so charmant macht. Es erinnert ein bisschen an die Anfangszeit von Minecraft – alles fühlt sich handgemacht an, du bastelst dir Stück für Stück deine kleine Mining-Welt zusammen.

Was Hydroneer für mich besonders macht, ist der Moment, wenn aus deinem kleinen Schlammloch plötzlich ein richtig funktionierendes System wird – mit Rohren, Maschinen, Förderbändern, Sortieranlagen. Ich habe stundenlang an meiner automatischen Anlage gebaut und war einfach stolz, als endlich alles lief. Klar, manchmal ist’s ein bisschen fummelig, aber genau das macht’s für mich authentisch.

Die Entwickler geben sich richtig Mühe. Es kommen regelmäßig Updates, neue Features, mehr Tiefe – man merkt, dass da Herzblut drinsteckt. Und die Community ist superhilfsbereit, falls man mal irgendwo hängt.

the game is extremely grind-heavy.  The only way I can enjoy some games is playing in creative mode or with dev tools enabled, and this is one of them.  The biggest problem I personally have is that Hydroneer has no inventory system at all. Hydroneer is basically a factory sandbox game combined with elements of idler/clicker games.  Incremental games, I guess.  Compared to fullblown incremental games, you might not find it that satisfying.  Compared to other factory-type games, it's sort of basic and you might not find it that satisying either.  When I wrote it out like that, I'm wondering to myself, "Why did I spend 30 hours playing it?" which means a ramble is coming in.

I mean, first off, it has splitscreen coop. I figured I'd coax my wife (and best gaming buddy) to play it as well and it would stream so very well, because if I was doing something dull maybe the other player wasn't.

But also basically it gets me right in the engineering gland. I have found myself spending a few hours at a time trying to work out how I'd set up a processing line on the surface, while getting a bunch of drills deep in a mine, and how I could do this tidily.  (Currently:  By digging a careful diagonal trench through the earth which I can then tidily cover up.)

So that leads me to somethign this game does differently:  It has diggable terrain.  Techtonica does too, but you can swiftly see the digging matrix, if you will.  This game lets you dig out essentially random balls and blobs and swiftly make really lumpy, messy tunnels that look like a maniac with a pickaxe went crazy.  Though it also gives you tools to smooth out the digs and make them polished again, which is way more satisfying than just having a pre-polished cube hacked out of the earth.

And if you get bored with that, there's also a digging machine you can purchase that you can drive and dig with.  It requires a very deft hand to use well, and maybe presurfacing tunnel floors so you don't overdo it. So it's sort of the reverse case of too much power in the hands of a player.  It's possible to, with a lot of patience, gradually undo digs, but far better to not mess it up in the first place.

Not to say this isn't without quirks, granted, some of which I'm... uncertain about. Overall game direction, and the inherent clumsiness of object manipulation.

The clumsiness of the game is something that will make or break you, frankly, and I should have discussed that at the top of this review.  But, aha, I didn't.  I'm not getting paid for this, so there's no editor.  But what makes the game clumsy is that the player can only hold one item at a time, regardless of its size.  Carrying a one-tonne drill?  Want to carry that shovel?  Put the drill down.  Done with the shovel and need a pickaxe?  Put down the shovel.  Saw a little loose nubbin of dirt the size of a marble?  Put down the pickaxe so you can pick up the dirt.

There are a few conveniences to make this somewhat less onerous - a toolrack exists that you can load up with four tools, and you just haul the rack around, set it down, and pull out the tool you need.  Not great, but less onerous than running back and forth for your tools.  There's also a few transport vehicles (a cart, a truck) you can get hold of right away, which you can load with a number of items and transport them all about as required. Working around this clumsiness is part of the game, and I usually solve this with my weird tractor-pickup hybrid, pulling it up as close to the workspace/shop/quest-client as I can, so I can pull things in and out of what's become a rolling inventory.  I can live without a massive inventory/toolbar the way most games tackle this, but for heaven's sake I must surely have pockets.  Let me keep my money in there!

The game's direction is another issue.  Basically, you start off penniless with just enough basic tools to get you to process a bit of minerals, and those bits of ore can be sold for money.  Money will let you start buying tools to improve the processs, and then automate the process, and after a few hours it's more-or-less entirely automatic and your gameplay revolves more around expanding your workspace, a bit of maintenance, and getting more machinery to dig things up faster... and "quests".

There's a bit of blacksmithing in the game.  It's relatively basic.  People will request a bit of jewelry, a melee weapon or maybe an ingot,  and will offer you payment in "tokens".  Those tokens are needed to buy tier 3 equipment.  I forgot to mention there's tiers of dirt; as one digs deeper, superior tech is needed to do anything with it.  The first two tiers can be purchased with regular cash (selling your mining leftovers will soon earn a ridiculous amount of money), but the third is had only with tokens, and that requires quests.

What makes the quests annoying (ish) is they'll ask for, say, a sword to be made of at least 150 "weight" of gold, or whatever, and to keep the game's item count down it's optimal to keep each resource as a single, giant lump.  The only manipulations possible are "cut in half" and "merge", so you wind up cutting a 62k "weight" ingot down to 123.5 or something, and then casting about for even tinier slivers to try to get up to (or past) 150, and then casting that random collection of slivers together to get the singular ingot you need.  (To be fair, later on you can afford to be like, "Aaah, 242 is close enough.  Let's go!" and the quest-giver is happy either way.)

There might well be some quest chain, but the second step requires a tier 3 resource I've only just started to harvest at 30-something hours.  Because I wasn't rushing it and just goofing off, having fun.  So I can't speak to that.

And with all that out of the way, there's apparently farming.  Which can be pretty awfully clumsy.  And it starts you off with a little trowel, dripping water onto a singular seedling out of a singular bucket.  And, in time, you'll probably have it all automated and harvesting great fields of it using a combine harvester I've been making googly eyes at for awhile now.

Anyway.  All I can say is that this review feels really disorganized, but I've enjoyed the game as I've been using it mostly as a cornball sandbox and just making things a bit harder on myself than I strictly needed to be.  Plus maybe I guess I like driving steamrollers around or whatever.  For the price I paid I certainly can't complain one bit.

We may eventually stream this thing, if I can convince the missus we should do it.  Who knows?  But we're chatting and affable 99% of the time, so if you got to the bottom of this review, you're exactly the sort of people that'd get on with our style.  http://www.twitch.tv/fdejeuner.  Hope to see you there.  (And thumbs up for this game, all things considered.)

TLDR; In its current state, I would only [b]pick it up [u]when on discount[/u][/b]

Hydroneer sets out to be a sandbox / automation game [b]with NO UI[/b], this is a choice the developers have made early on and have restated multiple times as a core principle of the game. This means among many things [b]no inventory[/b], [u]you WILL have to carry, move & place [b]everything[/b] one at a time.[/u]

[i]As you can imagine this creates many UX challenges[/i], which the developers have clearly thought quite a bit about, but there are still some issues; 

You do have [b]vehicles[/b] such as the hydro truck(s) that basically let you transport an infinite number of items (due to how all "containers" in the game disable clipping of items). But the truck controls feel a bit cluncky, which does have some charm with their oversized wheels, [i]but the roads are way too bumpy and the street lanterns have giant hitboxes,[/i] making driving feel more annoying than fun.

Due to not having an inventory, you [b]WILL HAVE TO drive back-and-forth between your plot(s) and the main stores in the towns CONSTANTLY[/b] (This will take up about 70-90% of the mid-to-end game, along with actually loading your truck with the items you purchased.)

[b]There is visible (positive) progress:[/b]
+++ The Construction Hammer, which was added since the last time I played, lets you lock/unlock items you constructed, which stops you from picking them up accidentally instead of the resources you were probably aiming at. I wanted to highlight this since it really shows the developers are working on QoL improvements too.
+ The developers are still actively working on Hydroneer. :)

So to summarize, there are still big QoL improvements that [b]must be made[/b], but I can see positive progress in that aspect since release. I will now give my QoL-istmass wishlist;
- We NEED some kind of fast travel, because ~80% of the mid game is just driving, instead of building machines or mining (which is the fun part). (While i understand a UI fast travel map is not "Hydroneer", we could maybe get an interior view of the truck, with a "dashboard" with 3 buttons that lets you select any town you already visited and plots you purchased? This could be something only Mk.II trucks can do?)
- A common QoL problem is managing where you left your money, there is a popular mod that does involve UI, but a more hydroneer approach could be being able to open a "bank account" for a large initial payment, then you can simply bring your giant stacks of money to the bank, and any shop will be able to subtract the money from the bank? That way we can have a single place to store/bring our coins, and there can be some transaction fee or something to make up for it?
- The roads need to be repaved lol

配管とコンベアといくつかの装置を使って採掘を自動化するゲーム
おまけ程度に農業と漁業もできる

自動化できるのは採掘作業の部分のみ
採掘した素材を組み合わせてクラフトする作業は手動でしかできない
なので複雑なラインを作る必要はない　というか非常にシンプルなものにならざるを得ない
ラインの美しさや効率化で頭をひねる余地はないので毎回同じものを作ることになる
やりこむとすればスピードランの方向

一度自動装置を完成させればお金はすぐに余るほど貯まる
しかしお金で買えるのは低Tierのアイテムのみで、高度な装置や乗り物の購入に必要なギルドコインはNPCの依頼を受けることでしか稼げない
各地にいるNPCに会いに行って依頼を受領→拠点に戻って依頼品を用意→またそのNPCのところに行って納品という流れを延々繰り返す

買い物の際も自分で店まで移動する必要がある
そして配管の1本・コンベアの1マスに至るまで、アイテムは1つずつ掴んで精算台に持っていって精算する必要がある
パレットやトラックを使ってある程度効率化はできるものの、一個ずつパレットに積む作業が生じるのでやはり時間と手間がかかる
どの形の配管がいくつ必要かなどは実際に作り始めてから気付くことも多く、そのたび店まで戻らなくてはならない

結果的に移動と買い物がプレイ時間の大部分を占めることになる
これがおすすめできない最大のポイント

DLCは新機構を追加した味変版といった趣
DLCエリアは完全に別個のマップであり、アイテムの持ち込み・持ち出し等一切できない
実質的に独立した別のゲームとしてプレイすることになる
こちらもラインは至ってシンプルであり頭を悩ませる余地はほぼない
水用配管・溶岩用配管・修理ツールが揃っている街がないので買い物のたびに複数の街を回る必要があったり
アイテム強化に使う岩がランダムスポーンだったり、それを使う場所に持っていく前に別の場所に行ってしばらく待つ必要があったり
むしろ移動時間を増やす方向に調整されている

総じて自動化ゲームというよりも単に作業ゲームの色が強い
そういうのをやりたい時には向いているが、但し書きなしにおすすめはできない

Ignoring for now all the other criticisms about the overall gameplay loop which may or may not have their own merits, once you enter the "late-game" full automation stage of the game, you'll be wrestling far more with the core engine limitations of the game than any actual system design challenges due to buggy optimizations of rigidbody physics (partly from Unreal Engine, partly from game design decisions directly), as well as how the developer seemingly refuses to fix such issues because it somehow means that you aren't playing the game in the correct way in their eyes, whichever way that is.


Now, putting it simply:
[b]The one thing stopping you from leaving ANY automated mining setup to run AFK is a bug that causes items to randomly freeze midair.[/b]

There doesn't seem to be a pattern to the occurrence of this bug, it's been around for years, and the only way to solve it reliably is to clear the block manually (some irony for an automation game). Leaving items to pile up on a stuck object will eventually crash the game, usually once you reach the tens of thousands of free rigidbodies range. This is related to an optimization which freezes objects that have been still for a while to avoid the need to calculate unnecessary physics for each of them, but it doesn't always seem to trigger at the right times, and is also semi-permanent - lasting until the object is manually picked up, or attracted by a logic magnet, regardless of other objects colliding with it.

Certain setups can reduce the rate at which such stuck objects occur, such as auto-cycling magnets, but they are not always reliable and can produce jams on their own as well.

Powering stuff in Hydroneer is "free". Hydro power is unlimited, but production machines eventually break down due to contaminants. You can however automate the repair process on each individual machine, or use water filters (which also break down but can be repaired in the same way). The most basic auto-repair filter setup which doesn't divert based on repair exhaustion can run an entire network of machines for 10-20 hours without any human intervention - if not for the fact that the items you are processing will crash the game.


On the other hand, let's take at the engine limitations of other popular automation games:

Factorio is extraordinarily stable without mods. Usually saves will break down due to UPS (updates per second) limitations because there are too many machines and conveyors running, but this just slows the game down and doesn't cause crashes unless you run out of memory. This can be alleviated with speed module beacons, which allow machines to run faster at the cost of increased power consumption, usually a minimal issue by the late game because solar power is very light on performance given the power grid just counts how many are plugged into the network at any given time. Combined, this makes the performance more than enough for even the most diehard factory planners.

In July 2023, a bug was [url=forums.factorio.com/107837]reported on the Factorio Forums[/url] where a save would stop working if it was running for 828 days total (slightly over 2 years), due to a 32-bit integer overflow for the game tick. This was [url=www.factorio.com/blog/post/fff-388]fixed for the 2.0 release[/url] by changing the tick integer to 64-bit, allowing for savefiles that run for 2+ million years.

Granted, Factorio runs on a custom C++ engine with excellent development practices and the support of an experienced and dedicated team, but the point still stands: Performance and optimization form a core part of sandbox games with no hard caps on the growth of player creations, which most automation games fall into. However, there is another game which is much more similar on a technical level, working with similar restraints on optimization capacity:

Satisfactory is another example which also happens to run on Unreal Engine. Here, conveyor logic runs separately from the actual rendering of items moving on top, which are represented by offsetting item mesh instances from the conveyor with data passed through the GPU every frame using a 2D texture, that has values representing the location and rotation of each item (with the texture size being a partial reason for why conveyors have a limited maximum length per segment; bit of further technical reading [url=drive.google.com/file/d/1JsAlduRg7-KV0jxEUjK-LLANwHUH7gRZ/view]here[/url]). With the combined effort of these optimizations, Satisfactory can afford global illumination casting shadows with hundreds if not thousands of moving conveyor items lit by dozens of individual light sources, assuming you have a powerful enough GPU.

One might say, "Well, Hydroneer has to always simulate each individual item as a rigidbody object, and rigidbody physics is CPU-bound! It can't benefit from the parallelism that GPUs offer."

The game really doesn't need to have physics enabled for every free object at all times. In fact, this is already a gameplay mechanic: "Container-like" objects such as pans, buckets, and vehicles deactivate objects on or inside them using the same optimization for objects dropped on the ground, but instead they are glued to the "container" object, allowing you to move items, machines, and piping without having everything flying out after you hit a small bump.

Just doing the same to conveyors would fix one of the largest outstanding, game-breaking bugs. Have conveyors deactivate objects dropped on top, offset it along the conveyor's direction at a static rate, and if the item would fall into the input of another machine, since everything is grid aligned - just have it follow a roughly correct preset trajectory with no physics simulation into the receptacle.

This change alone would probably fix a good 80-90% of crashes resulting from an overabundance of physics objects, since dirt and raw ore are only travelling as intermediate forms; once ore enters a crucible it's added as a value to the molten contents and removed from the world.

And what does the game give you right now to address this problem?

A checkmark, when loading a save, which deletes all loose dirt and ore in the save file.

This really is not rocket science.

Hydroneer takes the familiar satisfaction of digging for treasure and builds an entire engineering sandbox around it. Developed and published by Foulball Hangover, it begins with basic manual work before steadily opening into a much larger experience involving mining, machinery, automation, crafting, construction, farming, and exploration. There is no need for an elaborate storyline to keep things moving because the real motivation comes from watching a primitive mining operation gradually transform into an efficient industrial complex.

The opening hours deliberately make resources feel valuable. Digging dirt, processing material, collecting minerals, and selling the results require direct involvement, making every improvement feel useful rather than cosmetic. The terrain itself can be excavated, so players are not simply interacting with predetermined mining nodes. Pits, trenches, tunnels, and enormous excavation sites emerge naturally as the search for better resources continues. Deeper mining eventually encourages better equipment and more ambitious infrastructure, giving the progression a satisfying sense of physical scale.

Automation is where the experience becomes particularly compelling. Hydro-powered machinery can take over jobs that previously demanded repetitive manual labor, but getting everything working efficiently becomes a challenge of its own. Pipes need to supply water, machinery must be positioned properly, resources have to move through processing equipment, and the entire arrangement can be redesigned whenever a better solution becomes apparent. Building a working system is satisfying, but improving an inefficient one can be even more rewarding.

Construction provides plenty of freedom rather than pushing players toward one ideal layout. A mining site can remain relatively small and practical or expand into a sprawling collection of machines, pipes, storage areas, workshops, and buildings. The best moments often occur when several independent components finally work together as intended. Watching raw material travel through a system that was personally designed creates the kind of satisfaction normally associated with factory-building games, while the direct physical interaction keeps Hydroneer feeling more hands-on than a conventional management simulator.

Mining is not the only activity available. Valuable materials can be processed and used in crafting, including the production of jewellery and weapons. Farming and cooking add another economic activity, while fishing offers a quieter alternative when excavation and construction become exhausting. Vehicles and specialized equipment help with larger operations, transportation, and resource discovery. Multiple parcels of land also encourage expansion, giving players reasons to establish new operations and reconsider how their infrastructure should be organized.

The game's progression works particularly well because upgrades have visible consequences. Instead of merely increasing an abstract efficiency statistic, new equipment changes how the player actually works. A tedious manual process can eventually become automated, freeing time for construction, exploration, or another expansion project. This creates a strong cycle of earning money, purchasing better tools, improving production, discovering additional resources, and reinvesting the profits into an even larger operation.

Its physics-oriented design contributes plenty of personality, although it is also responsible for some frustration. Moving objects, arranging equipment, and dealing with large quantities of physical materials can occasionally feel awkward. Complex installations may require troubleshooting, and an apparently simple modification can sometimes turn into a larger reconstruction project. Players who demand extremely polished building controls may find these moments irritating. Those willing to experiment, however, may see the inconvenience as part of the challenge because solving practical problems is central to the experience.

Cooperative support adds another dimension by allowing mining and construction to become shared projects. Working together can make large operations more entertaining, particularly when responsibilities are divided between excavation, transportation, processing, construction, and general maintenance. Workshop support further expands the sandbox possibilities for players interested in community-created additions, while achievements provide optional objectives for anyone wanting more direction beyond the game's largely self-driven progression.

Visually, Hydroneer prioritizes readability and sandbox functionality rather than realism. Equipment is easy to distinguish, excavation visibly reshapes the environment, and a developed mining site becomes a physical record of the player's progress. There is something appealing about looking back at a once-empty piece of land after it has become covered with buildings, machinery, pipes, vehicles, and enormous holes. The transformation of the environment communicates advancement more effectively than a conventional level indicator could.

Steam Deck compatibility is currently listed as Playable rather than fully Verified. The game can therefore be used on Steam Deck, although some aspects of the experience may not meet every requirement associated with Valve's Verified classification. Given the amount of construction, object manipulation, inventory handling, and precision involved in larger facilities, players who prioritize maximum control convenience may still prefer a desktop setup.

Hydroneer ultimately works best for people who enjoy creating their own objectives. Its mixture of physical mining and increasingly elaborate automation provides a rewarding journey from shovel-level labor to industrial production. Some interactions can be cumbersome and the open-ended structure will not appeal equally to everyone, but the freedom to excavate, construct, automate, optimize, and rebuild gives the game impressive staying power. Few things are more satisfying here than standing beside a complicated mining operation and realizing that every pipe, machine, building, and production route exists because you decided how it should work.

Hra je v mnoha ohledech svérázná a netypická. Dokáže tak vtáhnout a fascinovat, ale zároveň i frustrovat a mnohé snadno odradit. 

Těžíte zeminu se ziskem kovů a šperků, které pak můžete dále formovat, zpracovávat a něco málo i vycraftit (opět velmi svérázně). Proces lze časem postupně vylepšovat a automatizovat.

Ale nyní k té svéráznosti. Kromě krátkého popisku předmětu, který aktuálně držíte ve hře neexistuje žádné UI, nemáte žádný hotbar, žádný inventář, žádna minimapa nebo velká mapa v menu mapu NIC.

Jediné co existuje jsou fyzické objekty ve světě s kterými můžete ručně manipulovat, a to vždy pěkně po jednom. Takže i ta mapa je samozřejmě objekt který musíte tahat sebou, použít, podívat se a pak zase do ruky něco jiného. Každý kousek základny, stěnu, okno, nářadí, pás, semínka, ... musíte v obchodě po jednom vložit na paletu, koupit (jak jinak než fyzickými mincemi, které taky všude sebou taháte), poté naložit na váš Hydrotruck (který díky bohu nemá na své korbě kolize a vy tak aspoň můžete naložit více než pár itemů, které by se jinak nevlezly), odvést k sobě na pozemek a všechno opět vyskládat, než to individuálně všechno někam přenesete / postavíte.

Pár základních věcí naštestí není daleko, ale i tak budete furt jezdit do města pro každou blbost co vám zrovna bude chybět. Tohle je frustrace ale i hlavní krása hry, která ale pravděpodobně není po každého.

Nejvíce mě ale frustrují dva konkrétní hlavní problémy, které se asi nikdy ani nevyřeší a opakují se stále dokola v herním loopu.
A) Pouze krátký neintuitivní a ne moc povedený tutoriál, který ale ani mnohé neřekne a bude stačit na prvních pár hodin hraní. Vše ostatní musíte zjištovat na internetu nebo se ptát AI... Přitom by stačila možnost si libovolný předmět vyhledat přímo ve hře v nápovědě tak, jako to mají všechny ostatní podobné hry

B) Často potřebujete položit předmět, který držíte v ruce, ale vertikální linie, po které padá dolů není uprostřed obrazovky, kam se díváte a kde je i vyznačený ingame kurzor (tečka uprostřed obrazovky). A tento problém je jen a jen horší na mém ultrawide monitoru. Ve dne má předmět alespoň malý kulatý stín, podle kterého jde vidět, kam přesně předmět dopadne, v noci nebo jindy ale vidět nebývá a vy tak opakujete proces kdy podíváte se přímo na předmět abyste ho sebrali, otočíte se doleva protože předmět má centr v právo nahoře obrazovky, pustíte a doufáte, že se trefíte. A když ne, tak znova.... Naprosto příšerný design mechaniky a nebo se nepočítalo, že existují i širší monitory než 16:9 (kde je to ale pravděpodobně taky off centr)

Takže takové craftění pak vypadá následovně. Vyberete si recept klikáním na kovadlinu. Zobrazí se který předmět máte kam hodit a pak už jen to nejhorší. Porovnat rozpečené ingoty správně po kovadlině. Tedy sebrat ingot, přesunout se a narotovat kameru tak aby tržený předmět vpravo nahoře obrazovky dopadl po puštění přesně na to místo co potřebujete, když svítí slunce, dá se to vidět dle stínu, ale jinak vám nezbývá než vždy sebrat, hodit, kouknout kam dopadl a podle toho upravit svoji polohu.... Nesmyslné, otravné a a celkově prostě a jednoduše debilní systém... A to doufejte že vám ty ingoty mezi tím nevystydnou.

Přesto bych hru spíše doporučil. Je to něco jiného a na pár hodin zabaví

From the lack of inventory, constant item clipping, terrible terrain management tools, completely jank progression setup, and the worst part by far has to be the currency that you have to PHYSICALLY HOLD and carry around with you while trying to buy items instead of simply having them in your inventory or a wallet, instead you have to constantly keep track of your currency and ensure you don't leave it somewhere which only gets worse by the fact there are TWO types of currency. 

I got this game because Crowmeda looked like he had fun even with the struggles, but this game feels impossible unless you're going to dedicate at LEAST 20 hours into just getting a base FUNCTIONING not even well adapted, just functioning to a degree where you can try to accomplish side objectives without babysitting your base every waking minute to ensure that something doesn't break or that ore isn't spilling out all over the ground because you can only pick up one item at a time and if by some unholy miracle you miss a bucket because there's no other way to store ore and gems in this game you have to pick up EACH peice of ore ONE AT A TIME! Оценка 3 из 10. Добро пожаловать в симулятор носильщика/грузчика.
Коротко о главном:
+++ Плюсы игры:
+1. Медитативная, спокойная, размеренная.
+2. Есть оптимизация.
Плюсов больше нет.

--- Минусы игры:
-1. Отвратительная прогрессия развития. По сути прогрессия развития практически отсутствует.
-2. Отвратительная игровая механика покупки/логистики предметов.
-3. Отвратительное обучение (по сути его нет). Отсутствуют вменяемые внутриигровые подсказки.
-4. Отвратительная механика техники (комбайн/гусеничный бур/прокладчик тунелей и пр.)
-5. Полностью отсутствует какой бы то ни было сюжет.
-6. Некрасивая графика, отвратительная работа с яркостью/контрастностью/светотенью.

= Лирика =
33 часа игры на момент написания обзора. Из этих 33 часов 15 потрачено на отвратительную механику покупки/переноски предметов. Разработчики приняли очень неудачное решение заставить игрока таскать руками каждый предмет для покупки на специальную платформу, а затем всё то же самое только с загрузкой предметов в грузовик для транспортировки, а затем ещё и по одному предмету размещать при строительстве (по идее можно вылечить, если играть в творческом режиме без достижений и пр.). И это ещё низкий поклон, за то, что убрали коллизию при загрузке предметов в грузовик, иначе 95% игры пришлось бы на логистику. Игра про строительство! Зачем?! Вернее за что, разработчики?! Что побудило вас заставлять игрока кучу времени тратить на скучную переноску предметов?! Хорошо, предположим вы пожелали "выпендриться" особой игровой механикой, так сделали бы возможность заказывать доставку нужных предметов прямо к строительным областям! А лучше сделали бы как в любой нормальной песочнице про строительство - инвентарь со стеками предметов! Правда в этом случае весь игровой контент закончился бы за 2 часа!

В игре всё очень плохо с прогрессией. Скорее даже не просто плохо, а отвратительно: существует всего только 3 вида развития игровых механизмов, при том, что в игре существует всего пара основных агрегатов: бур и дробила, всё остальное так, приложение. В итоге как только игрок накапливает хотя бы немного игровых денег, он сразу же покупает конвееры и полностью автоматизирует добычу полезных ископаемых, выстраивая единственно возможную оптимальную композиции игровой базы. В игру зачем-то добавили логику, комбинаторы, провода. Это всё бессмысленно из-за чудовищно малого количества контента. Производственная линия работает отлично и без логики (максимум только можно собрать примитивнейшую комбинацию для автоматического ремонта, задействовав лишь 15% предоставленных элементов программной логики).
Дополняет картину отвратительной прогрессии совершенно неуместная механика различных валют, при которых игрок не может купить самую продвинутую кирку/лопату, пока не пройдёт ряд бестолковых квестов, построенных на принципе "принеси мне вот это на столько-то цифирек". Так вот когда игрок уже может выполнять эти бестолковые поручения неписи, ему уже не нужно ничего из того, что он может купить за приобретаемую валюту.
И в довершение, тяжёлая техника типа комбайна, гусеничного бура, прокладчика туннелей покупается только за валюту. Мало того, что к моменту игры, когда игрок уже накопил нужную для покупки сумму эта техника уже полностью бесполезна, так ещё и сама техника ущербна чуть менее, чем полностью. К примеру, прокладчик туннелей не способен копать в горизонт, т.е. он всегда будет лажать и копать либо чуть ниже, либо чуть выше уровня горизонта или слоя почвы, из-за чего невозможно будет прокопать ровную площадку, остальная техника работает ещё хуже...

Как итог - очень жаль потраченного времени, 35 часов мучений в ожидании того, что игра вот-вот раскроет свой потенциал, может всё же "слюбится", но нет. Игра про строительство, добычу ресурсов и развитие, в которой строительство заканчивается за пол часа, а развитие отсутствует...
При таких негативных аспектах уже даже не мешают мелкие проблемы типа периодических провалов под текстуры и незначительные, но раздражающие баги с коллизией предметов...

This review is on the cusp of being a yes, but it surprises me that this game isn't marked as early access.

There are so many little things that are such a pain. Dropping items into the correct location (make sure to change the drop crosshair color) shouldn't be this annoying. It might collide with something above it, or it might bounce off something in your container. crouching probably won't help you either way.

Terrain manipulation sucks unless you're using squares like Minecraft. you're not cutting a smooth tunnel. Jumping out of the pits you make is a miserable experience. 

One part of the map has a lift, but there's no fall damage. There's no point in waiting. you can drive through the lake between the first plot and the main town because the water is ankle deep no matter where you go. 

I appreciate the gameplay loop, and will put more hours into it but there's something disapointing about the level of polish. It strikes me as a bit unfinished.

Игра о повторении одних и тех же действий, разнообразия в этих самых действиях очень мало. Возишься с рудой или рыбачишь, еще есть садоводство, но мне оно не интересно. Рыбалка очень скучна, нужно просто в любую точку воды кидать и кликать один раз, не важно в каком ты биоме или водоёме. При этом даже таймер поклёвки через одно и то же время. Нет ни рыбных точек, не тем более квик тайм ивентов. С рудой возиться чуть веселее, но строительство и развитие базы слишком затянуто. Учитывая что заработать быстро можно только на рыбалке, это придется делать часами реального времени, и я не преувеличиваю. Эта игра очень быстро начинает утомлять. Мир очень пустой, кроме торговцев для развития шахты, рыбалки и садоводства больше ничего нет. И всё настолько скудно тут, что даже у нпс набор фраз только из трех вариантов. А музыка в этой игре очень спокойная и расслабляющая, что усиливает эффект сонливости и вызывает желание удалить игру и больше не возвращаться в неё.

🔧 Gameplay Mechanics
In Hydroneer, players start with basic tools and must dig, pan, and refine resources to earn money. The absence of an inventory system means that every item must be physically carried and placed, adding a layer of realism and challenge. As players progress, they can automate processes, build complex machinery, and expand their operations. The game also features a variety of vehicles and machinery to assist in resource gathering and transportation. 
pcgamer.com

🎮 Visuals and Performance
Hydroneer boasts a stylized, voxel-based art style that is both charming and functional. The game's environments are richly detailed, with dynamic weather and day-night cycles that enhance immersion. However, some players have reported performance issues, particularly in larger bases or when using complex machinery. These issues can affect the overall experience, especially for those with lower-end hardware.

🧭 Learning Curve and Accessibility
The game does not hold the player's hand, which can be both a strength and a weakness. While some players appreciate the freedom and challenge, others find the lack of guidance overwhelming. The initial stages can feel slow and repetitive, but the satisfaction of building efficient systems and seeing progress can be rewarding.

🧩 Multiplayer and Updates
Recent updates have introduced multiplayer support, allowing players to collaborate on projects. The game has also received several expansions and updates, adding new areas, mechanics, and content to keep the experience fresh.

✅ Final Verdict
Pros:

Unique gameplay mechanics with manual item handling

Deep resource management and automation systems

Charming art style and immersive environments

The game doesn’t really have any clear objectives. Once you figure out how everything works, it hits you that you’re basically just grinding to get better tools so you can dig deeper... just to get even better tools. That’s pretty much the loop.

It works better as a sandbox, but even then it has issues. Leveling terrain to build is frustrating. There's a roller vehicle that's supposed to flatten the ground, but it doesn’t line up with the build grid. If you want anything to look neat, you have to use a hoe and flatten one tile at a time. It’s honestly one of the most annoying building systems I’ve used in an automation game.

There are mods that help with this, which seemed like a good fix. The problem is that enabling mods disables achievements. The game can auto-save before you realize that, which is a bit of a trap. At that point, your only options are starting over, using a third-party tool to get achievements back, or just not caring about them.

The best parts of this game revolve around its building systems - conveyors, water piping, and logic/automation. It does take hours of repetitive grinding to get a decent automation system going, but once you do you'll be making money as fast as you can spend it. And it feels satisfying to see it all at work.

The low point is the repetition. Digging by hand (before automation) is tedious. Building is fun, interacting with materials one by one over and over is not, especially when shopping or setting up a new area. The lack of any bulk grab or blueprint system is frustrating.

The lack of anything driving the game - no enemies or failure conditions etc. - is something some people will love and others will find increases the dullness.

It's a solid game if you love building small scale systems with no pressure and you don't mind (or even enjoy) repetitive grind. Otherwise skip it.

I had a hard time trying to decide how to rate this game. I did sort of enjoy it and I put a lot of hours into it, but I couldn't help but feel like the core gameplay style was flawed. It's a game that's hard to like. It's an okay game if you've run out of simulation or factory automation games and need something more. But for everyone else, I would pass.

For me, the core flaw is that the gameplay is small. I don't mean the size of the world, I mean the way you play. It's very manual and very much one where you do things one item at a time. In most automation games, you would buy or build a bunch of conveyor belts and then click and drag to place a whole line of them down. Not in this game. You have to do everything one segment at a time.

You have to go to the store and pick up each segment of a belt one at a time, put them into a cart, buy them and drive them to the mine. Then again, one at a time, you have to place each belt segment. Actually, it's double that because the belts all run on water power so you have to place the water pipes first, one at a time.

If you decide you need a corner piece, you have to get into the truck, drive to the store, pick up the corner piece, drop in on to the purchase shelf, drop your coins in the bucket, purchase the piece, pick up your coins, pick up the belt and put it into the truck, drive the truck back to the mine, and then you can place it. All that for one piece of your belt. Oh, and if you forget to pick up your money, you have to go back for it.

The result is that all the automation in the game amounts to building a scaffold of belts to get resources from out of a mine and then a short belt to process and filter the output. And it takes a lot of work to do that. You won't be building any sprawling factories.

Hydroneer — симулятор брудного бізнесу для тих, у кого на душі теж трохи багнюки

Якщо ти завжди мріяв копати яму на городі, але сусіди викликають поліцію за кожну лопату — Hydroneer для тебе. Це гра, де ти можеш безкарно рити землю, будувати гігантські труби, і потім ще й радіти, коли випаде шматок золота розміром з мозок розробника гри.

Починаєш як безхатченко з каструлею, який миє багнюку в надії знайти щось цінне. І от уже за кілька годин ти інженер-гірник, з системою автоматичних бурів, насосів і труб, що працюють краще, ніж водопостачання в деяких районах.

Графіка — казкова. В сенсі, казка про трьох поросят, де всі будують з багна. Але має свій шарм: краще копати цю землю, ніж свою яму на дні життя. Музики майже нема, але навіщо вона тобі, якщо твій мозок вже співає «шурш-шурш» від звуків води та металу?

Фізика в грі особлива. Якщо ти випадково кинеш лопату, вона може відскочити через всю мапу й убити твою самооцінку. Але й у цьому є шарм — якесь відчуття, що всесвіт тебе не любить, але дає копати далі.

Сюжет? Та ти шо, який ще сюжет? Тут твоя мета — стати багатим або хоча б не здохнути з голоду, продаючи самородки розміром з яйце динозавра за копійки. Це економіка нового рівня: більше копаєш — більше втомлюєшся — більше питаєш себе, чому не пішов на ІТ.

I think the game has a great concept but I can't recommend it because it's massively frustrating to play.

You can only hold one thing at a time so you will frequently be picking things up and dropping them. Moving ore into a pan requires pressing E on each individual ore, and then pressing E to drop the ore in the pan - you will be doing this likely tens of times for each panful and it ends up being uncomfortable, and for me - painful. The indicator for where items drops is difficult and finicky - some players say this gets easier to work around with time but I still find it annoying and difficult in a frustrating way.


The lack of an inventory or hotbar for tools is a deliberate design to create challenge - you are meant to manage what you carry and use carts/vehicles to move things around. This is good design for moving things around the map, but when you're fighting against your keyboard, hands, and game physics to move things a matter of meters from the furnace to an anvil, the floor into a pan, etc, it is frustrating and bad gameplay - there is no challenge here, just slow, methodical, repetitive movements. I think it would have been cool if you had a hotbar usable within your plot to make building, digging, and processing easier.


I found building in the game to be very difficult. Structures like drills have specific ports for connecting to water, this is fine and forces you to build structures in specific set ups. Pipes have limited configurations (straight sections, bends, and T shapes) and this also creates challenge. This is all fine and is expected, the issue then is that the act of building is highly frustrating in what I've played. You have to buy each individual pipe, concrete block, etc, in the shop by moving the individual piece into the buying spot, then moving it to your cart, then to your base. This has the same issue as moving items in that it's difficult to move items in any quantity and the process is designed to create repetitive busy work - this is especially bad when buying concrete blocks since they're so big that it's difficult to place more than a couple in the buying spot.

Once you've bought the pieces you'll need to place them - this can be fine but if you have to dig out dirt then you'll struggle with getting stuck in holes and trying to move up any steep gradient. You'll also struggle trying to tell how much space you need to dig to place a given structure/pipe. You'll frequently dig some space with a pickaxe, drop the pickaxe, pick up the pipe, try to place it but there's not enough empty space around the location you're trying to place the pipe so you drop the pipe, pick up the pickaxe, mine a bit more, etc. For me building my first drill setup was immensely frustrating because of this, but it was made so much worse by digging out a space and then realising that some of the space I was working with couldn't be mined since it was at the edge of my plot - the walls of which curve inward as you dig down. I felt like I was fighting against the game.


The quest system seems like it could be good but it is not at all friendly to newcomers. People will ask for things which you can't do at the start of the game - for example request you make them tomato soup, and there's no explanation of how to do those things so you'll have to look it up and realise that the quests the NPCs at the starting area give can't be completed for quite a while. They'll also ask for items to be made with specific weights of metal - sounds fine but how do you know how much a tool will weigh before you build it? Scales are available at a different town's shop and there is no mention of this in-game. You can see the weight of the tools you make when you pick them up, but you can't see the weight of the ingots you forge without buying scales so without knowing about the scale item you're semi-blindly trying to fulfil the conditions of the quest. I wrongly assumed that if someone wanted a dagger with 200 weight of gold that it maybe meant 20 pieces of gold ore, looking at Steam discussions I know other players have had the same issue. The inconsistency of when your character can tell weights is weird.


I wish the game was just a bit easier. Having a hotbar so I could immediately switch between a tool like the pickaxe or shovel and structures like pipes wouldn’t really make the game less challenging, but would make it more accessible and make it much easier to play. It would be much less frustrating. As it is, building was not fun. In a game like factorio it’s incredibly easy to build a layout of machines, realise they don’t work and tear them down - in Hydroneer that process takes a long time and requires lots of walking back and forth, finding space to drop items in an orderly way, picking up a tool, and repetition. In Minecraft everything is a uniform size so it’s always clear when you can place something - in Hydroneer it’s a process of guesswork and then trial and error whether you’ve successfully mined out space for your building. In most other games like this building is fun, but here I was left frustrated and put off from playing. Perhaps this gets easier once you’ve acquired better gear, etc, but the experience as a new player seems really poor.

I want to recommend this game, I really want to, but even though I've had some enjoyment out of it I have to acknowledge that the game deliberately wastes the player's time. There are so many design features that make you perform mundane tasks over and over, for example: If you want to buy anything from a shop, you have to pick up the item, carry it to the payment pallet, drop it on there (making sure it doesn't roll off), then repeat that for all the other items you want, then drop your coins into the bucket, hit the button to pay, then load all of your purchases into your truck ONE AT A TIME, then drive off. Of course forgetting to retrieve your money from the bucket and having to travel back there to get it back.

I get the idea of having every item be a physical object in the word, but only allowing the player to carry one item at a time makes things so infuriatingly tedious. Sure it encourages you to automate your mining operation, but there are so many task you're required to do that can't be automated, like forging items requested by villagers. If you're asked for a dagger made of 50.5 weight iron, you can't just smelt a 50.5 iron bar and forge it, you have to smelt a 50 weight bar and a 1 weight bar, cut the 1 into 2 0.5, smelt the 50 and 0.5 together, THEN forge the dagger. And with other items requiring multiple bars to forge, soon you're just performing busy work over and over to meet ordinary tasks to earn enough cash/tokens to buy larger mining gear. And what does it add to the playing experience that money/tokens are a physical object in the world? Why can't you just have a wallet that the money/tokens are in so you don't have to worry about it? It would be a minor addition and save so much hassle. But no, the rigid adherence to the design philosophy that the player can only carry one item at a time just makes the game tedious.

The annoying thing is I do like the parts of the game where you can build your mining operation, planning out how the machines and conveyor belts are going to be laid out, There's a huge amount of satisfaction watching your factory run, drilling, processing sorting, smelting the various materials, it's all great but it's buried under so much tedium.

Another example of the game not respecting the player's time are forge marks. These are found in blocks of ice scattered around the DLC island. You need to use the lava hauler truck to pick them up and transport them over to the Shattered Outpost (usually on the other side of the island to where you found the mark). There you need to load the block onto a giant lava grid to melt it. In real time. You have to stand there and wait for several minutes while the ice melts to reveal the mark. After which you can then add that into a forging recipe when making new equipment. Already time consuming, it then turns out you only learn what bonus the mark gives AFTER you've forged the machine. Oh, and it can also add a penalty, not a bonus. So after all that work you could end up with a near-useless machine that took you several hours' worth of play time to assemble.

WHY? WHY WOULD YOU DO THIS?

I recently gave it another go, and while I got a little further into it this time, I was pretty disgusted with it by the end. This was after the experience of setting up a new dig site in the Icehelm mine, which I think must be the absolute worst place in the entire game to operate. It takes forever to get between the mine area and your vehicle, and there is no way to bring things like vehicles or carts anywhere near the site. Instead, they give you a conveyor/teleporter you can use to send things up or down, but it is implemented very, very poorly.

When I sat and thought about it, I realized just how horribly tedious the process was. I needed to buy hundreds of items to place, and if I wanted to avoid dozens of unnecessary trips in the truck with awful handling on narrow roads filled with obstacles and uneven terrain, I had to figure out and remember exactly what I'd need in advance and get it all in one trip--at broken low FPS because even though the game turns off collisions between items in your truck bed, it's still apparently doing some kind of useless collision detection calculations between them all.

Every single item required me to individually pick it up, move to buy platform, place it. Once the platform is full, buy, then pick each thing up again, move to truck, place it. And do that on repeat until I have everything I need. Then take it back to Icehelm and the real "fun" begins. Pick up each piece of crap again again and place it on the conveyor, and it creates a glitched out, unstable garbage mountain at the bottom of Icehelm. The items are all interlocking, and the physics engine goes bananas, dropping FPS to 0.05 to 1.00 for minutes at a time before things (usually) settle on their own. Or crash. But each time you pick up another item (again again again) from Mt. Trashheap in order to place it where you actually need it, reality breaks down again as chaotic clusters of trash jerkily float around the room and FPS drops to virtually nothing until the physics finally stabilize. Again and again and again and again and again and again and again until you finally get your base set up and all the trash clusters are gone. Which you cannot accomplish until you mine out a solid wall of dirt by hand, because you can't get vehicles in there and there is no dirt surface or room to place everything until you dig.

All in all, it was one of the biggest wastes of my time I've ever experienced in a game, and looking back, it's kind of nauseating that I actually subjected myself to it. It's hours of valuable time off work that I'll never get back, and the worst part is that nothing about it was a novel experience. I didn't need to do anything different than I did at the starting dig site apart from trash chaos mountain, digging out the whole area by hand, and frustrating transit times to/from the truck. The actual pieces I used and how they fit together were--in all meaningful ways--exactly the same as they were at Ember Cradle.

This is game feels very unfinished. It has many ideas implemented that seem interesting when described casually, but when you look at how they have been implemented, it quickly becomes clear that it all comes down to slow tedium. And this is from someone who deeply enjoys Factorio, Satisfactory, even Dwarf Fortress.

The main issue is the limitation of only allowing you to handle a single item at a time, combined with a very clunky control scheme. An important secondary issue is that there is nothing in the game to motivate you to do anything, other than making enough money to do some of the other things for which there is no reason other than making more money to... you get it.

In Factorio, you want to build the rocket, and there's joy in scaling up. In Satisfactory, you want to know what the company really wants from you and what's at the end of the last tier on the space elevator. In Dwarf Fortress every playthrough kills you with something weird and you feel like you just had a unique playthrough. But in Hydroneer, all the stuff sits there in sterile stores, waiting for you and only you to buy it with money that's no good for anything else - it's pointless tedium.

Too bad, because a lot of work clearly went into making this, and it's somewhat interesting that everything is subject to physics. It's definitely unique, but I simply can't bring myself to keep playing - and from what I see from others that have played for longer, it doesn't improve.

O jogo tem uma mecânica relaxante e até prazerosa. Mas tem um problema de otimização que quebra a mecânica principal dele. Quando muitos recursos começam a se acumular, o jogo não demora a ficar pesado até o ponto de crashar e fechar. Esse problema não permite que vc jogue ao estilo "fabricação industrial de larga escala", ele simplesmente não aguenta a quantidade de recursos. Você pode até jogar mais de boa, low profile, lidando com poucos recursos, mas logo esse problema aparece pois é comum recursos ficarem enroscados em funis ou separadores e começam a se acumular. Vc saí pra dar uma volta, e quando você retorna, ha muitos recursos acumulados, enroscados, e o jogo estará travando. O pior é que o jogo se rende ao problema e apresenta uma opção de "limpar objetos do mundo", que quando vc aciona, apaga tudo que está solto por aí, isso destrava o jogo, mas joga fora uma quantidade imensa de recursos que estavam enroscados. É uma pena, pois tinha potencial pra ser um bom jogo, mas é inviável de seguir por muito tempo, vc se cansa de ver esse problema acontecendo.
Outro ponto é que o multiplayer infelizmente é apenas Remote Play e não funciona direito, os controles do jogador remoto não funcionam, e quando funcionam, logo param de responder.

やる事なすこと全部面倒な作業を徐々に自動化させるもやっぱり面倒臭い。

後半パイプを１００単位で使うのに１つずつしか買えなくて禿げそう。
荷車に荷物を置けば当たり判定がなくなり積み重ねることができる。
大量のアイテムを管理するなら荷車とトラックが複数必要。

自動化において絶対にしないといけないのはコンベアと採取機、溶鉱炉の固定（建築ハンマーで）。
不定期に起こるラインの詰まりを解消するはずがラインの撤去という暴挙になり土や鉱物が周りに撒き散らされることになる。

自動化が終わってお金に困らなくなったと一安心してると別通貨じゃないと買えないエンドコンテンツの足掛かりになるアイテムが必要で禿げる。

農業の方が恐ろしく面倒で改善できる頃には農業しなくても良くなってて禿げた。

一通り済んだのでDLCを始めてみたが持ち込み一切不可の最初からやり直し状態。
初期の資金源の釣りもできない＆整地ツールも無い面倒臭さが更に強化されている。

最初にお使いクエをして資金を調達し、青く光る膜で覆われた町で溶岩パイプと採取機、鉱石や宝石等の分別用の皿と宝飾品まで加工できるツール一式を買い揃えて一番最初におつかいした場所で鉱石採掘する。
ある程度鉱石を貯めたら宝飾品に加工して膜の町でTIER１の箱を購入し、町内の空き地に設置し、資材を納品する事で店ができる。
店を完成させる事で採掘機の型と整地ツール一式がようやく手に入れれるようになる。

コンベアを動かすには氷を溶かして水を供給する装置が必要で溶岩ドリルが掘る場所が悪いと出てくるアイスロックは水にできない。（表層の雪の上ならアイスロックは今のとこ出てこない）
深場の方がコンベアの速度が速いからと欲張ると酷い目に会う。

（溶岩ドリル+アイスメルター）+（溶岩ドリル+収穫期）でDLCの初期自動化ができたらお金を稼ぎつつ溶岩フィルターロックを５つ配管に付けて機械を故障しないようにする。
（アイスメルターで作った水は溶岩を止めても作った水が無くなるまで動き続けるため目詰まりが余計に酷い事になる。）
フィルターを付け終わったら初期採掘所の最下層まで掘り進め自動化でクロウチウムが掘れるようにする。
金属バーや宝石を加工して売ったお金でハードストーンリファイナーと鉱石分別、宝石分別、精錬所、自動研磨、宝石圧縮の順に自動化をしていく。

水供給用に溶岩ドリル×２、採掘用に溶岩ドリル×１０を稼働し終わったらもうお金に困ってないはずなのであたらしい採掘地を買う。
（お勧めはWATERSIDE　コンベアの町と膜の町の中間位にあって溶岩突っ切ると物凄く近い）

新規で採掘地を購入したら船のチケット屋を購入し建て膜の町の住民に指輪や鉱石などを食わせて２００ギルドコインを貯めチケットを買い、船に乗って溶岩ローラーを買いに行く。
次にＴＩＥＲⅡの整地ツールを買い揃え、ローラーで整地→整地ツールで掘り下げを繰り返し掘れるところまで雪を全部取り除きながら掘れるとこまで掘り下げ自動採掘化させコアストーンを集める。
自動採掘できるようになったら初期採掘地の稼働を止めて溶岩ドリルを移設し20機くらいで採掘する。
その間にギルドコインを貯め重いドリルと収穫機の型を購入し、溶岩ホーラーと溶岩解凍機+溶岩解凍ブースター×２かＴＩＥＲⅢの整地ツール一式のどちらかを用意する。

重い収穫機は3×３×４、重い溶岩ドリルは2×2×５と大きく人力では動かせないので溶岩ホーラーで移動させる。
（荷台に乗せると当たり判定が無くなるので複数乗せれる）
（設置する時は地面ギリギリまで降ろしてから置かないと地面にめり込んで配管が繋がらない）

やった感じだと重い溶岩ドリルは自体がデカすぎるのと設置に使う溶岩ホーラーもデカいので思った以上に設置できないのと最下層でも初期の溶岩ドリルで掘れるので無理して使う必要性が今のところない。

developer_response:
Hey there! Sorry you're experiencing problems with performance.

Firstly, I think its a bit unfair to compare us to games such as Satisfactory - Hydroneer is built with a team of 4 people, which is a huge difference to the hundreds that work(ed) on Satisfactory.
To clarify, Hydroneer is not dead, it's finished. We are still supporting it with bug fixes and patches - last month we actually fixed a pretty large bug that's been around for a while.

If you're struggling with performance, it may be due to having lots of resources in the world. Hydroneer allows the player to be limitless with the amount of resources they can spawn, which is fun but on the downside can lead to bad performance if there's too many items in the world. Try using the 'Clear Raw Resources' and 'Clear Dirt Chunks' buttons in the esc menu. They'll clear up the resources and bring you back to better performance. Hope that helps!

Please consider updating your review if this has been useful, we're a small team and reviews mean a lot to us, thanks!

I have Windows 11 Pro x64, AMD Ryzen 7 5700X3d 8 Core Processor, 32 GBs RAM and a AMD Radeon RX 7600 XT. I mention my hardware specs because the moment you make more than 12 miners and any amount of mined dirt builds up on your conveyor belts the game becomes unplayable and drops to about 5 frames a minute. When I check Task Manager it is hardly utilizing my CPU or RAM. developer_response:
Hey there! Sorry you're experiencing problems with performance.

The game isn't utilizing your CPU or RAM for certain options because that's not really how things work. Hydroneer mainly uses the GPU as the processes involved are GPU dependent (like rendering graphical elements). These operations can't be dumped onto the RAM because the RAM isn't used for rendering.

If you're struggling with performance, it may be due to having lots of resources in the world. Hydroneer allows the player to be limitless with the amount of resources they can spawn, which is fun but on the downside can lead to bad performance if there's too many items in the world. Try using the 'Clear Raw Resources' and 'Clear Dirt Chunks' buttons in the esc menu. They'll clear up the resources and bring you back to better performance. Hope that helps!

Please consider updating your review if this has been useful, we're a small team and reviews mean a lot to us, thanks!

On very rare occasions Hydroneers save files can be corrupted. This generally happens when someone closes the game while it is saving. We’ve added in measures to prevent this from corrupting but there are some outlying cases. 
We have also noticed that some anti-virus programs prevent Hydroneer from saving. Please list Hydroneer as an accepted program or consider disabling your anti-virus programs. (Windows Defender is fine, but other AV programs can have this issue)
We also have added in ‘backup’ saves to prevent total data loss. Try finding this backup, by opening up the game, pressing ‘continue’ on the main menu, then ticking the ‘Show Backup’ box. This will show a backup save file which hopefully won’t be corrupted.

If you’d like any more help with this or another issue, you can reach out to us by email: support@foulballhangover.com. If this has resolved your issue please consider updating your review. We’re a small team and reviews really help us out, thanks!
