I REALLY LIKE THIS GAME! It can be fun and its great to lose yourself in.

However, optimization, control precision, and design choices seem pretty bad. And the lack of content. Unless your a masochist, beyond elden ring masochism, I wont recommend this game.

TLDR 
Pro, Its a fun game when working, has nice graphics and flavor. Has some interesting options. 
CON'S shoddy aiming even though your expected to be precise and even when you are precise it may all go horribly wrong, No inventory and can only carry one thing at a time. Impossible to optimize unless they change one of the mechanics of the game, and they won't. Lack of ACTUAL content. If your going to have a mining and crafting game, then you need more then 14 recipes with only 3 usable by you at any 1 time and more then 4 metals, gems, and power crystals to mine. Which you can get all of the resources with your pan shovel and scrub brush. Mining really has only 1 goal. Get a auto mine and smelting setup and then its done. 5 miners, 1 crusher, 5 smelters and some gem sorting. Water pipes, pressure increase and conveyor belts is all you need to get stupid rich and able to make anything. Which most of the time you don't need.
END TLDR

First, optimization. There is none. The game specializes in having tons of tiny chunks of resources laying about. And it can't handle it. They could have made it so that multiple chunks of the same type merge when placed together like the money does. This single action would fix the biggest cause of lag. I left a couple drills running for about 5 minutes. When I got back, the pan had a good amount of resources all ready to go. Until I picked up the pan and got a slide show of 1 frame per 5 seconds. Quality. Later game you can mostly deal with this by using sorters compressors and auto smelters. Can just conveyor belt it all around with no problems, but since the whole point is to start pan mining and to work your way up, that's not a possibility for quite a while. And you will be handling thousands of chunks well before you can stream line it. They did do something with chunks attached to surfaces like pans though. Well, until you pick up the pan. Speaking of the pan, you will mess up at some point and spray hundreds of chunks all over the ground making a huge mess. Which leads to my next point.

Number 2. Precision controls. There are none. Have you ever wondered what it would feel like to have a prosthetic arm thats fully extended at all times forward and to the right and the only way to release the items is from 4 feet up at that exact angle despite where your looking or whether you look up or down? Ever wonder what it would be like to try and place things  carefully with no actual aiming mechanic? Well, you will find out soon. Not to mention, all you get is a small shadow to show where it 'should' go. If your looking at your feet you might see it. Sometimes. Just not what you need precision for. Like pouring a pan of ore into a smelter because you can't see the shadow in the pot. Oh well, 300 gold nuggets spray all over the place as you slightly misjudge and it hits the rim and flies everywhere around you. No big deal. Pick each piece up and try to do the same thing again, with every single piece. 1 AT A TIME. WTF. I suppose there is a 'easier' way. There is a magnet on a stick. Of course, any sudden movements, moving forward, turning, jumping, all of that can cause disaster with your telekinetic floating blob of hate inducing disaster in the making.

Number 3 Design decisions. So the god awful aiming mechanics, the fact that no matter how big or small something is, you can only carry one at a time. Walking simulator whenever you go shopping. Sometimes you can ferry stuff around with a vehicles. Not always. This deep underground forge/store/mining location does not have room for vehicles. The shop is 5 floors... ish from the place you can mine. Even with virtually unlimited money it takes FOREVER to ferry everything from the shop to your work station. To automate 1 miner to a smelter (which would leave you a ton of resources just sitting somewhere, takes well over a hour of walking back and forth. And thats with me walking out the shop, throwing it all over a cliff edge towards my mine. And then jumping over the edge myself so i can start running them all to the next room with my mine and setting everything up. You will do so much pacing back and forth that you will become tired and turn the game off even though you have not physically done any of the walking. Your a blacksmith and miner... and farmer. You create up to 5 items that you can't use. Dagger, axe, sword, ring, and necklace. Those are for missions or money. For yourself, you can make 9 things. Only and they are really only 3 with 3 tiers. Miner, Crusher, and a water pressure increase item. Even though pipes and other items are made out of the different resources, you can't make them. And since you can have unlimited money quick with just the tier 1 items I don't even see the point. Even the late game stuff is just weird ways of doing old things. Often more complicated and less useful in my opinion. Then we have farming and cooking. I have not done much with farming and cooking. Realized it was more busy work and lost interest for now. Dig hole, Plant seed, drop pan in water cause you can't scoop it up. chase it down and go pour the WHOLE PAN OF WATER on 1 plant. Repeat for every plant you want to water. Woo. There may be better tools but they are locked behind special currency that you can only get from farming hundreds of tomatoes because everyone wants a small bowl of tomato soup. Small bowl = small reward. Which means not enough currency to buy stuff unless you grind. 

There is so many design decisions that blemish this game, yet, if they were removed, the game would become start to end maybe a hour if they fixed it. So they left it. Instead of content, the game was built around tedious poor control mechanics. I mean, every NPC says basically 2 lines. 'Ey up lad', and 'I need a bit of scram'. There is a few other phrases but thats the jist of it. There is no survival or fighting mechanics. So it lives on its mining and self made experiences and construction.

Oh... Construction. Every survival game or even other primarily crafting games get construction better. You can't pull items in or push them away when trying to place them. You can't push a button to snap to points, like pipes snapping to the end of other pipes. You cant even choose to raise or lower items. And everything is picked up with the same button. You pick up and drop items with E. Thats for resources dropped on the ground, or if you miss, the floor under them. Until you buy a construction hammer, a tiny misclick can cause massive problems. Remember, you cant raise, lower, recess, pull in or push out the placement of a item. You have to move. Carefully place a block, place other things around it, accidentally click it, and you may never get it back in place.


All that said, I enjoy the game when its not making me go bald. I like calm simple games sometimes. This has a beautiful world, graphics and some great animations and play options. And I know there is more for me to see and do. But, its impossible to look past the MANY flaws. I will continue to play. I have gotten better at the shoddy controls, but every time there is a unexpected resource explosion I like the game a little bit less. I don't recommend the game, because I don't want people to suffer such bad mechanics. Unless your a masochist. Honestly. I get more upset when resources go flying then I do in elden ring after my 20th death to the same boss.

Sometimes keybindings can bug out and need to be hard reset. To do this.

- Close the game
- Open the Run prompt by holding the WINDOWS key and pressing R.

%localappdata%\Mining\Saved\Config\WindowsNoEditor
- Delete the 'input.ini' file and relaunch the game.

Hydroneer is a sandbox game where you, a simple engineer in a pseudo-medieval world, must harness the power of water to make your fortune. Run pipes from the nearby river into your quarry to power mining equipment. Grab a fishing rod and earn coins selling buckets of herring and prawns. Use watering cans and sprinklers to grow a vegetable garden to feed the citizenry. Hop in your water-powered truck and go joyriding around the island, running into NPCs and sending them flying with a satisfying *thump*.

The game isn't without flaws. In the 20+ hours I've played, I've experienced one hard crash and several bugs like vanishing ore and extreme framerate drop, though most issues have been resolved by saving and reloading. As the game is still in early access as of this review, these are to be expected and hopefully will be resolved by release. Overall, it's been a good time.

From a programming perspective, I am truly amazed at how the developers managed to create such advanced physics in this addictive and time-consuming automation game. Although there are some issues such as peculiar bugs, imbalanced gameplay, and lack of progression, the game is still quite enjoyable and user-friendly. The integration of the Steam workshop is a great feature, and the mods created by some talented developers are definitely worth trying out.

I strongly recommend this game due to the exceptional value it offers at its price point, surpassing the quality that is typically expected. Furthermore, the developers have been diligent in adding new features to the game. While there are some aspects where the game feels incomplete, it is best observed through gameplay rather than described. Fortunately, there are excellent creators who have made videos about the game that can help form your opinion.

Although the game could use some improvements, such as adding multiplayer instead of just remote play split-screen, as well as further customization and progression, it is still a fantastic game as it is.

It's pretty hard to recommend Hydroneer.  Once you get over the novelty of the interface you have kind of done and seen everything the game has to offer.  Yes, you *could* then proceed to build some large scale mining or farming operation or whatever but I don't see why you would.  That's kind of the issue here: there doesn't seem to be a reason to *do* anything.  I guess that isn't, in itself, a problem but check the store page: craft weapons?  It feels very deceptive.  It's true, but only in that its a list of "things that are in the game."  There are weapons and jewelry in the game, but there isn't say, equipment or combat.  Yes there is farming and cooking fixtures, but again, there isn't anything *else*.  Food, like weapons, is just a thing you can sell.  You might be tempted to think these features lead somewhere, but they do not.

It honestly plays a lot like a first gen VR game where the novelty of using your actual hands is supposed to make you ignore that the game isn't going anywhere.  I think this has some merits, contrary to complaints, as the unique control scheme is kind of what the game has going for it.  Remove that and you have any number of other games on Steam.  Even so, I had to double check Hydroneer wasn't actually in early access because it definitely *feels* unfinished.  For example, there's a little indicator that shows where something will drop but it's like... what everyone will want is to point where they'd like to put something down.  That this game has been out for two years and the best it can offer is an alternative precision mode that doesn't work ... well, I gave it seven hours but I would kind of like that time back.

I'm not sure who this game is for, but I can say for sure it wasn't for me.

Ways to improve the game

1: A inventory system.

DEAR GODS you can't even pocket your money?  That is unbelievable and immersion breaking somehow?  Okay so you dont want someone carrying an anvil around in the same slot that a much smaller item would go into on a toolbar, how do we deal with this?
.
..
...
TADA: In Game Backpacks and classifying each object already in game with a size and mass category.  The backpack would only be able to hold so much mass and within that mass, it also would have a size limit.  BUT WAIT, THERE'S MORE!  Different kinds of backpacks.  Farmers Pack which is meant to hold onto a TON of seeds, harvested crops and the like and possibly even upgradable via quests!  A Market Pack whose entire purpose is to bring raw materials or processed materials to the market.  Lots of Small space to fill up.  Then of course the Hauler Pack which would allow a person to carrying one additional Large item.

"But wait!" I hear someone cry out "Thats alot of material to go back and add an extra couple of tags to, the author is clearly working on upgrading the game as it is, get off their back!"  Its really not, but for those of you who don't understand how easy it is to mass add tags to groups of in-game objects, we could go with something else that would add some QoL.

A Purchase Mule at the front of each Plot.  This mule can be an actual donkey, a person or just a cart, but the entire point would be that it has a catelogue of all the things being sold in the game that you have access too, and for a small fee and a tiny bit of time-cooldown, this Mule could let you buy and then deliver objects to the plot you are working on.  This isn't game breaking and could easily be tweaked about, with its own Guild whose quests can be done to upgrade the speed and decrease the delivery cost.

AT THE VERY LEAST THOUGH
If nothing else gets added, if NOTHING else gets added.
PLEASE add a money pouch.  Having to run around with our arms stuck out infront of us holding our money infront of us like some kind  of subway goblin with a pile of Shiny Things they found.  The character wears clothing, it has pockets.  One can be sewn on if need be, its not that hard.  IRL I have crap sewing skills and I could easily make a ♥♥♥♥-job-pouch to hold a few coins at least.

*Sigh* and no, stacking a bunch of ♥♥♥♥ up in a bucket so that it literally stacks and goes static doesn't count as a inventory system.  It counts as a unintended side-effect glitch.  You are not Bethesda,  This isn't a 'quality feature', its a bug.



Now, past the complaining.  The game itself is neat and does everything it sets out to do: Panning for gold, smelt stuff, sell it, use a lego-system to create structures.  Improvements and additional content are constantly being added so its likely this game could mutate far beyond what it currently is.  Perhaps they already have a inventory system in the works but are holding off until other things get updated instead of having to create a system then recreate it for a planned upgrade.  Even if nothing else gets added, its a decent adhd burner though the need to drag objects huge distances can really destroy the appeal for those who like zone into building structures and machines.

"But creative mode!" Do we really need to cheat for some basic QoL functions? Once you start with creative mode the entire purpose of the game for most would be over.  Thats not a suitable solution.

2. A combat mode?  Random creatures and monsters that will wander in from the Surrounding Wilds.  Could include water-machinery turrets that could fire anything loaded into it, from ore chunks to processed materials and even fully made weapons, belt fed of course with a possibility of the 'ammo' being recoverable.  The creatures would of course drop things upon defeat.  They could just be elementals so they drop ore when defeated and their main goal is to get to the biggest hole on the map, jump in and fill it with a self-destruct dirtbomb, which would let starting gear like the shovel be a semi-effective weapon, against dirt golems at least.  it would provide a reason to make weapons and armor, outside of selling it.

There are occasional bugs, but the game is in active development, and most get ironed out quickly.

Would recommend this game to anyone who wants a automation game, that's just that little bit different to everything else.

review:
This was a hard call for me but in the end I'm recommending it because for the cost it's not bad.

To me this feels like an early access game and as the developer is still adding content it's possible it will reach where I feel it is a released product.  The tutorial is okay but I'd prefer some pop up help on various things.  

The beginning game and mid game are almost different games and I almost wish they would find a faster way to get to midgame that didn't have you play another game.  You can pan for resources (tedious with okay rewards) or you can fish (less actions but also less money per item)  In the end you will spend an hour or two as a new player before you can start with midgame content.  This is not a new player friendly game.  

Once you have the game mostly figured out and understand how the majority of ths game works there is a very interesting design here.  This is not the massive factory systems you get in other games.  The 4 minable resources are just as avalible in the tedius early game as in the mid and late game.  You are not going to have to figure out complex mixing and processes to get to better content.  The various stages maily get you resources faster and with less manual processes.  

There is something interesting about not being able to interact with more than 1 thing at a time.  You don't materialize components out of thin air.  You have to go buy the parts, transport them where you want, and then install them one at a time.  This level of tedium is interesting and while it may not be for everyone I think a lot more people will like the automation building a lot more than the tedious panning for minerals or fishing.  

Once you get going you begin to see the limit of the current content.  I'd like to see a bit more to the game,m not just in resources or automation options but also in reasons to get the resources.  Once  you are making your components your only real thing to collect resoruces for is quests so you can get the tokens.  And while that does give you next tier stuff it doesn't really deepend the game play.  Id love to see a system to rebuild areas or install a delivery depot on your lands so you can have someone deliver stuff for you.  A new smelter at T3 or T4 that opened you up to alloys.  Farming and fishing are nice deversions but they don't really deepen the game  play for me.  

In the end for the minimal price this game asks for I really can't complain too much.  I do think the mid and late game mining automation are interesting and something new and fun.  Those two are why I recomend this.  It is my hope that either the developer will continue to deepen this game or consider making a Version 2 based on some of the core features of this one.  It's a good but not a great game.  But it has some really intriguing design choices that belong in a great game.

Но как только развитие доходит до 3-4 буров и ты понимаешь, что пора переезжать...тут начинаются первые проблемы. 
[spoiler] Многа букаф, не осилил [/spoiler]


[b]Физическая грязь[/b]. Это конечно очень интересно, но на первых этапах, всё, что у тебя будет, это маленькая кирочка, и если ты хочешь закопаться поглубже, да так, чтоб места под 4-8 буров хватило, доставай чашечку чая, это будет долгая смена. (Справедливости ради, существует полноценная техника, для копания, но она добывается за токены, о которых речь пойдёт дальше.) [spoiler]Мод на динамит или на кирки в помощь[/spoiler]

[b]Переноска предметов[/b]. Физические объекты, это, конечно, прикольно...но вы перетаскивали более сотни предметов ручками? Взять, подойти к грузовику, положить, вернуться и повторить так ещё 99 раз. Или ещё интересней, покупка 100 предметов. Подойти, взять, отнести, положить, подойти. Кайф? Кайф. Не удивительно что мод на ящики так популярен. (И снова, да, есть поддоны, позволяющие таскать ~8 труб или же 4 конвейера, но это всё ещё очень мало. Ящики, one love. Хотя и с ними проблема, т.к. они забаганые)

[b]Строительство[/b]. Если вы не можете поставить предмет ниже себя, перезайдите, это решит проблему. Если не получается поставить трубу в правильное место, потому что она постоянно, вверх, вниз, вперёд, назад, не беспокойтесь, это норма. Чаю с ромашками?

[b]Квесты[/b]. Идея хорошая, придаёт смысла тем добывающим мощностям, которые уже удалось настроить. К квестам кузнечного дела (меч, кольцо, ожерелье и т.п.) претензий нет, на токены от этих квестов можно покупать технику, новые трубы, инструменты и т.п. Но вот к квестам на еду и "королевкие квесты", вопросики созрели. 
- Добавили фермерство, хорошо. Единственный способ покупать фермерские штучки (разбрызгиватель, лейка, корзинка, ящик и т.п.) - выполнять задания на доставку еды. Без них на первых этапах тяжеловато, но жить можно. В среднем, с квеста удаётся получить ~70 монет, предположим, нам везёт. Нужно сделать [b]30[/b] заказов, чтобы упростить себе полив растений. Накопи чуть больше и ты получишь себе ТРАКТОР. Ещё раз. Разбрызгиватель стоит почти столько же, сколько и трактор. Только разбрызгиватель делает *пшик-пшик*, а трактор и собирает, и сажает (кста, единственный способ ускорить посадку растений). Кто устанавливал ценник, моё почтение.

[b]Королевские квесты[/b] - это особенная степень бдсм. Щас объясню. Это полноценная "ветка" квестов. Пока не выполнишь один, не сможешь перейти к другому. Всего квестов пять. Три из которых задействуют основную механику - добычу ресурсов и минералов. Один - это квест на фермерство. Пока всё хорошо, да? 4 квеста из 5 - это основные механики, интересные, почти проработанные. Вот ты выполнил квест на золотой меч, тебя пускают внутрь, у тебя слегка лезут глаза на лоб от фермерского заказа, но ты думаешь что ладно, дальше будет интересней, идёшь, ЛАПКАМИ ФАРМИШЬ 600 КГ ОВОЩЕЙ(5-6 часов), приносишь, делаешь второй квест(на меч), отдаёшь, всё хорошо. У тебя уже есть схема, поток ресурсов автоматизирован и следующий квест будет интересным, и захватывающим, верно? Там же, можно будет, не знаю, собрать снаряжения для небольшого войска, снабдить его едой, да? 
Нет.

[b]ЛОВИ. МНЕ. ЛОБСТЕРА.[/b]

И ты идешь и ловишь. 5-6 часов. Просто садишься на причал с удочкой, тазиком. И ловишь. Рыбка каждые ~7,3 секунды.
Да, есть сетки для ловли рыбы. Но за два часа ожидания, в куче рыбы, которую они наловили, не было ни одного лобстера. 
[spoiler]Мод на креативный спавн вещей приходит на помощь.[/spoiler]
И вот ты пришёл, отдал лобстера, дальше тебя встречает финальный квест, кольцо для короля, которое ты идёшь и спокойно делаешь, ведь у тебя гораздо больше ресурсов чем нужно...и ты получаешь, палку для генерации земли. 
Это сейчас не шутка. За основной квест ты получаешь палку, которой при нажатии на землю, вот ту, которую ты киркой копал, ты её делаешь больше. Это буквально всё.  

[b]Третий тир земли[/b]. Ему пока не нашли применение. Да, появились новые механизмы, 3 тира, но, помимо увеличения получаемых ресурсов, ничего нет. Корстониум можно и на втором тире добывать. Учитывая существование рудных жил, смысл от третьего тира остаётся просто как достижение. Возможно ему придумают смысл потом.

[b]Кстати, о достижениях[/b]. Они почти не работают. В обучении получишь несколько, а дальше, в основной игре, делай что хочешь, ничего не получишь. А за сбор 4 реликвий, ты вообще получаешь ЦЕЛЫХ 62000. Вау, точно не 5 минут афк у буров.

[b]Оптимизация[/b]. Оптимизация Шрёдингера. Со временем, увеличивая число построек, фпс выше определённых значений повышаться не будет. Хотя...если под капотом i9 или такой же мощности, наверное, можно хоть весь мир застроить.

I really thought I'd enjoy this game but only after about 6 hours I feel like there is no point in continueing even though I haven't really even explored the map or most of the features.

The start was interesting, short amount of grind to purchasing my first things, meaningful improvements in my operation with almost every item bought. The gameplay also changes from all-manual to mostly automated gradually. Going around the map to find there are more items to find in a bigger town is also nice, I like it that there is motivation to pick where you want to build.

However, this is where the game ended for me. It looks like from here on all I need to do is wait, buy more drills, wait, dig 1 level lower, build the exact same setup with tier 2 and repeat. There are the relics to find, but it seems like a trivial side quest rather than actual content. There is farming and some new machines but ultimately I could basically leave the game running for a day on my tier 1 starter setup and end up with enough money to not make anything else relevant. I'm sure that people with more creativity than me will find arbitrary goals to set and get more out of the game, but for me it severely lacks depth.

Aside from the lack of content, the world feels dead with a few NPCs with very basic quests, nothing really moving aside from myself. The building feels rather clunky and aiming to drop things inside buckets and similar felt similarly annoying.. I understand each piece of dirt and rock has physics but it'd be nice to be able to throw them into a bucket 10cm away rather than just hold in your hand and let go wherever it falls.

I realise that the game never promised to have an objective being a sandbox, but for a sandbox it feels there is very little to do for the price. I got it on a discount, but I couldn't recommend it for more than £5 to be honest at the moment.

Extremely janky, charming game. One of those games that has its own logic and limitations. 

Pros:
- Extremely open-ended play your way experience.
- Neat mechanics
- Wide variety of gameplay
- Very unique feel
- The jank.

Cons:
- The jank.
- The whole "carry 1 item at a time" thing. It's a neat concept, but turns every single ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing into an exercise in patience, especially buying items from a shop that does not have vehicle access. Have fun running from buy pad to drop point 50 times.
- NO MULTIPLAYER. Come on, where's it at?! I've been following this game since launch, and it would be SO much better with up to 4 in some co-op.
- Illogical mechanics sometimes. Want to build your conveyor system this orientation? Sorry, the splitter conveyors only push one way even when spun about, so your entire contraption must be altered because of this.

Final Thoughts:
7/10 exercise in patience. When it works it works BEAUTIFULLY. When it doesn't, it's rage inducing and makes me regret having not refunded it. The lack of being able to do A N Y T H I N G fast is just atrocious. Structures go up slow, they get torn down slow, and when things don't work it's just a huge mess that is slow to clean up. And it's not even like the pieces can be gathered into a centralized location or into a storage container, nope, just giant piles of pipes, and pyramids of conveyors.

In a nutshell:
What this game has  but other games don't – you physically transport currencies, resources and 3-dimensional machines with your flatbed truck from a shop to your quarry. THERE IS NO INVENTORY.
What other games have but this game doesn't: you actually build factories. Here you just build a sorting station and keep adding more drills, pipes and conveyors.

In a game like Satisfactory, expansion requires you to increase raw material production, expanding low-tier refining, mid-tier refining and even high-tier refining, as well as transportation (conveyor belts/pipes/trains/trucks etc) and energy production, and on top of that constructing buildings, but you build with a magical gun.
In this game, expansion requires you to (I'm serious) add miners and water pipes, and connect them to your sorting system with conveyor belts. Energy is free and only requires one pump.

That's the game past the point where you have a sorting system. You can also farm (and you have to in order to finish the quest line).

Giving [i]Hydroneer[/i] a thumbs-down makes me somewhat sad, but unfortunately it leaves me no other choice. There's a lot of good stuff in there, starting with the attractive premise of a mining simulator sandbox. The graphics are serviceable, setting up an automated mining outfit feels quite satisfying, and there's significant potential for more advanced builds including logic gates for that extra bit of fine control over your operation.

Sadly, almost all of this is locked behind an incredibly tedious grind. This game not only disrespects your time, it actively hates you. Yes, you. And your family, and your dog. Especially your dog. Don't get me wrong, I know that construction and sandbox games tend to have a slow-paced start, and I'm completely fine with that, but [i]Hydroneer[/i] takes it to such a ridiculous extreme that I can no longer tolerate it. A game that's all about automating production shouldn't gate its automation features behind hours and hours of manual grinding. While this can be circumvented for the mining part by playing the fishing minigame (which isn't what I bought this game for), other features like farming have no such recourse. 

Let's stick with the farming example for a rundown on how this game does its best to waste your time in the most agonizing way it can. 
Farming equipment can't be purchased with the game's standard currency, because why should it? That would be way too convenient. No, you need special tokens, which can only be earned by completing farming-related quests, which in turn literally boils down to cooking bowls of soup for the NPCs wandering around the map. To make soup you need to plant and harvest crops, starting with tomatoes. Like all other pieces of equipment (yes, all of them; no exceptions), seeds can only be purchased individually. The packets stack to a limited degree, but you still need to pick up a seed packet, drop it in the purchase area, walk back to the counter, pick up another, drop it on the first, rinse and repeat. Sounds tedious? Oh, you sweet summer child, do I have more bad news for you. 
Now you have your seeds and your starting equipment, the only farming gear you can purchase with standard money. You haul it back to your claim, plant the seeds (individually of course) and water them... individually. You literally have to take your mining pan, fill it with water, pour it on one single aspiring tomato plant, refill the pan and repeat with the next plant. Sucks? You bet it does... and that's just the first round. You need to repeat the whole thing about once a minute until the plant is fully grown. For every. Single. Plant.
Okay. After what feels like an eternity of manual torture, you finally have a bunch of tomatoes. You cook the soup, take it to the quest giver and receive something in the ballpark of 40 tokens. That's just enough to purchase a watering can, which allows you to water an incredible FOUR plants per refill. Certainly a step up from the mining pan, but still mind-numbingly tedious. You want to automate this crap. That's what you bought this game for, after all. You vaguely remember seeing a sprinkler attachment for your water pipes back at the farming shop. You check the price tag and feel your hopes evaporate before your eyes because the damn thing costs a whopping 2,100 tokens. That's about 50 quests' worth of work just to automate the watering of a single small area of your fields, and it does nothing to help you with the harvest, the next seeding, the preparation of the harvest for cooking, the cooking itself, or any other part of the farming system. Isn't this great game design?

I freely admit that farming is the most extreme example of how [i]Hydroneer[/i] actively fights your attempt to have fun, but the rest isn't far behind. And if the game isn't wasting your time for a change, it's making your life difficult in other ways for absolutely no good reason. 
For instance, equipment comes in several tiers of increasing quality, but tools of the same type aren't readily interchangeable. A T1 drill has its power input on its backside near the ground. The T2 drill has it on its left side near the top. So instead of simply removing the old drill and plonking down a better one in its place, you have to tear apart your entire automated production line to accommodate this random BS. Oh, and it also makes it impossible to place T2 drills side by side, making them less efficient overall despite being higher on the tech tree. Again, just one example of many.

I could go on for at least another dozen paragraphs about all the nonsensical stuff in [i]Hydroneer[/i], the incomprehensible design decisions, and the near-psychotic level of contempt the devs seem to have for their customers' time, but I think I've made my point clear by now, so let's wrap it up. [i]Hydroneer[/i] has a lot going for it. It has many neat ideas and a solid core so that sometimes, when all the stars align and you squint real hard, you can just sense an echo of the fun you might actually have with this game. And then the next BS roars around the corner and slams you back down to the reality of how much potential was wasted in its development.

After 4X and Turn Based Strategy games I am a sucker for Base Building type games.  I have seen Hydoneer for a while now but for some reason never added it to my list of similar games.  It wasn't due to the price, which is even at full price is a great deal.  I guess every time I saw it I had other things on my mind.  Well thanks to the most recent deal the game was just under $10.50 USD so I had to finally try it out when I say it on the front page.

So far I only have one session in the game, at just under 3 hours played but I wanted to give my initial thoughts.  First off I installed on my i5-7400, 16 GB RAM, SSD, 1060 GTX which is what I played with at this point, and also my Steam Deck which I will come back and re-review after some time with it played and compare controller vs. KBM play as well at that time.

Cons First:
While I did not have any crashes to desktop, I feel that I need to note that I had at least three minor freezes for upwards of 25-30 seconds that I almost went to task manager to end task.  Each of these times was during an auto-save.  I am not sure why this was as I have the auto-save set for ever 5 minutes and I only had it happen 3 times and nothing major was going on during those three times of note.    

However during general game play I had no lag or other issues.  I am going to have to do a little more research to see if I can replicate and see what the issue is.  I am up to date on my SSD and Nvidiia Drivers so I should be okay there and I haven't had problems with more intensive graphics games.  But like I said, this did not lead to crashed to desktop and resolved after less than 30 seconds.

The only other slightly bothersome issue I have is with the game play it's.  While there is a visual center dot for things like clicking on items to pick them up, press buttons and so forth, this dot / interact button is separate from the button to drop items (I am sorry I forget the actually name of said indicator at the moment).  It defaults to black, which I highly recommend you  seek out under settings and game play and change to white, or a brighter color, I went with the magenta color myself because when you are dropping it's into pans, on the anvil, the cart, a table and so on, this indicator is where the item will fall to.  

If you are like me your brain is pretty trained to expect your focal dot to be where an item will fall, but since it isn't this may throw you for a loop, even more so at night when you will have a hard time seeing the drop point.   However once you change to a brighter color it becomes a lot easier to deal with.  Maybe no one else has fought against this issue, I haven't looked at other reviews or the forums, but I would imagine it is a common problem that people new to the game run into.

Okay, so that's the Cons that I have at this point.  Not bad, both are more annoying than major and the secondary one I mentioned is fairly easy to work around with the color change.  So now let's look at the pros.

Pros:
 1) The game is done in a nice cartoonist art form.  Sorry but for decades I played Warcraft and then World of Warcraft and I like my dwarves to be cartoonish, and they are spot on here.  Technically I don't even know if they are Dwarfs of just strange looking people.  I am going to think of them as Dwarfs since it's a mining game.  I love the art work, it has some great detail, some cell shade landscape looks, and as started cartoon looks.  All in all a very enjoyable look for me verses many of the survival / crafting games I have that go for a very realistic look.  I appreciate it myself.

2) While I am still using tier one gear, I like to gaming flow.  It feels good.  Even before I really even think about automating anything I am already doing so myself with multiple buckets, pails, furnaces and so on.   Coming up with a new way to speed up my processing even with the basic tier one items has been fun.  My next session I should be about ready to move to truly mining down and becoming a Hydroneer but even before that part as it is I could easily spend a couple more hours just maximizing how to increase my output with the bottom line equipment.

3) Other than the few lockups I mentioned during autosaves, I had no other bugs or issues with FPS or studdering.  I experienced zero clipping issues.   All in all the game feels pretty solid.  I would highly recommend it to my friends.  I do not feel my money was wasted in the least purchasing the game.

As of my experiences so far with just under 3 hours I would rate the game a 9/10.   I would have rated it higher but I am not a fan of how there is a second marker for where items are going to drop, maybe if there were different difficulty levels, but to me the only parts that frustrated me were and still are to a small degree that issue..

I have to applaud the dev(s) for making such bold decisions when making the foundation for controls/UI in this game. Inventories in other games can feel too small or unorganized, sometimes lacking the ability to quick deposit or "grab all"; rather than go through any of that nonsense, this dev team decided not to build an inventory at all. So, you have to pick up items one at a time and place them with yet another bold approach no one asked for: an off-center drop cursor. If that wasn't spicy enough for you they throw another curve ball at you with the currency system: drop money piles on top of each-other (with the aforementioned trash drop cursor) to combine them or smack them with a tool to break them. When you go to buy an item you have to drop your money into a bucket, purchase and re-locate the item then go back for your money later. If you thought they were done with radical ideas there, think again. They took it another step further by using Steam's Remote play for multiplayer, read through other people's reviews for comments on how fun and exciting that is. Considering this game was released during lock-down when everyone was stuck inside, why would you not release a full multiplayer? 

If you're interested in wasting your time, this game is for you.

Hydroneer is a game that oozes charm initially, with a neat pitch of it being this big, expansive mining simulator that lets you create mighty forges and simplistic machines to simplify the digging process, while driving along in a big vehicle and playing with a friend. Sadly, the trailers and the actual game play simply don't match up at all. It drops you in with effectively no tutorial. Curiously, you'll find a button to launch a direct link to the wiki, which I immediately don't see as a good sign--I shouldn't have to leave the game to understand how it works. Pushing that aside though, I read the abysmally small quick-start guide, and got to work. It took awhile for me to notice there were tools provided at the start, so after hunting those down, I began the process of shoveling dirt into a pan, filling that pan with water, brushing the dirt, and getting little chunks of whatever in it. From there, it was sprinting uphill to sell it, to then...have to carry the money physically back, and rinse and repeat (quite literally). Again, there's no in game tutorial--and the quick start guide only covers up till blacksmithing. There's drills on sale, but the in-game description and the constantly yammering NPC next to it says that it's damaged by unfiltered water. Seeing as I don't see any sort of filter available at any of the nearby stores, I refrain from buying it--due to seeing the cost of repair tools being pretty steep. After fiddling with smithing, dumping an obscene amount of ore into making a bar, only for the resulting dagger to only be worth 20 coins, I simply put the game down. It's frustrating in so many little ways, whether it be needing to drop money on top of other stacks to combine it (Why? What does this provide?) to your character making obnoxious grunting noises any time they can't interact with something for one reason or another, to just the complete lack of any kind of explanation as to how to get started beyond the barebones boring basics, I found myself feeling scammed out of my $10. Honestly, this game is nearly 3 years old now--how is it still in a state where the wiki has an in-game button dedicated to opening it, but the wiki isn't even fully filled in? In the 2 hours I played, I'd rate it at most, a 3/10. It's very far from the worst game I've ever played, but for all the charm this game has, it is a mechanically annoying mess.

Hydro Porter and the Planned Obsolescence
The game used to be a lot more entertaining but every update adds content while also making that content worse.

In the old days, the goal seemed simple - build a huge row of drills, get an obscene amount of materials, sell those for money.
Only because the dirt under the drill never diminishes and it's pretty easy to run them forever while AFK, money gets worthless real fast and there's nothing more to see.

Minerals now rely on more depth. OK, so move the drills a little lower but no big change there. There are even drills that give better materials that require that depth - it's a little more progression but ultimately just about colour that works the exact same way

OK, so farming comes out. People all over the map demand soup. You need to grow veggies, get the weight right for the ingredients, then run the soup out to them for a new variety of money. Only, cut veggies stack and you can only halve them. You now need to spend a while splitting and combining to try and get the quantities right. Add into this the fact the rewards barely cover the cost of the seeds and since seeds give 1-3 items and each turns back into 1 seed you feel slowed down. Now finally, add onto this finding the NPC on a map you have to stop, pick up, and check, and the distance you're running items out. The distance that would be much easier on the fast vehicle, but that barely fits anything on it.
That's all pretty tedious but the only thing the farming money rewards give is more farming goods (colours of the same mechanic) and a set of (cosmetic) greenhouse parts.

So now prospecting is a thing. Another type of money. It's the same as farming for getting quests > weighing > making > delivery but even worse because your big strip mine doesn't give nice tidy weights to make items to specification. No, you need to halve a huge 60,000 ingot over and over and over to get maybe 50 weight for maybe 80 special mining money.
Automation is going to take doing that several times since a tool to cut to weight needs the currency you're being paid for this time-sink. Oh, and you still need to collect the quests and run the products back out.

Overall, it's just becoming grindier, slower, and less intuitive. The balance in the old version was not good but instead of fixing it, the dev has just made things more punishing instead of more rewarding. You're still working towards the exact same goal of making your life automated and giving up, you're just now doing it with weights around your ankles.
The only thing the new update has added is a fix to a problem it introduces, and a new colour of goods that works in the exact same way.

Oh, and the worst part. Returning players better enjoy creating a new save because if you want achievements you better start over again from scratch.

Go look up Automachef. It's going to give you a much better experience and respect your time a lot more.

The game is very poorly optimised. If you put too many (~50) items into a bucket, or onto the back of your car, the FPS will drop to ~2. After 50h of gameplay and capturing just one of ~6 available dig sites, the game became unplayable.

[hr][/hr]

The first impression, with no tutorial in the regular game, was rather bad. And then I was told the tutorial is available from the main menu - as a separate scenario where you lose everything you do.

Then I had 20-30 hours of fun, doing things by hand, then building up, automating, and so on.

The lack of any kind of interface is an interesting approach - there is no inventory or any kind of information displayed on the screen, all items are objects that have to be carried around; checking the weight of an iron bar requires putting it on a scale; and so on.

And then came the end game which is again rather poor:
[list]
[*] Big purchases become problematic, as you still have to move items one by one
[*] Very poor logic circuits:
[list]
[*] Logic circuits are non intuitive and have no tutorial whatsoever - e.g. sending signal 0 and not sending a signal at all are two different things.
[*] Despite ~30 different logic blocks, very little can be actually automated (no automation for fishing, picking plants, taking bars/gems from the smelters/compressors, crafting items on the anvil).
[*] Even the simplest circuits take a huge amount of space (and blocks to move).
[*] No modulo operator - have fun building a circuit of ~20 blocks for something that should be possible with just one. 
[/list]
[*] Conveyor belt sorters sometimes glitch and let the wrong items through.
[*] You and your vehicles often get stuck - and using the “unstuck” option often moves you or your vehicle to another stuck position.
[*] Clean up option that removes all loose piles of dirt from the map actually removes them from the sorters as well.
[*] There are two pointers - one for aiming and one for dropping held items, but there are inconsistencies which one is used by the item held - e.g. emptying the bucket will use the dropping pointer, but pouring a soup into a bowl will use the aiming pointer.
[*] Scale has a display on the wrong side - you have to put the item on its left side, but the display is on the right side. Putting the item using the dropping pointer, which is on the right side, therefore you cannot immediately see the weight of the item you just dropped.
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

I am really torn whether to recommend it or not. I did have 30 hours of fun for £12.79, but on the other hand I was expecting more from it. I will be definitely looking forward to the updates.

This game is janky as hell and I love it for that very reason.
Reasons I love this game:
- The gameplay loop feels different from other games were you mine resources and craft things out of them. It's mellow, there aren't really goals set for you and as of 2.1 the tutorial consists of mostly self direction and self education, otherwise a *lot* of trial and error. To my understanding, there is a playable tutorial coming in 2.2 which is supposed to launch today. I'm writing this review while I wait for it to drop.
- I like when numbers go up, and this game makes every tier or progression, every new tool or piece of machinery feel special. I enjoy when I have enough ore in a single pan that my framerate drops to zero. Sure, there can be some frustration with it but ultimately it's a game and it's not like you're punished really for the bugs and quirks. You just... keep playing more of the game.
- The game has a lot of different things to do, but nothing forces you or even nudges you in that direction (except for that NPC you end up walking by all the time who could really do with some scran). It's a lot of self-directed exploration


If you're looking for the following, you won't find them here:
-This is not a survival game. There is not hunger or thirst, you don't have to sleep
-This is not an RPG. You don't have skills or levels, the progression is more baked into the materials you find and use.
-The gameplay loop is fun, but it is not efficient. If you're looking for a really clean experience free of bugs or quirks of the physics engine, look somewhere else.

Wanted to recommend this one, love Factorio (over 1000 hrs on it) and the Lets Game It Out videos, so figured it would be a hit for me... but I just cant understand how anyone can interact with the game. You want to put some dirt blocks in a pan. You drop the pan, it tips over on the ground (even if its fairly even ground). Try again. You get that and pick up the dirt, look at the pan and hit E. It drops to the ground to your side. You can't look directly at the pan, you need to aim away and try to judge where the dirt is going to drop in the bottom right of your screen. Its not just dirt, but the ore you get from the dirt, the pan again, the bars from the smelter, the gold you get, etc. But not everything, some things work like you would expect - pour out the crucible and you want to look directly at where you want it to go.
So so so much time wasted trying to just put things where you want to go. Honestly its an actual strain on the eyes and very very frustrating. You can hold E for a second or two to get a more precise dropping, but its still a bit hard to aim and the thing might still just bounce or roll over - and with how many things your picking up and dropping those seconds add up, which goes to the next thing.
It takes forever to get any automation going. Played for 1.5hrs and finally got my first machine, a mining machine but everything else is still a huge manual process, and think it would be another hour before I can get an automatic grinder.
Technically the game is solid, impressive as a base building/mining style game - it looks great, love the art style - sounds great - but just can't recommend it.

Is it a digging and ore game? Is it a fishing game? Is it a farming game? The game has felt extremely clunky to play for years and nothing has been done about that, and the the developer decides to release DLC lol

The controls for picking stuff up and dropping them sucks, it should work like grabbing stuff in Halif Life 2 or Amnesia The Dark Descent where the player has a lot more freedom, or better yet, Voices of the Void has the best controls for picking stuff up and putting them down exactly where you want and how, it could be similar to that.

The early game sucks, I understand using the shovel to manually do things for a while before getting money to afford the resources to automate stuff, but some things like the hand sorter yeets the ores in a direction with a slight variation making it miss the pan FREQUENTLY for example, and stuff like the funnel not helping at all in the early game since stuff falling with some momentum will mostly fall outside of where you wanted it to land anyway, having to position the pan in a near pixel perfect spot to actually catch the resources being sorted while they are yeeted around... It is just pure frustration and stress for the first 3 or 4 hours of the game.
And the game doesn't even have an in-game guide, so you are left to guess how things work and how to position them. all you have is a brief and simple description of what the item is supposed to do.
Also when digging further down a lot of tiny floating dirt pieces simply exist and make it annoying to do literally everything, and good luck trying to see them to then attempt to remove them.

After you get through all that though, when you manage to finish your first fully automated machine, doing all the steps for you, things do get a quite a bit smoother going forward and actually fun. Only buy this game if you are certain you're willing to go through some stress to get a grip of the mechanics and also watch some youtube videos to understand what the f*ck and you're doing and supposed to do since the game has no built-in UI guide to aid you, just some cryptic signs on walls giving you hints.

Despite all of what I said, I love this game and want it to see how far it is going to get in the future, usually I don't like these kinds of games but Hydroneer simply isn't as boring or stressful as other games are, I've been following this game's development for a few years already and it has evolved quite a bit since it's older versions, a lot of mechanics have been improved, but the main problems with the early game are still present  which is why I decided to make this review and talk about all of them, hopefully the developers are gonna fix all of those problems and make the early game not as annoying, that probably turns away a lot of people who give the game a try.

If you're looking for a fun and relaxing game that combines resource management, exploration, and creativity, Hydroneer is an absolute gem. This game has everything you could want from a simulation game, and it delivers it all with stunning graphics, smooth gameplay, and an addictive soundtrack.

From the moment you start playing Hydroneer, you'll be immersed in a world filled with possibilities. The game puts you in the role of a gold miner, tasked with exploring the world around you to find valuable resources and build up your mining operation. You'll need to manage your resources carefully, balancing your budget with your desire to expand your business.

One of the best things about Hydroneer is how much freedom you have to explore and create. You can build your own mining operation from scratch, designing everything from the layout of your mine to the equipment you use to extract gold from the ground. The game encourages experimentation and creativity, so you'll never run out of new things to try.

But what really sets Hydroneer apart is its attention to detail. The game's physics engine is incredibly realistic, making mining feel like a genuine physical task. Every tool and piece of machinery has its own unique properties, and learning how to use them effectively is both satisfying and challenging.

Overall, I would highly recommend Hydroneer to anyone who loves simulation games. With its gorgeous graphics, immersive gameplay, and endless possibilities for exploration and creation, this game is a true standout in the genre. Whether you're a seasoned miner or a newcomer to the world of resource management, you're sure to find something to love in Hydroneer.

Hydroneer is an indie simulation game is set in a fantasy world where players assume the role of a miner who must extract valuable resources, such as gold and silver, from the ground. The game play of Hydroneer is a mix of resource management and puzzle-solving mechanics. Players must build and operate a variety of machines to extract resources from the ground and process them into valuable materials. The game also features a variety of puzzle elements, such as finding hidden treasure and solving riddles to progress. One of the standout features of Hydroneer is its charming and colorful art style, which creates a whimsical and relaxing atmosphere. The game's mechanics are also straightforward and easy to understand, making it accessible to players of all skill levels. Additionally, Hydroneer offers a variety of customization options, allowing players to personalize their mining operations and machines. The game also features a multiplayer mode, allowing players to collaborate with friends and compete against each other. However, Hydroneer can become repetitive and grind, with players performing the same tasks over and over to extract resources. The game can also be short, with the main campaign only lasting a few hours. In conclusion, Hydroneer is a charming and accessible simulation game that offers a relaxing and enjoyable experience. Its charming art style and straightforward mechanics make it accessible to players of all skill levels, while its multiplayer mode and customization options add depth and replay ability. While it can become repetitive and may be short for some players, those looking for a casual and enjoyable mining simulator will find a satisfying experience in Hydroneer.

Hydroneer is the best terrible game I've ever played. On paper, it sounds great. A mining game that makes Factorio-style promises of automation and engineering, machine maintenance, piping, all the good stuff you wanna see in an industrial sim.

Then you get in and find out you have 1 hand. No toolbelt, ever. No way to place anything besides throwing it on the ground at full force like those old milk challenges. You are told to dig... with a shovel that makes a tiny indent and a bucket... Not quite as glamorous as Factorio or Satisfactory where you are bringing stuff from space with you. Oh and there's only 2 individual machines for sale at the start. You can't even craft. 

If you stick with it, though, the janky charm ramps up very quickly. So far, my favorite part is how drastic the production techniques have evolved as I played. I went from shoveling dirt into a bucket then hand washing it, to a hand-wash production line with like 6 buckets, to having 1 machine that I dump my buckets into, then 2 machines, and I pick up the dirt myself and put it in, and now I just bought a huge load of (EXPENSIVE) conveyer belts. Whereas Factorio is about progressing into more and more complex but fundamentally similar recipe flows, this one seems to be about scaling up into entirely new production processes.  Hydroneer is pretty small scale overall, and most of the game seems to be about trying to process more and more (and then more and more valuable) dirt. 

It's kind of like a job... and the game got MORE fun when I thought of it that way. That's not going to be a game for everyone and I'm not even sure I would PREFER it this way, but it's interesting. 

Overall, that's what Hydroneer is. Interesting. I got it on sale and find it very worth it. New updates are really adding a lot. Cooking is fun diversion and there's a lot of cosmetic building pieces, but it's all expensive. This seems like it could be a basis for a SUPER SUPER good MMO down the line. For now, It's mainly odd, but worth your time if you're a fan of the genre.

Excellent game! Where a lot of games employ a farming/grinding mechanic and keep things simple (for the engineers) by limiting the impact of physics; the developer(s) of Hydroneer shouted "YEET" and decided to let physics play a significant role in the game. I love it - placing a bucket just a few inches off from where you wanted it to be could result in hundreds of raw resources just piling up on the ground next to it, requiring you to loathe your sloppiness, move the resources into the bucket manually, and move the bucket to a better position. It's certainly not enough of an occurrence to be frustrating but I absolutely love the reward for "being organized". Items like tables, walls, etc have true value because of the organizational benefit they bring - it isn't just cosmetic. Getting excited to bring home a new tool rack to your dig site is a legitimate experience because of this and it's just perfect IMO.

As a fan of survival games, I was looking for a laid-back and relaxing experience without the added pressure of managing hunger or thirst. This game fits the bill perfectly, with gameplay centered around optimizing your own mine and/or farm, without any particular end goal other than to enjoy the process. 

Initially, the game may feel a bit repetitive, but as you progress, you can automate many of the more tedious tasks, allowing you to focus on the more advanced aspects of the game. I found myself getting lost in the decorating and optimizing of my mine and farm, which added a fun and creative element to the gameplay. As you continue to play, the game becomes more complex and satisfying, with plenty of challenges to keep things interesting.

What really sets this game apart is its welcoming community. In my experience, the community is incredibly supportive and helpful, and I was pleasantly surprised to be able to reach out to one of the developers and hear back in under 48 hours helping me with a game bug, and based on what I read from the patch notes after that, it looks like it may have been addressed. Having played many games over the years, I can confidently say that this community is one of the most helpful and supportive I've encountered.

Overall, if you're looking for a laid-back game to relax and unwind with, this game may be worth checking out. It has a lot of animal crossing appeal, where you are never really done as it wasn’t the point. While it may not be the most adrenaline-inducing game out there, it offers a stress-free experience and a supportive community that can make for a truly enjoyable gaming experience.

Decent game. Feels like a mobile version of satisfactory with very limited progression. After you get mk2 miners there's little progression aside from making your "factory" bigger. It feels like minecraft pre 1.16 (nether update); there's huge potential and the possibilities are endless but you are limited to the "build more bigger" gameplay loop. There's NO automatic crafting except jewel compression and smelting which functions as a lag reducer masquerading as wealth and utility conversion. The UI is creative and I love the immersion of a physical inventory system but it's not very user friendly or intuitive. Performance is also pretty bad. If you want a factory game with a 3rd dimension and a polished "feel" spend twice the price and get Satisfactory. 

If this game doesn't add a bunch more content in the next year and fix performance I am going to change this to a dislike. Currently, I believe in what this game can be one day and the dev(s) is clearly creative and competent.

I have a fairly good rig that runs far more intensive games, so I was surprised that this game (which does not look good compared to say, dyson sphere program) still cannot consistently run well. The game is mechanically simpler than minecraft and should not have performance issues on high end hardware.

I appreciate that the developer has put in work to add things like NPC's and more locations and even streamline the code, but when the performance is this bad and basic UI/UX stuff is still missing 2 years down the line, I can't recommend it. 

If the game ever moves away from it's busywork dropping/carrying gameplay and fixes the performance issues I will update the review.

Without mods, it's tedious transporting materials. It's a physical inventory and not a virtual one. This is likely why I like the game so much - because you have to touch everything. May not be your cup of tea if that turns you off.

Highly recommended.

I was on the fence for a while, but overall I have to say this game isn't well done.  
Somewhat fun, yes, especially early on, but it's really frustrating overall.

Main problems:

1) bugs.   

Items disappearing, random freezes, long freezes during saving, and a total slowdown if you try to move too many items (few hundred will do it, eg a pan of resources)

2) tedium

Digging a bloody hole takes ages.  Moving earth takes 10 times more.   Moving items around  is slow.  And you have to re-build every single bit.  The program forgets item orientation, and rotating is not that intuitive either. (it's not even explained!)  Need I go on?  

3) total lack of information

Apart from some very basic youtube tutorial you get nothing.  Unless you consider hieroglyphs helpful.  (We have invented proper writing, why try to communicate with ambiguous images?)  The in-game descriptions of machines, logic pieces, etc are skeletal at best.  It's nearly impossible to figure things out on your own, since they aren't entirely logical - it certainly is very hard without some prior knowledge of some parts at least.   


[b]Summary:[/b]

Unless you are a time millionaire and want to punish yourself, I can't recommend it.  

You're expected to build logic circuits and networks of machines, building takes a significant amount of time due to the lack of proper building tools (eg multi-select), and you'll have to keep running to the shops (slow, you have to pack up 10 items to buy 10, no way to do it on one go!) and re-build things because of the lack of information.  

This combination is unforgivable in my opinion, hence the negative review.  

Alternatively you can copy/build stuff others have already figured out and posted online - but where is the fun in that?

The developers tried to explore new inventory mechanics by simply completely doing away with an inventory, requiring you to use buckets and carts to carry anything beyond the single object in your hands. I appreciate the attempt at originality, but it is utterly atrocious.

One might dismiss the tedium of picking up and dropping 4 or 5 different objects to accomplish a basic task like panning for gold so you can get started. That can be said to be a matter of taste. However, when you've got a pan full of hundreds of nuggets, you have no options except insane infuriating ones. Sort them by hand? Will take you an hour. Dump them into a sorting machine? You'll probably miss, and the machine will miss the pans you set up to catch the output. Use a magnet tool to police the mess you just made? It's garbage, won't attract what you want it to, and will attract what you don't want it to. Plus more than a few dozen nuggets will destroy your framerate and make you vastly more likely to miss the toilet bowl. No words can express how rage-inducing it is to see an explosion of nuggets go all over the place because you missed your lay-up.

My advice to the developer would be to abandon this failed attempt at item mechanics, and give the player pockets, at LEAST for resources. You don't need an inventory screen, just give the player a non-physical way to police nuggets.

Mecánicas no tiene demasiadas. Tienes una pala la cual usas para sacar tierra, una cubeta donde llenas tierra, un balde donde pones la tierra de la cubeta y agua para finalmente usar un cepillo y obtener los recursos. Conforme avanzas podrás comprar un yunque y una fragua para transformar estos recursos. Tu meta es conseguir automatizar todo ese proceso con maquinaria y cintas transportadoras.

Si tengo que ser bastante sincero este no es un juego que apunte a un público en general, sino para gente que le guste mucho el tema de construcción y automatización de recursos, ya que normalmente tendrás que buscar la manera de hacer tu fábrica cada vez más eficiente y hay varios terrenos para hacerlo, así que puedes elegir el que más te convenga.

Ahora, el juego no tiene un objetivo en particular ya que no hay un "final de juego" en sí y en un inicio estarás haciendo una cantidad considerable de grindeo manual.

Si te gustan juegos de construcción de base y recolección/automatización de recursos, te digo que vale la pena darle una prueba a este juego que te divertira bastante... Y con los nuevos NPCs definitivamente te sacará sonrisas... Lo único que sí te recomiendo es que averigues cómo conseguir Clothium antes de empezar a hacer tu fábrica ya que no es tan intuitivo.

It's actually quite amazing that this game is built with Unreal ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and manages to run almost always at 114ish fps.

There are a few bad pracrice coding issues the devs should probably address, like - I'm willing to bet - Tick Aggregation on mining machines (add enough and the frames start to drop, which indicates their on tick event is individualized).

Collisions are ♥♥♥♥, that's the engine however. There really isn't all that much a developer can do. Maybe buy and use a different physics engine - like Havok - which sure does cut into the profit margin a wee bit but is much more reliable than anything the Epic team touches...

Overall, the item progression / money acquisition is simple and logical enough that you can just sit there and figure stuff out.

There are some lazy design choices that the devs are peddling as "wanting people to have to think to build".
They appear most obvious in the logic nodes proably, where you have >= but not <= (and all you have to do is turn the piece around). One of the not so clear ones is the lack of cross intersections on all pipes.

I haven't even began to peruse the house building items, and there is a ton of them, which makes playing and building fun, as you wait for resources to gather up.

Overall, the game is well worth its money.

Special note, the voxel system for digging is nicer than one would expect. And the tools provided are rather spot on. It's not even close to no man's sky in terms of *fun factor* of terrain manipulation, but if you want to go full dwarve and dig up a copy of moria by pickaxe, this is the game for it XD

The game is one huge annoyance, it makes the worst thing the game can make - it gives hardship to player when doing most basic tasks like placing bucket on the ground, jesus. It's unacceptable that I struggle to do such thing in a game which core is constant manipulating with objects and vast majority of them just won't cooperate, constantly tumbling over, rolling down, misguiding themselves and generally doing everything except what I want them to do. Also, recent addition of NPCs was absolutely unnecessary. Game become even more annoying when I have to listen to bunch of the same lines in same moments with same voices all day long.
If anyone responsible would ever read that - really simple change to behavior of dropped items would have enormous impact on quality of player's life, consider that. And in general, manipulating the props feels like constant struggle and battle against the game. More annoyance than enjoyment.

At present, no, can't recommend due to motion sickness issues. The idea is fine and it's a neat concept that everything is a physical object instead of just an image in an inventory, but that concept is also a problem as it means you have to constantly move tiny little things around.

Starting with the very basic mechanic of dig dirt and put dirt in bucket requires constantly moving the camera from side to side. Once you put dirt in basin and brush the thing, you then again have to move every single nugget one by one, which again means moving the camera all over repeatedly. This constant and repeated need to moving the camera back and forth is nauseating and by itself makes the game unplayable for anyone prone to motion sickness. And it does not help that the drop marker is always somewhere off to the side instead of where you're looking, so you have to look around to figure out where the stuff you drop will end up.

Given the basic mechanics of the game I don't see any simple fix to avoid the motion sickness because it requires changing how it works so you don't have to move the camera as much. Basic things like make stuff drop where the crosshair is pointing and being able to pick up more than 1 thing at a time would go a long way (and make the game a lot more intuitive), but the digging mechanic has to be totally redone for this to be possible.

Essentially, the biggest problem with the way the game works is that it's first person. If it was in third person the mechanics would be far less nauseating, but not any less tedious.

This game is GREAT!

It does have its ups and its downs, but it is definitely more positive than negative.

It has a steep learning curve in the early game and little more than a YouTube video from the Devs to help guide you. This video (or at least watching another guide to starting from YoutTube) is critical to success as it’s not intuitive!

But getting over that learning curve, you learn some of the many charms of this game!

You have no inventory, so you have to manage everything a little more than you might in most games. You can only pick up one item at a time, so you end up having to put things in a container and carrying that. Or you load up one of the vehicles and move things about that way. This can get a little annoying when doing a big project, but mostly adds to the complexity/problem solving aspect of the game!

Next you have 2 cursors - one for picking up items or using them on things, and another for where you’ll drop items. Again, not intuitive, but once you get used to it, can be used to great effect.

The begins the grind - you start at the beginning of your mining journey panning for resources - dig dirt, wash it, get stuff. This can be painful, but there are strategies to optimise this (YouTube to the rescue again). But basically you do a bunch of panning & earn a bit of money selling your resources to the Jeweller.

Some people then use this money to buy a fishing rod & go fishing - personally I find fishing a bit boring and beyond completing the quests to upgrade to the T8 fishing pole rarely do it - and then only when I’m waiting around for other things. I also find this to be much slower than going back to mining more.

The alternative is, you can use your money to buy some equipment to make things easier - unfortunately, you likely didn’t make lots, so you’re still on the hand panning, but you can make this a lot easier for yourself with the new equipment. Also new equipment will make it easier to get as low as possible - the lower you go in this game the heavier the resources you get from the same action. So, another hand panning session, and possibly a bit of processing (depends how much you got from the first session, if you had enough to buy everything that would be useful) and it’s off to the Jeweller again!

You’re likely to have enough money now (if not it’ll be another panning session for you) to start moving into automation. Then it’s drills (that perpetually dig dirt for you) and harvesters (that do the cleaning for you) and conveyors (to move it all around) and pipes (to power it all).

If you’ve done your research beforehand, even at a leisurely pace, it’ll only really take you an hour to get to this point.

There are more dig sites available to buy for reasonable prices (if you’ve done particularly well with your panning, you’ve probably got enough to go buy one before setting up automation) the starting plot is limited to only a certain depth.

More drills (including the next tier) can be crafted at an old dwarven mine “Icehelm” which is a cool little progression mechanic.

There’s farming as well now! I recommend having made yourself a fair bit of money before diving into farming - it’s totally optional, gets you a different currency, which only buys more farming items - but could probably be started as soon as you have enough money to buy the basic equipment.

Farming is fun - not only do you have to make a farm, you have to find customers who want soup, cook soup to their orders, then deliver it to them. Again, it can feel a little grindy at times, but the progression feels real and purposeful.

There’s a load of vehicles to help with things like moving stuff about, but also more specific things like collecting crops, sowing seed and flattening land.

There are building pieces which can be used to construct buildings and interiors. Some players have made pretty buildings, others have made entire complexes of buildings.

There’s even a logic system to automate the automation further.

There’s a lovely discord community full of friendly and helpful players if you get stuck/need help figuring something out. And a whole community of modders, adding in community requests, the devs don’t feel fit the game.

Yes, there’s problems - the obvious lack of an in game tutorial system. The game occasionally throws a spanner in the works when someone does something not anticipated. Early game/late game needs a bit of a rebalance. The game eventually “runs out of content”. But these are mostly being addressed - there are regular bug fixes whenever something becomes apparent, not just someone derping into ridiculous situations. Things are regularly reviewed to improve them (the game balance is much better than it was). There are regular free major updates adding more content.

The multiplayer (up to 4P) is only streamed split screen at the minute, what’s more, only one person can use mouse and keyboard - everyone else needs to use controllers. This might be a deal breaker for some people. Personally I don’t multiplayer that often, and when I do, it’s tolerable. The devs explain that the tools aren’t available given the mass of objects in a normal hydroneer save - it’d be like your playing a game of pool and on player 1’s screen the black ball goes down the hole, but on player 2’s screen the black ball jumps the cushion and rolls away from the table - you want everything to be the same for both players, else things are gonna get funky real fast!

The game starts using the best settings it can - I’ve got a good pc, but my game turned into a slideshow. Unless you have a serious computing rig (graphics are key to this game) I suggest the first thing you do is reduce the graphics settings.

Couple of things to bear in mind before complaining - This was mostly created by a single dev, and the team is still pretty small. The cost for this game is still really low, given the quality of the game.


SUMMARY

As I said, this game is great. It’s original and quirky - in a good way. It offers progression and development. At the time of writing this, I’ve played 150 hours and I’m far from having experienced everything. Yes I can see content running out, but they are adding more all the time. Also, it’s a sandbox game, there’s more than one way to skin every cat, obviously some are more efficient than others, but figuring out all the variations adds many hours of fun. While not for everyone, I do recommend checking it out and giving it a fair chance to get used to the control system.
