Great value. Very zen, relaxing.  

Core Gameplay Loop:
  dig the earth, sift it in a pan by the river for valuables.  Sell at the market.  Buy equipment to improve and automate.  Fish the fish, load them in a cart, sell them at market.   (coming soon:  plant the seed, harvest the plant, sell at the market)
As you earn more money, you can buy better tools, and buy machines to begin automating mining.  Fishing and (coming soon) Farming don't have obvious automation options yet.

Pacing:
Early game is well paced, but scaling of resources gathered is dramatic.  For experienced players, 2-3 hours before money becomes pointless.  For new players, maybe 6 hours before money becomes pointless.  Then the constraint becomes a relatively rare ore, this remains the constraint for another 10 hours or so, give or take.  By this point you will be producing more materials than you can reasonably find a use for, and may need to buy the item destroyer to dump everything except the 1 rare ore in order to keep the game from choking out on stockpiled gold/iron/gems.

Difficulty:
   Low difficulty, but satisfying and relaxing gameplay.  More tedium than difficulty.  With the need to physically handle only 1 item at a time, no inventory, and no item stacking... even the most mundane of building efforts will require lots of mindless back and forth hauling with carts/trucks, and hand placing every block from wherever you dump the items to wherever you plan to install them.

Visuals:
  Very surreal cartoony vibe, I like it.  The decision to not have a UI is very creative.  I like the tedium of hauling logs around one by one and zoning out while I listen to an audio book.  There's no build menu, no inventory, no tool slots.  Everything is 1 item at a time, by hand.

Diggy Diggy Hole!:
  I love digging.   This game does have an issue shared with other games, where you get these little tine pieces of dirt that stay floating in the air, blocking things.  You almost can't see them, but you have to pixel hunt with your tool to try to clear it.   The rake item lets you level your terrain, but it won't add dirt unless the square is already over halfway full, and it won't fully clear the dirt unless it's under halfway full.  So there's a lot of fiddling required for smooth surfaces.  Best to rough it out and use wall segments if you want precision smoothness.  There are explosives of 3 different sizes available for quicker excavation.  And a dev pickax if you want to go in to creative mode and have fun digging without the very very slow default tools.

Performance:
  Just like any other game of this type.  Our modern world doesn't offer a good multi-threading solution for core physics calculations.  All of these physics must be rendered in real time, and the results must be delivered in the order they happen.  This means everything ends up being constrained to a single core physics thread.  And like every other game with parts and physics, the more parts you have, the more crunchy your game becomes.  This game is beautiful and renders smoothly and fast for early and mid game.  Once you start crossing over that 10 hour mark, you are going to need to watch closely for random hitches where your ores might become stuck coming out of a chute, or randomly stuck on a belt.  My most common source of game crashes has come from stuck ores that clock up the belt and create a deadly physics clump.  (there's a handy button in the main menu to delete all loose raw resources, but this only helps if your items are clumped up before being refined).   The game offers trucks and hand cards that disable item meshes to allow you to drop multiple items on top of one another without collision, but be careful, if you stack too many items you'll be barely able to move due to the physics hit on your framerate.

Advanced Play:
  Tier 1 and Tier 2 are established.  But even though the game says "2.0" it is not feature complete yet.  The developers have not added any mechanism to dig/process the bottom tier of dirt present in the plots of land you can currently buy.  The focus for the next system to be added sounds like it will be farming, so it may be quite some time before the bottom dirt can be worked.  Automation is available for use, but the only practical application I have found is to auto-repair your water filtration system.  I've tried to use it to automate smelting, but the way the piping system in this game works, you end up consuming a MASSIVE amount of tiles trying to do even the most basic of logical operations.  Personally I find the simplicity of clicking on the manual smelter to be vastly superior to the convoluted eyesore that automation provides.  And even the best youtube videos I have seen on the automation side of things still suffer from increased likelihood of logjams and creating messes, not to mention how hideous it all looks.  If you plan to automate, I'd say leave about 6 squares in radius around any automated equipment so you can fit in enough straight pipes to hold all the delays, switches, diodes, flippers etc.   Because the game rewards you for digging as deep as possible, it's difficult to create a basement where you can hide all this mess.   Also, note that after you get more than 10 miners going of any tier,  money and resources are no longer an issue, so you are really just being "creative" at that point.  Switching to creative mode is a good way to skip some of the more tedious aspects unless (like me) you enjoy the mind numbing bliss of hauling logs back and forth.  Don't buy this game for logic builds. (at least not in its current state)

Super giereczka z ogromnym potencjałem (praktycznie nieograniczonym!). Miejsca do rozwoju jest od groma, ale przechodząc do tego co mamy aktualnie:

Satysfakcjonująca zabawa - dużo frajdy daje patrzenie na to jak działa to co zbudowaliśmy, te poruszające się kawałki surowców na taśmociągach które każdy jest osobnym obiektem w grze.
Duża ilość zawartości - można budować bazę, wydobywać surowce ręcznie by potem wszystko zautomatyzować i dalej optymalizować oraz ulepszać o nowe maszyny dodając więcej możliwości naszej kopalni. 
Realistyczna mechanika gry - w tej grze nie ma plecaka czy innego wymyślnego ekwipunku w którym schowamy tysiące przedmiotów. W tej grze każdy przedmiot i surowiec jest osobnym obiektem który ma własną fizykę i aby go podnieść, potrzebujemy go wziąć do ręki bądź wrzucić go do jakiegoś pojemnika. Potem to wszystko można przewieźć za pomocą wózka lub pojazdu.

Grafika - Stylizowana, całkiem ładna - choć to zależy od gustu. Moim zdaniem wystarczająca do tego typu rozgrywki.

Z optymalizacją bywa różnie, zależy od komputera - przy i5 4690k gra z 40 działającymi wiertłami była niegrywalna (1-5FPS), przy i7 12700k - gra działała bez zająknięcia i pewnie działała by dobrze przy o wiele większej ilości wierteł (ponad 75FPS). 

Większych problemów z grą nie uświadczyłem, wiem że niektórzy mają problem z blokującymi się obiektami na taśmociągach, fizyka nie wyrabia i dzieją się dziwne rzeczy. Osobiście dużo takich momentów nie miałem, wręcz w ilości pomijalnej ale chciałem o tym wspomnieć

*Opinia z przed aktualizacji 2.0.6:
Pojazdy lubią się dziwnie zachowywać, szczególnie jeśli zapakujemy na niego dużo sprzętu (silnik gry nie wyrabia) i te oprócz ogromnego spadku wydajności gry powodują że zaczynają podskakiwać a niekiedy odlatują (Samemu tego nie doświadczyłem). 
*Ponoć twórca już to naprawił.

My review is a bit mixed. 

I was watching this game for some time and waiting until there was a multiplayer before diving in.

When approaching this game, be forewarned: 

There are some issues.

if you go into this look for a "game" you will be disappointed. Right now the game is mine, smelt, sell. There is no real item production or automation. Mining appears to be the only thing you can do. You can build houses that don't impact the mining operations at all. Fun if you want to spend your earned in-game currency on building an elaborate empty town and mining outpost. 

The building mechanic is interesting, You buy the machines you need and place them down. You need to lock them in place with a hammer, otherwise you tend to pick them up accidentally. The placement of these machines on terrain can be a little tricky, especially around other machines.

What kills this game for me is the implementation of "multiplayer."

I wanted to try this with friends and was disappointed that the only MP solution is a split-screen remote play with steam. In order to work, both players are forced into a split screen to receive the other player's stream, and the remote player MUST be using a game controller (keyboard wont work)

This isn't going to work in terms of a multiplayer experience. Knowing the complexity of a project this scale, I can understand the developer's choice to go this route; however, doing so seems cheap, incomplete and too much trouble to even bother. 

Hydroneer is as much a sandbox about clutter as it is about moving dirt balls around on a conveyor. In my view, there is no workable multiplayer because the halved screen-space completely breaks the experience, making building a further chore.  

On the upside, the game's atmosphere is very pleasant. You can tell a ton of TLC went into the artwork because the world is beautiful. The lighting appears to be, by default, a bit too dim, especially at night, likely to force you to use the light objects.

All in all, Hydroneer is a visually pleasing sandbox with a unique implementation of mining & processing. 

There is no significant crafting or automation beyond mining, nor a player inventory. Everything is carried or trucked around. 

Bottom line:

You will enjoy this game in single player. 

In "multiplayer," you are less likely to enjoy it because the implementation is poor.

I am a huge fan of the factory building genre.  I have spent thousands of hours across games like Satisfactory, Factorio, Dyson Sphere, and FortressCraft.  I want to like Hydroneer, but I can't. Factory building games are supposed to be long and a grind.  Normally, this is a natural result of tech advances and progression, but Hydroneer is made artificially so.  

There is no item bar.  I can only pick up and use a single item at a time.  This makes digging an ordeal.  You need to pick up your pickaxe, dig out an area, drop it, pick up your rake, flatten an area, drop it, pick up your pickaxe, and continue.  You aren't doing this quickly either, even the upgraded pickaxe takes a lot of time to dig.  You aren't going to be able to dig out a large area unless you spend many hours to do so.  

There is no backpack.  Again, since you have to handle each item individually, you have to buy, transport, and build each item individually.  If you want to build out a modest 10 drill factory, you will need hundreds of items including multiple  types of pipes, conveyors, hooks, drills, etc.   Each of these must be picked up, purchased, transported, stored, and built.  It is going to take a while.

There is no tech tree.  This is an essential part of any factory building game.  You need to research and discover new technologies that give you a purpose to build and upgrade that factory.  Here, there is no purpose.  There is a drill, and a tier 2 drill which is superficially different.  The factory you upgrade to is the exact same factory, but lower down.  It produces the same resources, in the same ratios.  Not that the resources matter anymore, because you just sell it.  

The end result of all of this is a game with no driving force.  You aimlessly build the same thing, only bigger, but the mechanics in the game makes it more frustrating to build until you decide to call it quits. 

There is hope.  They are still updating the game.  The new vehicles might take the tedium of digging away.  Playing in creative takes the tedium of handling items individually away.  I don't see any tech tree coming in the future though, and so for me that is the deal breaker.

I'm becoming increasingly aware that I've only just scratched the surface of this great game (there's a pun there somewhere I think) but I'm already enjoying it more than enough to give the thumbs up to others. I really like the beautiful neither overly simplistic nor cheesy cute graphic style (reminiscent, to me, of Torchlight) and I particularly like the intuitive nature of how most everything (I've encountered so far) works. Rarely do I start into a game such as this type without scratching my head and having to look around for tutorials and YT videos etc to get me orientated to how stuff works. This game I got pretty much straight into it and even the new stuff I found, like water pipes and associated components, all aspects of fishing (again Torchlight jumps into mind) with the help of the little popup descriptive notes, very easy to figure out and get working with without the usually somewhat annoying often frustrating distractions of seeking information outside the game.

Anyway, I'm really enjoying it and I recommend it to others. I'm looking forward to future developments. The Devs seem to listen and respond to the community and also have plenty of ideas of their own too. They also clearly have a handle on implementing and expanding the whole concept so the future looks exciting and bright. I can't wait to find out and enjoy more...

I've been here for over a year of the game's development. It started out as a nice little digging game with plenty of promise and has since become confused and shallow.

It is a digging game, yet as you progress in the game your success is defined by not digging. You get "better" by automating the digging and putting ore into crucibles to liquefy them, but it lacks any automation for making bars or any of the crafted materials. Thus you end up with a game whose end-goal is to... not play the game? Or perhaps to shift your set of chores from one to another.

That would be alright if not for the fact that development has been focused on things like player housing, character bodies, or even (Woah!) a single new kind of gem. There's only a small handful of resource types, digging is either tedious or automated with no sense of reward or accomplishment, and development of the game is going in literally any other direction (at the time of writing our big cliffhanger is farming).
Fun fact: I was also banned from the steam forums with a message of "touch grass" for bringing this up in a forum thread asking other players what they thought of the games' direction. So let's keep the negatives to reviews, lest the dev simply ban everyone he disagrees with.

I first saw this game on Lets Game It Out. I thought it would be fun to try, and it was, but let me give you a few tips.

You will crash your pickup truck about 10 times on the way to the next town over. You will spend an hour painstaikingly digging a hole and gathering ore to make your first tiny dagger, You will get way to excited when you make your first gem. You will take a little shopping trip with your measely earnings to buy 2 conveyor belts and 25 pipes only to come home and realize you left your money in the bucket at the previous town.

And my personal favorite, you'll get too close to the bed when going to sleep and find a terrifying man with glowing eyes standing over you. That man is you, but for a brief few seconds this game is a horror game.

And then it'll be 4am and you'll have been playing for 10 hours. Its tedious, its slow paced, and sometimes aggravating. But its worth it to see your drills and grinders start producing more ore, to see the bars you smelt get bigger and bigger, to watch a previous task that took hours automate and only take moments.

If you find satisfaction in hard work, this is the game for you.

I usually don't go for this type of game because there are hundreds of resources and just as much craftable items. This one keeps it simple. 5 types of resources (if you count all emerdoods as one), that's it.What you work forward to is no more resources but more efficancy. tier 2 items allow you to mine at lower levels, but that doesn't get you diamonds or some other things, it gets you the same as before, just more of them.
I can see some ppl taking this as a negative but I liked it. Most crafting games lose me because they overcomplicate stuff,, not so here.
Which doesn't mean you can't do some creative work. I just progressed from a manual sorter stack (kinda a misnomer, not really manual if it sorts automaticly, but you got to feed it manually) to a fully automated sorting system using conveyors.
But.. the previous one showed the shortcomings. This game is very prone to performance issues. It's really sensitive to too many mineral chunks flying around. I don't really know how it works but it seems to be fine if those land in a bucket/pan, up until you pick the bucket/pan up and suddenly, you got 0.2 fps. Literally. One frame in 5 seconds. So.. if you'r e new and can't afford conveyors and use manual sorters, make sure to make plenty of trips from your harvester to the sorting and smelt them early, Don't be like me and let it run for an hour or two and then.. Spend the next hour cleaning up the issues it caused.
that's another thig and I guess it only happens when processing too many minerals at once. The sorters and containers have (seemingly few) minerals stuck. Well there is the very helpful magnet on a stick. But one millisecond of magnet and the stuck resources explode into hundreds of junks because, as I guess, there were many resources holding the same space but the magnet demanded they act individually so collission detection kicked in.
TL;DR, either melt down your resources early or invest in automated conveyor belt to smelter systems, which'll cost yoiu probably around 20k.

While it is a far from perfect this game is really fun.

Hydroneer is a factory design game centered around mining.

Start with a pan and a brush, and slowly expand to massive machinery.  As the name suggests, the machinery is all powered by pipes with water pressure.  

The game allows you to build massive cavern and pit mines using a voxel-based terrain system.

The game is not without it's bugs, and you will find yourself hitting the interface buttons to clear loose raw resources from the world if they end up spilling everywhere.  

It works great on my Linux desktop under proton and reportedly works reasonably well in Steam Deck. 

Who will like this game: People who like building big complex machines and sandbox gameplay.
Who won't: People who can't stand bugs in their games, people who can't play games that don't have clear goals, and people who think all games should be like Halo.

Comecei a acompanhar a produção deste jogo nos meados de 2020 e fiquei bastante interessado pelo Hydroneer. Fiquei extremamente decepcionado quando vi que o jogo não tinha COOP e fiquei xingando a humanidade por algumas horas, porém decidi comprar o jogo mesmo sendo uma pessoa que não costuma jogar jogos offline. Jogos por algumas boas horas e cheguei a um ponto que cansei de jogar sozinho e parei a minha jogatina, porém continuei acompanhando o produtor principal da Foulball Hangover.  Alguns meses atrás vi que estariam atualizando o jogo e colocando um modo multiplayer e assim que foi lançado voltei a jogar, só que desta vez com amigos. Vamos para a análise...

Hydroneer é bem diferente de qualquer outro jogo que já vi. É extremamente divertido para jogar, principalmente com amigos. Ainda há vários bugs e glitchs, sendo que alguns deles podem causar perda de itens e outras coisas, porém a equipe desenvolvedora é pequena tenta remover todos os bugs de acordo com os feedbacks da comunidade. O jogo conta com várias atualizações e agora com mods, que melhoram significativamente a gameplay. A mecânica do jogo é bem peculiar, mas não é tão ruim. Os gráficos são bons, porém é meio mal otimizado e a coisa que você mais vai necessitar é de memória RAM. Em geral é um jogo bem interessante que ainda pode progredir muito. Pelo preço, você terá um ótimo custo benefício e várias horas de diversão.

Hydroneer has similar gameplay to Factorio or Satisfactory.  Plan out a system, implement it and then fix any problems that happen after you turn it on.  Fun game overall if you enjoy that sort of thing.

The game is a bit slow at the start but picks up speed pretty quick once you're able to get your hands on some mining machines and the stuff to go with them.  The game's very minimal UI (you get tooltips when you grab something and that's about it) takes a bit to learn, but works well enough.  

Hydroneer is definitely not finished yet though.  The game has two main issues right now: lack of late game goals and managing large number of items.  

It appears that the developers are working on adding more materials and more things to do with them but, for the moment there aren't a ton things to do with what you dig up.  You can use two materials to make mining machines, and the other two are for making money.  You also get the same materials regardless of how deep your mine is (depth just increases how much ore you get).  I hope that deeper mines will eventually award rare materials that can be used to make cool stuff.  The game needs some sort of goal or project to push you to expand and optimize your setup because after 50 hours I am now capable of making more money than I will ever be able to spend.

The other problem stems from the developers choosing not to give the game a traditional inventory system.  This makes moving things around messy.  There are containers you can use, but putting too many items into those containers tanks the game's FPS and cause a variety physics glitches.  This issue is easy enough to avoid once you're aware of it but, it makes transporting a large amount of equipment anywhere take more trips than it should.  The game does have a creative mode that alleviates this issue somewhat since one of the items you can borrow from that mode (creative mode can be toggled on or off in Hydroneer) is a wand that duplicates items, allowing you to avoid having to transport large amounts of pipes or any other cheap items that you need a ton of.

I hope the developers can fix how the game handles large numbers of items though.  I'd rather not have to worry about my truck or pallets launching themselves into orbit because I stacked too much stuff on them.

If you do choose to buy this game I would recommend checking out Hydroneer's steam workshop.  There are a variety of mods that make the game more enjoyable to play.

Very poor and frustrating gameplay experience. Requested a refund, don't bother.

Recommended, but only just. For a game announcing its "2.0 release" it really feels like an early beta; there just isn't a whole lot to do, and there are bugs aplenty. Once you finish your first fully automated build, you've basically experienced everything the game has to offer, the progression just stops. There's basically 3 stages: mining and smelting by hand, mining using drills and combination smelters, and mining using logic-based automated drills and using logic-based smelters. That's pretty much it, and you fly through them before you even need to move to a bigger plot than the one you start off with. After that, you just earn insane amounts of money, but there's nothing to really spend it on, as you cannot buy any drills or refiners, all the hand tools have infinite uses, and only one piece (the filter) ever breaks down on the machines. Sure, you can build a house/base, but if that's your thing, there are plenty of games that do it way better (dragon quest builders and minecraft for example). 

HOWEVER

For what is there, you'll get $10 (or less) worth of entertainment out of it, and I really like the concept of digging (mostly) fully destructible terrain and selling whatever you can pan out of the clumps you mine. It's a pretty unique concept that I haven't really seen elsewhere, I just wish there was more to do/buy. For what it's worth, $10 is an appropriate price, and it's a relaxing experience, but the monotony and lack of meaningful progression is a definite drawback. The good news is that the devs seem to be pretty invested in making more content and listening to community feedback about what to add next, so, very much like an early-access beta, there is potential for the game to grow beyond its rather slim current state.

Seeing gold bar getting heavier and heavier with every hard-earned nugget merged into it is enjoyable. Bit less when I realise there isnt much more. 

You start a game with basics - shovel, bucket, pan and a broom. Fill the bucket with shovel, drop its contents into the pan, fill it with water and use broom on it - boom, you get first batch of valuables. Then sell them to buy some equipment - gem polisher to turn rocks into gems, and furnace with crucible to smelt ores into bars. When you collect enough coins, you can get water-powered machines that will make your job easier - auto digger, machine that breaks contents out of dirt clumps, and pipes to keep machines working. Then get some sorters and conveyor belts to connect everything together with a basic automation rig to make an automatic money factory. And then... well, what then?

The moment i built my first automatic mining rig, I felt like I completed the game. Sure, i could've made it more efficient, improved pipes to make everything work better (better pipes offer better pressure, which makes things work faster). There are 5-6 dig sites I could expand to. There are house building materials for me to make my own home. 
But why do those for? To get more money to make more efficient rig, to make more money to make... bla bla bla, you get it. Building in grid-based 3D game can be a bit annoying - navigating a piece into specific cube you want it in isn't that easy - thats general problem of grid-based 3D building, not the game. I know the main goal of the game is automation, but I didn't felt like there was enough incentive to do so. 
There are few available dig sites as well. Problem is, they don't offer different minerals as far as I know - they are just deeper, and nuggets found deeper are heavier, thus more valuable. But all I have to do now to get money is wait a bit, maybe fix a machine, so... why bother? 
House building. Sure you can store your metal bars in there, play decorator and so on, but that's not something everyone enjoys. Plus, this still is building in 3D grid. 

What else... The bads:
-Physics sometimes gets creative - a few times my truck or cart went flying just because it could. At least once something got stuck. But to be fair, reloading save, or using a nifty menu that lets me get unstuck or reposition nearest vehicle to more manageable spot. Sure, had to look for it every once in a while, because placing spot is a bit arbitrary, but thats still something neat. 
- There is not inventory, and everything is an object. Need to buy a single conveyor belt? Grab a truck, because thats the only way you can do it in one trip - load your coins on the truck, drive to the shop, buy what you need and load it and coins on the truck because you can carry only one thing at the time. 
- I feel like all shops could offer everything, since everything is an object, and map is a bit big. You can buy basics near the first dig site, but to get some of the advanced stuff, you need to drive to next town, which can be a bit annoying when you need just one item.
-I feel like gemstones are too cheap - they are kinda less common that gold or iron nuggets, which those can quickly accumulate value in form of bars. 
-Tutorial is a button sending you to a short youtube video. I know it's a solution of some kind, but come on.

The good:
-Objects lose collision when placed in transport objects, be it a pan, cart or a truck. This way,  you can store all your nuggets in a single pan without them overflowing, or deliver entire kit required for your rig in one truck trip. Sadly this doesn't apply to the shops, so bigger purchases may need to be split into few transactions, as not everything may fit on the "selling spot". Still, this is an amazing solution, as it makes it less bothersome to transport stuff, and prevents physics issues of too many items close together. 
-There is fishing. Yea, i know, dont look at me like that. Maybe devs seen the meme about fishing minigames, i don't know. Fact is, you can fish using rods, or an item that when placed in water will spawn a fish in it every once in a while. Fish aren't too valuable, but thats something you can do.
-Metal bars don't seem to have any limit on how much can be merged into them. If you have large bar, and smelt it with more nuggets, you will get a heavier, more valuable bar. There is a visual size cap, but nothing stops you from having a gold bar with mass of the sun, or I just think so because it would take a while and I haven't tried that.
-With enough time and persistence, you can clean all dig sites of dirt, making it impossible to mine anymore. You can be overexploitative capitalist if you feel like it.

I had enough fun to recommend the game. If you have beefy PC, and are into automation, you may enjoy the game even more, but some more content would be nice. Maybe more types of ore could be added? Some dig site variety - one unique ore at each dig site? Achievements? I don't know. There is some fun you can get from this game, price is rather fair, quire good overall.

This is one of those times I kind of wish there was a neutral review option. I really WANT to like this game; it's charming and creative, with enough novelty in the automation/building genre to stand out, but right now there just isn't much to it. It has a very "early access" feel to it despite supposedly being fully released. 

Digging/modifying terrain takes absolutely forever, even with explosives. Placing objects is an absolute pain in the ass and nothing goes where you want it to. When you pick up a bucket full of ore to put it in a smelter, the game lags horrifically. These three things are most of the core gameplay loop, and they're just really not where they should be. There are just enough little quality of life annoyances to make the game frustrating instead of fun, but I do still keep wanting to come back to it somehow. 

This game is made by a very small team (three people total!) and should be given some leeway, but you should know what you're getting into: a really charming start to a game that REALLY needs work. I do think people should buy it and play it, and $10 is pretty fair for the amount of fun I did have. I really do hope this game improves, because it has a lot of room to grow.

Bugs, everywhere. If you are not playing the expected way in this sandbox game, you will encounter numerous game breaking bugs. Pallets do not work as expected and things get stuck in midair, placing lots of items into pans or buckets, often defy the laws of gravity and stay stuck in midair. Putting things in your truck allow for items to stack in infinite space on top of each other, but not when unloading and NOT when on a pallet.

I had to look on the internet to determine how the devs intended me to play the game to truly experience it, but at that point, its a VERY bland game without a lot of depth. I just read it has a half a million sales. Frankly speaking, the bugs and lack of gameplay content were forgivable if it was one dude in his basement, but with half a million sales, this is inexcusable.

So most of the negative reviews I've seen focus on the lack of inventory, the tedium, the lack of an endgame, and the early game minutiae. I'll not stick on those, accordingly. What "broke" the game experience was coming back after the big update or whichever one introduced the cloutium drills with a pipe inlet on a side that made them impossible to keep next to one another (yes I know how to engineer solutions to this, I'll get to that in a sec) + prevented swapping old drills for new without redesigning your entire pipe system from the ground up. 

aaaand also whatever made it so conveyors no longer automatically have pipes in them, requiring a nice doubling of the placement work/time, which is particularly noisome with diagonals only achievable with pipes using repeated hard right angles, including for verticality.

These problems wouldn't be as bad as they are if it were easier to place items/"blocks" what have you, but I have never had as hard a time doing so than I have in this game, very very literally. So unless I missed something huge, the placement system is vexing to levels that stray into disbelief territory. 

Changes such as the removal of plumbing from conveyor belts and the like just kind of pushed me into the territory of just seeing the game as a thing that invents annoying problems, just for the sake of them. Pros:
-Dieses Game ist vom Gameplay her ziemlich simpel und das ist ein Pluspunkt im vergleich zu anderen Spielen dieser Art.
-Die Möglichkeiten für Automatisierung waren/sind auch genügend vorhanden.
 (einige Features wurden wieder entfernt welches diese Möglichkeiten wieder einschränken)

- Das neue System für Förderbänder und Rohre ist sehr gut geworden, leider fehlen noch ein paar Rohrvarianten um alles zu ermöglichen und ist deshalb nur mit Mod möglich zurzeit.

Contra:
- Nach einiger Spielzeit wird das Game extrem langsam und laggy
Da ich einen sehr starken Computer besitze was die Leistung angeht sollte dies nicht passieren jedoch hatte ich im meinem angetestet von 2.0 sehr starke Probleme hiermit welches mich dazu gebracht hat das Spiel zu deinstallieren und auf Besserung zu warten.
- Die Fahrzeuge machten sich nach einiger Zeit selbstständig und haben das Spiel noch unspielbarer gemacht.
- Sehr lange Wegzeiten.
Aufgrund von der Entscheidung kein Inventar zu haben leidet dieses Spiel sehr stark darunter das Wege zum Transport 4/5 des Spiels ausmachen. Wenn mann einmal einen Stehende Produktion hat ist dieses weniger Schlimm, jedoch erst einmal alle Bauteile zu einem Ort zu bekommen und diese auf Aufzusetzen ist sehr Zeitaufwendig und Spieler-unfreundlich gestaltet. 


Pro/Contra:
- Das neue Gebiet wurde gut gestaltet ist jedoch rein von der Effektivität her das einzig lohnenswerte da sich alle nötigen Maschinen für die Herstellung weiter Maschinen hier befinden.
Da in dem neuem Gebiet auch ein Händler vorhanden ist, sind dementsprechend die anderen Gebiete nutzlos geworden.
Hierfür sollte die Möglichkeit von den anderen Gebieten bestehen diese dann auch herstellen zu können.
- Da dieses Spiel sich damit brüstet kein Inventar zu haben ist dies Geschmackssache ob Leute dieses bevorzugen oder nicht. Meiner Ansicht nach würde ein Inventar nicht schaden was den Transport von Gebäudeteilen, Maschinen etc. angeht da diese zu Transportieren echt nervend sein kann. Eine Option zum Anschalten oder Ausschalten eines solchen würde beiden seiten der Fraktionen für Inventar oder ohne helfen und glücklich machen.
Ich selbst finde es in Ordnung das für die zur Verfügung stehen Werkzeuge kein Inventar vorhanden ist, jedoch würde ich es wirklich bevorzugen nicht 200 Bauteile einzeln und mehrfach in die Hand nehmen zu müssen nur um diese aufzustellen.

Alles in Allem ist Hydroneer ein nettes Spiel für zwischendurch mit welchen man gut und gerne ein paar Stunden Zeit vertreiben kann, jedoch würde ich derzeit keinen Kauf in Rate ziehen da durch bestimmte Fehler das Spiel nach kurzer Zeit einen Neustart erfordert um wieder flüssig Spielbar zu sein. Weiterhin ist schade das dass Bauen so viel Zeit in Anspruch nehmen muss dadurch das einiges in Version 2.0 geändert wurde und hierdurch Zeiten für das Aufsetzen in die länge gezogen werden.

Falls die Fehler behoben werden sollten könnte ich einen Kauf Empfehlen. Allerdings werde ich selbst warten bis entweder ein Inventar als Mod erscheint oder die Entwickler ein Feature hinzufügen welches das Bauen von "Fabriken" nicht eine Qual macht. (Der Transport von Bauteilen von A nach B und das Händeln dieser Gegenstände nimmt ca. 3-4 mal so viel Zeit ein wie das Aufsetzen der Anlage selbst)

The game world is small but lush and well populated with trees, structures, bridges and streams.  You are the only character, instead interacting with tables, pallets, and buckets.  The shops are just organized enough to look haphazardly stocked by grumbling, mining town shopkeeps.  The ambient audio gives you the right feeling of 'outdoorsy.'  The core gameplay loop is fun and relatively simple to pick up and play.  You're manually digging and prospecting just long enough before moving into automated mining, and it's rewarding to see that automated system, and your resources, grow.

There's definitely some issues to work out - the heavy use of physics assets causes a lot of collision problems with vehicles which can often be unavoidable.  The game loads fast enough on an SSD that saving to menu and loading your game is a fairly quick fix to the problems.  

Moving from Tier 1 Iron mining equipment to Tier 2 introduces some complexity in your automation, but there isn't much incentive to do so.  By the point you can readily start investing in Tier 2 miners (which require 300 weight Cloutium bars), you've had to build up Tier 1 to the point you're making hundreds of thousands of coins before you can build up enough Cloutium for one miner.  That really hurts the pacing.

I wish there were other characters, even if they only stood at their respective shops selling things.  It would help the world to feel lived in.

Lastly, there's not much after that.  There's some fun to be had in building and filling in a home for yourself on one of the many plots, or working towards near complete automation using the logic circuits available (I only built up auto-repair).  I started to build out my home while waiting for Cloutium (I needed 8 miners), but burned out.

I built out automated mining, spent hours digging around in Icehelm (though didn't find anything interesting), and had fun playing with the physics.  50+ hours was a good investment to me.

I enjoy this game, and it's a game type I never thought I would, but Version 2.0 seems like it's pushed the game backwards more than forwards.

Pros:
-If you want an automation sandbox game, this can get surprisingly addictive. You can wonder why people like this game, as you sit hours and hours into a play session designing a build. If you like building huge frame rate destroying production factories, you'll like this game
-The new machine crafting is pretty good, although it makes it easy to create a huge setup very quickly
-Multiple dig sites so you can try different bases out
-So many more material types to make buildings out of (can't help it, I like constructing proper buildings to house my setups)
-It's a cheap game, for something you can easily lose a lot of time on (as I look at my game time)

Cons:
-The trucks are terrible to drive. And 2.0 seems to have made them worse, and I didn't think that was possible
-The placing system seems to have gotten more janky. It can take way too long to find the right angle to place a single item because the placing system is putting it everywhere but the spot you want
-Filters are now clip on items, so the auto repair system from version 1 isn't possible any more. If it can work still, then I really don't know what I'm doing wrong
-The crafting system now means there is less need for money, and means you have less to work towards. The only things to buy you get most of early on (splitters, gem compressor and smelters), then all you need money for is new land, pipes and conveyors, which are a pittance compared to the money you can rack up in a short space of time. But this also leads to...
-THE POWER SYSTEM IS GONE. I'm hoping the developers bring it back, everything was hugely expensive and made it all so satisfying to earn the money to afford it and set it up. It also means the removal of powered boosters and powered filters (which were useful for the auto repair system). Without all of this system, again, the sheer lack of things to spend your money on really hits home

(I can't comment on fishing as I don't really bother with it!)

At the end of the day, the game is cheap, it can provide hours of automated entertainment, but I really hope the developers balance the money stuff again, give us something more to buy so we can use the ridiculous money we can earn *cough*bringbackpower*cough*

This is a prime example of great idea, bad implementation. The controls in this game are so clunky and weird that you will constantly find yourself picking up random objects, dropping things you didn't want to drop and finding weird clipping/non-clipping issues which any first year game programmer would be able to solve.
Don't get me wrong, it's a good concept. The gameplay itself when you aren't frustrated beyond belief by the controls or trying to place something or drop something, is great! However I find myself constantly being frustrated to the point of tears by the bad implementation of game mechanics.
Also, when you pick something up, it's at cursor, no surprise there... But, to drop something, you literally drop it for 2 feet in the air straight down, you can't place objects in or onto anything without it falling down in a line. I wish that were the worst part, but it's not. The cursor for dropping objects is off centre and sometimes you can't even see where it is going to land before you drop it.
Next thing, it encourages you to build underground to get better resources... This would be fine if you didn't have to dig down under the ground further than you need to then place your equipment, then fill in the dirt under your mining machine. That's right, you heard me, "fill in the dirt under your mining machine". You can place objects anywhere you like, as long as there's nothing sticking into it, no clipping for convenience in this game. so you'll constantly find that you've dug a little too far, or not enough dirt and have to spend the next 10 mins to try and get the object placed. There is an in-game object that lets you flatten terrain though, just doesn't really help that much when your things are at different levels.
So if you want a game where you manually have to do the most menial tasks, and be frustrated by the controls the entire time, this is the game for you!
For me though not-so-much.

For a game that rewards working at depth it is a remarkably shallow experience. (I am sorry. I had to) My first few hours with this game I was sold. Its a cute game about mining and automating your way out of a somewhat tedious process until money is just rolling in. But honestly I am not sure it is right to call it a game. It is a sand box. I was excited as I transitioned from a bucket and broom to machinery and from hand sorting and smelting to automating, and I was excited to see how much deeper it goes. I put together a pretty basic setup with a single belt fed by a couple drills dropping into the harvester, a gem polisher, and the 7 splitters to drop each resource into a pale or auto-smelter. It worked great. time to set up auto crafting or something. Except that doesnt exist.  I quickly found out that my super basic first build is about as good as it gets. I can drop more drills in line, increase water pressure, and optimize distance between drill and source, but thats it. I had basically exhausted the progression in mining. Fine I have tons of money now lets go spend it! There has to be some awesome stuff to get with these hundreds of thousands of coins right? I can get a shiny chair and build a house that has no purpose. Seriously. I hit the end of this game before I finished my first build on my first mine. I opened up another mine and went through the process of loading my car with just enough stuff that it wouldn't take off into the atmosphere and spent hours digging out a nice cave and set up the same exact rig for higher numbers that I dont need on resources that have no use. No new resources, no new crafting, no meaningful purchases and no point to any of it. You might say the point is to optimize and find the best way to set everything up except that the best way is essentially the only way. If your rig works, its about as good as it gets. Hydroneer has a lot going for it, but it lacks purpose and direction, depth and reward. Oh and a ton of optimization and bug fixing. My played hours are vastly inflated by my save randomly corrupting, i lost a truck into the sky, crashes aren't uncommon, and lag is a real problem even at a pretty small scale. It can get there, but this is a top tier demo right now, or a shallow sand box, not a game ready for release.

Trying to empty a pan into a smelter that already has something in it, and you better have the cursor off the smelter because emptying the pan and emptying the smelter use the same button so the smelter pours a small bar and the pan of ore goes everywhere and has to be picked up one at a time.  

The no inventory concept was interesting, but ultimately made a giant pain.  I ended up with random pieces of equipment scattered all over the place because I didn't know what all I'd need, and I'd forget where I put stuff and what I had so a lot of duplicate purchases were made.  And if you try to load too much into your vehicle, watch out, because it might fly away - not sure how the physics works for that, but it does - luckily more vehicles cost almost nothing (once you have automated mining up and running), but then again, there isn't anything you can buy that costs much.

Hydroneer is a pretty builder, but very simple.  

At its most sophisticated, you get access to conveyor belts that can sort and machines that can dig and process the ore for you.  The only point in mining is to turn the ore into ingots and craft the ingots into weapons or jewelry and sell it.  You can fish and sell your fish.  Aaand... that's pretty much it.  Hydroneer is a very simple game; Satisfactory it ain't.  I wouldn't have recommended this game at a higher price than the $10 they're asking.

On the other hand, maybe you like simplicity.  Hydroneer is all about that.  Your character doesn't even have an inventory.  Everything has to be moved by hand, one at a time.  When you stop using a tool, you have to put it down somewhere.  Even your coins need to be moved around and plopped in the world to use them.  You don't craft any of the equipment you use.  Instead, you need to buy everything from shops, load it onto a wagon or your truck, and haul it where it needs to go.  This interface is so simple that it's novel in its simplicity.

A shame Hydroneer doesn't have a VR version.  This inventory-less approach would work well, and motion controls would help with the awkwardness of placement.

When this game was first released I very nearly bought it, but after watching videos showing a lack of content and glitches I held off. I bought this shortly after version 2.0 released and I wished I'd held off even longer.

This game is intentionally grindy. I think you've gathered that already from reviews and videos, and I knew this going in. But with mods such as the crate mod make it more bearable for moving dozens of items at once.

Ignoring Let's Game It Out's excellent videos that've brought hundreds to the game, Hydroneer has amazing polish and fully embraces that classic low-oly indie fantasy game aesthetic. Everywhere the game feels unpolished is counter-balanced with excellent attention to detail and thought put into features that one WOULD expect a developer to focus on in an effort to put their best foot forward. 

Once you get in the groove of playing with the game's main conceit (you don't have an inventory and thus have to manually carry every single item) you get into a flow state of setting up and automating your first mine. 

My main problem arises from the fact there's... not much to do quite quickly in. I've got 15 hours played and had an absolute blast, but I haven't even touched the game's automation circuitry tech and there's not really any emphasis for me to do so. I have two T1 miners hooked up to one T1 harvester and a conveyor sorting system. I basically have infinite money and there's zero monetary or plot reason for me to leave the first digging area. 

I mine, I make thousands of gold worth of product, I go to Bridgepour to buy everything expensive. I realize building a house out of the fancy furniture and individual items would be a pain. I return to my starter mine with thousands of gold and no real reason to upgrade to T2 mining equipment. 

Hydroneer is well worth your time and money, but there is no victorious summit to the mountain. You climb, you have fun, and then you realize you've been walking on a flat plateau for hours and no new challenge or puzzle has come along. Every save file not created by a streamer or YouTuber seeking to make content will end in the player staring around, full of ennui for the fact Hydroneer FEELS like it's a game that'll have hundreds of hours of content with tons of depth yet... here you are. Rich as a king with gear you can buy within two hours of play and nothing to spend it on.

I love me some automation games. They give me an immense amount of satisfaction. But this game doesn't seem to be sure if it's an automation game, or a wannabe VR simulation of blacksmithing from getting your own materials to smelting stuff.

To wit, this game perpetuates the ultimate sin in gaming: trying to do everything with as little UI as possible. I see it in game after game where design or art or whoever wants to have a beautiful game with no or little UI and the UX suffers immensely from it. And the developers are on record for that as well!

Everything in this game is interactable down to the individual nuggets. Which means you are hand carrying things everywhere before you get automation. Gold nugget to your bin, then hand carrying the bin of nuggets to the jeweler, then hand carrying the money in the bin to the store to buy more tools/automation stuff. Placing anything down is an exercise in frustration as you attempt to get it to land upright (assuming you can drop it at all). Heck, even picking up water is a chore.

If you want to create something on the anvil, you're manually moving the nugget into the crucible, which you manually move the crucible onto the forge. Then you pour the molten metal out into a mold (but don't miss the mold or you've wasted your effort!), then you grab those bars, and you have to heat them up, place them individually on the anvil, then make your thing. This might be cool with better controls or as a VR blacksmith simulator, but not really what I wanted

So aside from the absolute tedium of it all, none of this is explained in-game. Controls are awkward (though bonus points for *partially* supporting a controller), with no overlays or help on what controls *do* in-game at all. You're expected to go to view an external video tutorial that barely tells you anything. 90 minutes in I barely had anything done because I spent so much time struggling with controls and trying to divine what precisely these interactable elements wanted me to do.

Based on descriptions, if this tedium didn't exist, you'd experience everything the game has to offer in very little time. Add to that no NPCs in the world, all shops are weirdly automated based around this control scheme/no UI paradigm, and the game feels extremely empty. Who lives in that castle? Who's running the shops? *whispers* Nobody.

The game doesn't feel like a released game. And while it's quite cheap, it's not for me.

Well, I have to update my review. The game is still based on annoying things like not having a purse, not being able to carry more than one thing at a time (including money!!!), and for some reason not being able to put something down in front of you...

but if you accept that the game is like playing someone with only one arm and no pockets, it is quite addictive. The machines, when they work, are fun to build and to watch work.

I would like this game a lot more if they fixed the problems I listed above (the developer thinks they are features, so it won't happen), but then the fact that there isn't much content would be obvious.

Play this if you like grindy automation games.

OLD REVIEW:

More like 0.2 than 2.0. There is very little content in the game. If this was way pre-release, I would be excited about the possibilities.

The first two hours will be awful, as you learn to deal with the awkward, inventoryless game system, where you can only carry one item at a time for no obvious reason (you can develop automatic mining technology, but not...a purse????) and the fact that you can't put something down in the same place you picked it up (I learned to do this when I was 2 years old in real life).

Then the game is pretty fun for about 10 hours, as you build your first automatic mining, sorting and smelting machine.

Then you realize that there is no more content, and all you can do is repeat the same thing on a larger scale.

I bought it on sale for a low price, so I'm not too upset, but this is a very pre-release game that is unlikely to get finished enough to make up for the dishonest description.

0.2 hours. Maybe I haven't played enough of this game to be writing this. But maybe the developer should make something about this game crystal clear on the store page before you buy: This is a crafting and building game that has no inventory system. None. At all. No tool bar, no backpack, not even a wallet. You have to hold anything you wanna hold in your right hand in front of you. You don't even get a second hand to hold a second item. I didn't learn about this until I watched the game's official tutorial youtube video after the purchase was made. The guy in the video tries to make the whole lack of an inventory system sound like a feature, like it's some kind of new and revolutionary idea that will add actual value to the game. I don't know. Maybe if you're patient enough, you'll think that only being able to hold a single item in front of you sounds like fun. Here's what my entire 12 minutes of gameplay sounded like: Start the game. Watch the tutorial video, ok cool it's only 3 minutes and some change. Start game. Press E to pick up shovel. Click to dig. Take shovel full of dirt over to pan. Dump the shovel full of dirt on ground next to pan, dang it. Ball of dirt on ground now seems impossible to shovel or pick up. Whatever. Grab another shovel full of dirt. No, not there, you gotta walk a little farther. Ok. Come back, get the dirt in the pan. Ok. Press E to drop shovel. Press E to grab bucket. Look at water and click to fill up the bucket. Nice try, moron, but you're not staying dry through this. You got two choices, idiot. Jump in the river with the bucket, or throw the bucket in the river and go in after it. You're gonna get some practice with this since you're gonna dump the first two buckets on the ground next to the pan. But eventually you'll get it. Cool, E to drop the bucket again, and E to pick up the famous iconic tool of every gold miner: The brush. Wave your brush magically over the pan to change water and dirt into a single chunk of gold. Or maybe iron. Press E to drop your brush, then press E to pick up your gold nugget and stick it in your pocket. Just kidding! You don't have any pockets! You're probably not even wearing pants! So you think fast and throw your gold nugget into your cart. You go and sell your gold nugget, and the money is given to you in a stack of coins. At which point I exited the game and came back to reality where I was able to refund 10 bucks back into my inventory.

Normally I'd give an early access the benefit of the doubt, but we're two years down the road and the "big update" that just came out has seemingly changed little to nothing.

As a developer, you can add millions of new items if you want, but if nothing is changing or improving the core game play loop, then I don't know that it's genuinely an "update". As far as I've seen, they've just added ancillary content, some decorative, some methodical in the way you extract resources - but therein lies the main issue: the resources. Maybe I'm expecting something that isn't planned, but when a game about mining and crafting is released into early access, I'd expect that, within two years, there'd be some additions or changes to the resources you could acquire. I would argue that in a game like this, which does not have the deeper functionalities of genre adjacent games, such as Satisfactory, that most of the joy would come from collecting and refining a wide variety of resources.  However, here we are with the same iron, gold and gems as craftable and marketable materials. The other two resources, Cloutium (sp?) and crystal shards, are purely for functionality of more equipment to mine iron, gold and gems (and not even a wide variety of gems).

It's a very tight, repetitive loop - which I am not opposed to, IF there is enough variety within to keep it fresh or to add some degree of excitement or anticipation as to what you might pull out of the dirt.

I wish the best for the developers, and look forward to what they'll be doing with Hydroneer, but until there is some nuance or variety to the core game play, I cannot recommend it. This review can, and will, easily change to a thumbs up when/if this happens.

I like a ton of stuff about this game, unfortunately I can't recommend it unless you're part of a very niche community that wants a game that is purely self-led with the only motivation to keep going is to be more efficient 

I had a ton of fun in the starter area figuring out the game, but once I nailed automation of the mining and cleaning process (all I had to do was dump my single pan into two different sorters to filter out the iron and gold) and was able to produce mountains of money every 10 minutes, I lost all motivation to continue, the only things I could do with my money was purchase things that would allow me to make even more money if I wanted to completely rebuild my setup, and with the honestly miserable inventory system I couldn't bring myself to ever want to change my setup

I would really love a business side of the game to really give me a long term goal, something I could invest in and make me feel like the materials I'm gathering are actually going towards something, right now all I do is trade it to the jeweler and watch it disappear 

I also think the "inventory"/handling items mechanic is more than miserable, it's almost unacceptable how bad it is and prevents me from having fun. There really needs to be a "place" option, so I don't have to drop a bucket 300 times until luck is on my side and it lands right side up.. it would also be fantastic to be able to press a button and pour ores into a crucible without the terrible aiming minigame, where sometimes half the ores go spilling out all over the floor simply because the crosshair disappears in the shadows and art of the game.. when you're dealing with hundreds of ores at a time this is like a 20-30 minute oopsie that shouldn't even exist 

I understand the reason why they ceased development of online multiplayer (the only way I would be able to get friends to buy this game, this is an insanely quiet and dull game without multiplayer or NPC interaction of any kind)...but this really is one of the most lonely games I've ever played, I feel like this could still be an early access game

This game has a ton of potential... but currently, I wouldn't recommend it.  The premise and concept are great, and I wish I could say it was a great game, but the second you start to figure it all out... it's over.

That's when you realize, this game has no goal(currently).  You start out manually doing stuff.  Instinct tells you to automate it.  You probably need to move to newer more expensive areas right?  So you do that... but why?

There's no quest.  No score.  No goal.  It's simply a question of how high do you want to see your cash go for the sake of seeing it higher, and buying things via cash becomes meaningless very early on.  At most you can try to buy Tier 2 equipment, which requires a rare resource, but the benefit isn't there yet and again... to what end.

This game has amazing potential, but it's just not worth it yet.  I'm hoping in a few updates that will change.   It needs direction and re balancing badly.

Edit:  I stand by most of what I said when I first reviewed this.  I've since bought the DLC.  The DLC is by far the better version of the game.  The new map makes it more interesting to set things up.  I'm a big fan of not having to do the farming, wan't a huge fan of that mechanic in the base one.

However, even this new version still has the same problem as the original.  You finally thing you're getting things set up. You unlocked Tier 3... and then what?  The game basically loses all purpose and goes out with a whimper.

Sure, there's a trophy you can buy for T9999999 or something, but getting tokens is more about being willing to put up with the tedious "fetch" type quests this game relies on.  Driving all over the map to find out where the quest spawned this time, going back, Punching in weights on a key pad and crafting.

There's no reward for a better mine or a bigger one, the constraining resource is your willing ness to drive around and get those quests, then come back and manually craft. 

I wish there was more of an end game focused on getting a bigger mine or a more efficient one.  Something that focused on the mining side vs just driving across the map.

It has potential to be a really fun game.  Unfortunately there are several problems that make it tough to recommend.  One of the biggest issues is only being able to carry one item at a time.  Yes you can put many items in the truck, but hearing that "huh?" when something is in the way will drive you mad.  The physics are wonky.  Some people like that, but things flying off or just disappearing it unacceptable.  It's really bad early in the game if something you've grinded to afford gets flung off into oblivion.  

Don't put too many resources in a bucket if you like frame rate.  It's unplayable if there are too many, often times I only get 1 fps after picking up a bucket full of resources.  Trying to move around with a bucket like this is just brutal.  Also, when doing something with those resources, like pouring them into a furnace, causes the sound to amplify.  It can almost be deafening, and needs to be fixed asap.

It does have a "cheat" system, which makes the game more bearable, and in my opinion, does "cheating" correctly.  It gives you the ability to make it as easy or as hard as you want.  You can use the cheats via the magic wand to duplicate things as you see fit.  You can enable this and still play the game as intended without ruining anything.

Ultimately, without fixing the frame rate problem, and not having an inventory system, I can't suggest this game.

I wish there was a "meh" review option. The game is simple and fun. I love anything that's about automation and creating complex systems. But it has two major flaws for me personally:

1. There is no inventory. Every single thing you place must be carried to the location one at a time. This can be mitigated with carts and the truck, to carry multiple things closer to the build site, but even those have limits before they start lagging the game. I just do not have the patience to play until the endgame with all that tedium.

2. Endgame? I'm no stranger to games without any real goal. I've probably played 10,000 hours of minecraft. But this game really has nothing to do. You set up a system to automate mining, which gets you a ton of money which you spend to make a better system and then....nothing. You can build a house, I guess, but for what? A bed, a chair, and a safe? And a huge house plus furnishings will cost you .000001% of the coin you have by the endgame.

I think these problems are solvable. Dev wouldn't even need to add an inventory. Just add something like a "package" into the game. You put one item on a palette and it becomes a package of that item. Now any more of that item dropped onto the palette will disappear, and just add 1 to the count on that package. You could add hundreds of that one item without affecting the framerate at all.

As for the endgame...I don't know. The game probably needs some kind of goal; a story, a mystery, a problem to solve, something that must be kept at bay with money? IDK. As it is, the only reason to keep playing is just to see numbers go up.

 It can also be very annoying if you say want to switch tools, for instance you want to switch from shovel to pickaxe. But your shovel doesn't want to drop, because it often thinks it'll be clipped into the ground. Some items clip into others no problem, other give a big fuss.

Shopping sometimes just ain't fun, because you know big items in bulk will make your truck unstable/cart/pallet. And just not having an inventory.

2. It has a day/night cycle but it only adds inconvenience. As night just means you can't see anything. If you jump in a bed it becomes day, but its a darkish morning so thats annoying. And it goes from night to day fairly quickly. In old builds I carried around a a bed in my truck to take out any time like in town to sleep on, but you can't place stuff in towns anymore so that don't work. You don't have needs, you don't eat, drink, no enemies come out at night, night just exists to annoy you. It might as well be that a bed switches night/day permanently or a setting option to set day length so I can make it like 12 irl hours long or something.

3. Almost all your time is going to be spent crafting the same two objects. A gold necklace, and a long sword. The game had a craft system in the past where you could craft many useful things such as your own pipes and repair kits, but its removed now. Whats replaced it is a very grindy system you have to use to craft drills/harvesters (As you can no longer buy them anymore).

4. A lot of stuff from old versions is gone. Such as the harvester truck. And some of the new replacements are just worse, like the hand sorter which jams all the time.

5. Sometimes you just lose stuff. Like your tools do clip through the ground. Or you place something quickly and it's placed under bedrock, or place deep inside dirt you don't know where.

6. Theres minor frustrations. For instance one of the best items in the game, the magnet rod/staff which you use to pick up ores will also attract repair kits. Which is just annoying. Its also annoying how if you trying to use it to pick up ores to place into a pan, it'll pick up the ores already in the pan, and if you try to put them back in and its a big group, it won't work. Like if I want to empty the pan, I'll pick the pan up and turn it over.

You can lock a lot of things in place, but some things you may want to lock you can't, such as pans, crucibles. For instance if I locked a pan, maybe then it would indicate I want my staff to pick stuff up from the pan, or not.

You can only see the map if your carrying the map item. If you don't know the map, this can be really annoying. It don't take long to learn the map by heart. So its like....it adds a tiny bit of charm at the start, but then its pointless after that.

As far as I know you cannot scrap trucks, I've tried and couldn't. I got no use for the starter truck once I got the better trucks. So it just sits inside the scrap yard, sometimes getting in my way.

Things are spread out pretty needlessly. Like the jeweler, stockmarket, and a shop could all be at one place, which would be very convenient. but they usually aren't. Like I rarely go to the stock market due to how out of the way it usually is and how it'll only buy select items each day. And on top of it, while it can buy them slightly higher than base value, it can also buy under. Or I could stay home instead of go out each day and make extra money that way.

7. The game is very unhappy if you leave it alone for a while. The pan can fill up with so much ore than picking the pan up can reduce fps to near zero. Filters will break (which means your whole setup will stop running). Hand sorters will overflow and cause everything to get mixed up

8. The dev spends a lot of time making sure people can't steal from the shops, but at this point does it really matter? Money is easy to get. And what you really want, stuff like golith drills aren't in shops anymore. Its mainly a single player game that you can invite a friend to remote play with you. Why people that want to steal don't activate creative mode idk. I miss stuff like placing blocks anywhere such as my bed in normal mode. Its not a massively multiplayer game, its a single player game you sometimes play with your buds.


Do I think hydroneer is worth buying to try it out? Yes, its only ten bucks. Do I think it's a game worth spending hundreds of hours in automating things like factorio, modded minecraft, etc? Nah, it needs an inventory system incredibly badly, more than two tiers of items, to fix the sorter, fix its lag/fps issues, get a better progression system (Or drop it entirely and be a chill sandbox again)

Do I think it could be a great game? Yeah I do, but I doubt it'll ever happen while it has no inventory system. Because its just not fun to spend irl days unload/loading a truck. Then finishing that area and going "Now to do that all over again". The closest thing to a compromise we got was at dig site crafting, but thats gone now.

I think its recent updates have on the whole made it a lot worse of a game. Like I don't mean adding remote play. I mean most everything else and the great removing of a lot of old stuff. There is some good like the hook system is great, new dig sites is great, the new conveyers are a huge mixed bag, yes they gives you more pipe freedom (I love the gem cut hook for conveyers), but they are also a much bigger pain to work with in reguards to placing, specially up conveyers...but most everything else... Just seems like a worse game than it used to be.

And I'm again where I feel I'd rather restart than keep dealing with the hand sorter/lack of inventory/awful clout rates where I owned everything I needed or wanted from the shop gold wise, but still didn't have 200 of the 300 clout weight for just the golith drill.

I'm very sad to say that I can not give a positive review of this game as of yet.  I am still playing around with the game, but am fast becoming bored.

First the pros.  The concept is great and I love the feel of the game.  The automation of drills, belts, sorters, etc. is really interesting and a great mechanic.  The world is interesting and gives a slightly steam punk meets WoW feel.  The building is fun and interesting.  All in all, it is a very beautiful game.

Now for the cons.  There is a bug that I find annoying where if you leave your equipment running, your mined resources tend to hover over the bucket they should be going into, creating a mess.  I've notice that as long as I stay near the equipment, this doesn't happen.  There are some other small bugs, but none others that really bother me.  

The main reason I'm giving this a negative review is that there feels to be a lack of purpose to the game.  I can get the same resources from mining at the top level as I do at the bottom, just at a slower rate.  There's only 5 types of resources which are only used to craft items to sell or build new equipment and to speed up your equipment.  The game just feels monotonous with very little reward.  I am also wondering what the point is to have different mining locations that pretty much act the same way as the starting area.

From what I've heard, multiplayer is through steam link.  I won't even attempt to try this in multiplayer using that garbage system.

I truly hope that there will be more added to the game as it has a lot of potential, but i'm not holding my breath.  The latest big update was two years after the game was released and only included bug fixes, new locations, and some new pieces of equipment just to make mining faster.  This game desperately needs a direction for players and a reason to go to new locations and to upgrade equipment.

With calming music, fun SFX, and easy gameplay- this is going in the same relaxing category as simulators like Farming Sim and Lawn Mowing sim. Full review at bottom.

❤ Audience ❤
This game has no difficult elements, so it is perfect for beginning audiences. This is something I could see my mom learning to game with like how she plays House Flipper. This game is super fun and very easygoing for a relaxed experience.

-- PC Requirements --
This game has not been heavy on resources for the most part. The only time I have had frame loss is when I am working with a LOT of resources at once. Bucket been filling up with gold for the last half hour? Be ready for your frame rate to drop because you're carrying over 50 entities. It's easy to recover though, as there are options to delete all raw resources, or you can simply power through and get the resources to a smeltery. That should clear up your frames just fine.

☼ Graphics ☼
I personally love Unreal Engine graphics. I love the cutesy cartoon style that comes with the engine. The developer worked really hard to create a simple but beautiful game. The town Bridge Pour shows some of their more creative elements in design. The buildings are adorable and fun to visit, and everything is cute to look at and fun to work with.

♬ Music ♬
The music in this game is really simple, but don't let that fool you. This music is something I love to compare to the skyrim open world ost. The trumpets are very similar, and they give me the same serotonin boost of nostalgia and relaxation. I never get tired of hearing it, so the loop is long enough that you won't get annoyed or grow tired of it.

☠ Difficulty ☠
Literally the easiest game I have ever played. That's part of why I find it so calming to play. With no PvP or PvE elements, it's just you and your shovel, you're free to do whatever you want in the game. You can explore different claims, or stay in Ember Cradle the entire game. You're free. It's incredibly calming, and I can get lost in this game for several hours at a time.

§ Bugs §
Most of these aren't really bugs, but the game can be kind of clunky. Sometimes if you set your items down on the ground (like raw shards or gold), the game will actually place them *below* the surface of the dirt. You then have to dig with a pickaxe or use a magnet to get the resources back. You can also lose equipment if you aren't careful placing it, as you CAN place it underground. I have misplaced a couple anvils this way, and had to buy a new one because I didn't want to destroy my lot looking for it. 

☯ Story ☯
I have not discovered any story in the game so far. There ARE relics that you can find and place in this cave, but I have no idea what it does, so I cannot speak to the story at the time of this review.

⚔ Gameplay ⚔
Gameplay is super fun and relaxing, which I have already said a million times throughout the review. To beat a dead horse, I would say the gameplay is some of the easiest I have ever encountered, and the game is definitely worth trying. I highly recommend this game for people who are new to the gaming scene and want something peaceful to play without interruptions.

۞ Game time / Length ۞
This game you can point countless hours into per session. It's not something like hearts of iron 4 where you can dump thousands of hours, but it definitely has the capability to reach dozens of hours of play without completing the story. I am currently only at 10 hours in 2-3 days, and know there is a place I can go to build better machines and discover more equipment, but I am nowhere close to using the place yet. I imagine I will need at least another 10-15 hours of play before I am ready to go there.

$ Price / Quality $
Full price all the way. I paid 10 USD for this game, and it was worth every penny. Now I am going to finish this review and play some more Hydroneer.

Played for 23 hours in early access: most of the main instructional information currently comes from a sub-5 minute tutorial video on the main menu, and item descriptions that appear when you pick up an item; though they explain what the items are, they don't give in-depth explanations how to use them. The learning curve relies on trying out new items and seeing how they work first hand (Or you could just ask someone who's already familiar with the items).

Gameplay is very tedious: the two main tasks are managing your production system and traveling back and forth from the production system to shops that supply new and better devices than what you start with. The production systems are extremely tedious, at first you have to manually extract and refine each piece of dirt in hopes of finding ore; when you do it takes hours to get the drill and harvester, but that's not the hardest part, that's making sure that materials don't constantly fall off the production line, which happens very often. Next to the shop that sells the drill and harvester is a shop that sells cauldrons and their heating devices. If you place a raw material (except for gems) into an empty cauldron, it will only store that type of material and destroy all other materials upon contact. The materials you start with most early game are gold and iron, and a few others eventually, in order to not lose out on all those materials and organize them, you need devices called sorters to separate different materials toward different directions; this is where production get tricky: sorters have two outputs, one for items placed on it's tray and one for everything else, they each launch materials at different downward trajectories; this wouldn't be as much of an issue except for the fact that the starting plot of land has very limited depth, requiring multiple trips to another shop in order to get the vertical conveyor belts and figure out how to build an efficient conveyor belt.

Playing Hydroneer for inexperienced players costs an unnecessary amount of time planning due to gameplay features being either under-explained or undiscovered. If the developers refine the gameplay mechanics and add more depth to them, then Hydoneer could potentially be a 8/10 game in 2 years, but in early access I currently see it as a 6/10.
